solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the number of topological types of compact Kähler threefolds with c₁ = 0 is bounded; equivalently, a bound (or proof of unboundedness) on invariants such as the Euler characteristic or total Betti number of Calabi–Yau threefolds.
why: A finiteness result would give the Calabi–Yau landscape a finite topological envelope, directly informing the string-theoretic picture in which Calabi–Yau threefolds parametrize possible vacua; unboundedness would show this landscape is topologically infinite.

title: Are most cubic plane curves over the rationals elliptic
open: When cubic plane curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ are sampled by choosing ten relatively prime integer coefficients uniformly from a box $[-N,N]^{10}$ and clearing denominators, what fraction of them possess a rational point? Formally, if $E(N)$ counts the points in the box giving rise to a curve with a rational point, what is the behavior of $E(N)/(2N+1)^{10}$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$ — does the limit exist, and is it one, zero, or some other number?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 29, 4 answers); the question as stated appears open, per Poonen's answer referenced in the record. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/11349/are-most-cubic-plane-curves-over-the-rationals-elliptic
solved_when: The limit $E(N)/(2N+1)^{10}$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$ is determined: its existence is settled and its value (one, zero, or some other number) is proved.
why: It gives a precise meaning to the informal question of whether "most" cubic plane curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ are elliptic, turning a vague density intuition into a checkable asymptotic statement about rational points on random plane cubics.

title: Majorization and Schur Polynomials
open: Does Muirhead-style majorization comparison extend from monomial symmetric polynomials to the Schur basis? Formally, for nonnegative variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and partitions $\lambda \succeq \mu$ in the dominance order ($\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i \geq \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_i$ for all $1\le k\le l-1$ with equal total sums), does the corresponding pointwise inequality for Schur polynomials always hold?
status: Community-curated open problem on MathOverflow (score 29, 3 answers), arising from the proposer's experiments with variations on Muirhead's inequality $m_{\lambda}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\geq m_{\mu}(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for $\lambda\succeq\mu$; the Schur analogue has been verified in a few special cases but remains unproved and without counterexample. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/65194/majorization-and-schur-polynomials
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for the conjectured Schur-polynomial inequality under the stated hypotheses ($x_1,\dots,x_n \geq 0$, $\lambda \succeq \mu$); special cases suggest it is true, so a full proof or an explicit counterexample settles it.
why: Muirhead's inequality is a fundamental comparison tool for symmetric polynomials; extending it to the Schur basis would give a majorization calculus for the most widely used basis of the symmetric-function ring, with consequences wherever Schur positivity and dominance order interact.

title: Are there Ricci-flat riemannian manifolds with generic holonomy
open: Does there exist a Ricci-flat Riemannian manifold whose holonomy is not a proper subgroup of $\mathrm{SO}(n)$? Formally, does Ricci-flatness force a reduction of the holonomy group, or can a "generic" holonomy representation occur on a Ricci-flat manifold?
status: In Berger's classification (refined by Simons, Alekseevsky, Bryant, and others) of holonomy representations of irreducible non-symmetric complete simply-connected Riemannian manifolds, the cases $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ in dimension $2n$, $\mathrm{Sp}(n)$ in dimension $4n$, $G_2$ in dimension $7$, and $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ in dimension $8$ imply Ricci-flatness. The other holonomy representations are known not to give Ricci-flat metrics: quaternionic Kähler ($\mathrm{Sp}(n)\cdot\mathrm{Sp}(1)$) manifolds are Einstein with nonzero scalar curvature, and a Ricci-flat Kähler ($\mathrm{U}(n)$) manifold has holonomy contained in $\mathrm{SU}(n)$. The converse question — whether Ricci-flatness implies reduced holonomy — is posed on MathOverflow (score 29, 2 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/16818/are-there-ricci-flat-riemannian-manifolds-with-generic-holonomy
solved_when: Either a complete simply-connected Ricci-flat Riemannian manifold is exhibited whose holonomy is $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ (generic holonomy), or it is proved that Ricci-flatness always implies a reduction of holonomy to one of the Ricci-flat cases in the Berger–Simons classification ($\mathrm{SU}(n)$ in dimension $2n$, $\mathrm{Sp}(n)$ in dimension $4n$, $G_2$ in dimension $7$, $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ in dimension $8$).
why: A positive example would show Ricci-flatness does not constrain holonomy, while a converse theorem would complete the structural picture of the Berger–Simons classification, tying Ricci-flatness rigidly to special geometries like Calabi–Yau, hyperkähler, $G_2$, and $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$.

title: Can you flip the end of a large exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$
open: Can the end of a large exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ be "flipped" — that is, does there exist an exotic structure on the end that reverses its orientation-type behavior? Formally, for a large exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ (an exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ containing a compact smooth 4-submanifold $K'$ that cannot be smoothly embedded in standard $\mathbb{R}^4$), with end $R - D^4$ for a topologically embedded disk $D^4 \supset K'$, can one construct such a flip of the end?
status: Community-curated open problem on MathOverflow (score 29, 1 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/59046/can-you-flip-the-end-of-a-large-exotic-mathbbr4. Background definitions follow Gompf and Stipsicz Exercise 9, with the end defined as $R - D^4$ rather than the standard notion of "end."
solved_when: An explicit construction of a flipped end of a large exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ is given, or a proof that no such flip exists, for the notion of end defined via $R - D^4$ as above.
why: It probes the flexibility of exotic smooth structures at infinity, telling us whether the end of a large exotic $\mathbb{R}^4$ is constrained by its interior or can be independently manipulated.

title: Finite-dimensional subalgebras of $C^\star$-algebras
open: If a finitely generated unital $C^\star$-algebra $A$ — generated (with adjoints) by finitely many normal elements $a_1,\dots,a_n$ whose span gives a norm-dense $\star$-subalgebra $B$ — has every element of $B$ with finite spectrum, must $A$ be finite-dimensional? The question is the converse to the trivial observation that in a finite-dimensional $C^\star$-algebra every element has finite spectrum.
status: Open as a community-curated MathOverflow question (score 29, 0 answers); no simpler counterexample route is known to the poser, and no answers have been given.
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, showing that finite spectrum of every element of the densely generated $\star$-subalgebra $B$ does (respectively does not) force $A$ to be finite-dimensional.
why: The question sits at the intersection of $C^\star$-algebra structure and group theory: finitely generated infinite torsion groups suggest a plausible counterexample route via reduced group $C^\star$-algebras, where all monomials in the generators and their inverses (= adjoints) would have finite spectrum while the generated algebra remains infinite-dimensional.

title: Is the ratio Perimeter/Area for a finite union of unit squares at most 4
open: Is the ratio of perimeter to area of a union of finitely many unit squares in the plane always at most four? Formally, prove (or disprove) that for every finite union H of unit squares, Perimeter(H)/Area(H) ≤ 4 — a statement known as Keleti's perimeter–area conjecture.
status: Community-vetted on MathOverflow (score 28, 3 answers). The axis-aligned version of the statement is easy to prove; for unit circles the analogous statement is true and sharp with constant two. The best known bound is 5.551... by Zoltán Gyenes, whose master thesis contains much more about the problem. Discussion at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/15188/is-the-ratio-perimeter-area-for-a-finite-union-of-unit-squares-at-most-4.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the bound Perimeter(H)/Area(H) ≤ 4 for every union H of finitely many unit squares in the plane, improving on the best known bound of 5.551... due to Zoltán Gyenes.
why: Resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about how much boundary a union of congruent squares can carry relative to its area; the analogous statement for unit circles is true and sharp with constant two, so the square case is the remaining gap.

title: Point singularity of a Riemannian manifold with bounded curvature
open: Does the Riemannian structure of an incomplete manifold with bounded sectional curvature, whose metric completion adds exactly one point, extend smoothly across that point singularity? For simplicity, assume the dimension is greater than 2 and that every neighborhood of the singularity contains a smaller punctured neighborhood that is simply connected; in dimension 2 this should be replaced by an appropriate holonomy condition.
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow (community-curated, score 27, 5 answers). The poser and Penny Smith wrote a paper on this years ago proving extension under the extra assumption that no arbitrarily short closed geodesics exist near the singularity, but the poser could not remove this assumption and is seeking either a proof without it or a counterexample. Key record: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/1554/point-singularity-of-a-riemannian-manifold-with-bounded-curvature
solved_when: Either a proof is given that the Riemannian structure extends across the point singularity under the stated hypotheses (dimension greater than 2, plus the local simple-connectivity assumption near the singularity; in dimension 2, the holonomy variant), without any assumption excluding arbitrarily short closed geodesics, or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: Removing the short-closed-geodesic assumption from the known partial result would settle the basic regularity question for bounded-curvature point singularities; a counterexample would reveal a genuinely new type of singularity.

title: The quaternion moat problem
open: Is there an analogue of the Gaussian moat problem for the quaternions — that is, can one "walk to infinity" through quaternion primes using steps of bounded length, or does a moat of some bounded width block every such path? Just as it is unknown whether a bounded-step walk to infinity exists on the Gaussian primes, the question is what the corresponding statement, if any, should be over the quaternions and whether it is open.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 27, 1 answer). The Gaussian moat problem itself is unresolved: Gethner, Wagon, and Wick, "A Stroll Through the Gaussian Primes" (American Mathematical Monthly 105 (4): 327-337 (1998)), explain it is unknown whether one can walk to infinity on the Gaussian primes with bounded steps; Paul Erdős was reported to have conjectured this possible ("A conjecture of Paul Erdős concerning Gaussian primes." Math. Comp 24: 221-223 (1970)), and later reported to have conjectured the opposite [GWW98, p.327].
solved_when: A well-posed quaternionic analogue of the moat question is formulated, and it is either proved that no walk to infinity with bounded-length steps exists among quaternion primes, or such a walk is exhibited (or shown to exist) — mirroring a resolution of the Gaussian moat problem.
why: The Gaussian moat problem is a famous, long-standing unsolved question with reported conflicting conjectures of Paul Erdős; extending it to quaternions probes whether the obstruction is special to the Gaussian integers or structural to noncommutative or higher-dimensional arithmetic.

title: 0's in 815915283247897734345611269596115894272000000000
open: Is 40 the largest $n$ such that every 0 digit appearing in the decimal expansion of $n!$ occurs among its trailing zeros? Equivalently, does every $n > 40$ have an "internal" 0 in its factorial's decimal representation?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 27, 1 answers); the question is available at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/393993/0s-in-815915283247897734345611269596115894272000000000.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit $n > 40$) of the claim that 40 is the largest number whose factorial has all its 0 digits at the end.
why: It is a charming, concrete question about the decimal digits of factorials that resists easy resolution and has drawn substantial community attention as a long-tail problem outside the standard open-problem lists.

title: on consecutive integers with similar prime factorizations
open: Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ have identical prime signatures (that is, $n=\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{e_i}$ and $n+1=\prod_{i=1}^{k} q_i^{f_i}$ with $k=l$ and $e_i=f_i$ for all $i$, exponents in nondecreasing order)? Many small examples are known — $(2,3)$, $(14,15)$, $(21,22)$, $(33,34)$, $(34,35)$, $(38,39)$, $(44,45)$, $(98,99)$, and more — many of them almost-primes, but the question of infinitude remains open.
status: Community-curated and vetted on MathOverflow, where the question has score 26 and 7 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/32412/question-on-consecutive-integers-with-similar-prime-factorizations); numerous example pairs are documented but no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many $n$ are factorially equivalent to $n+1$; since no quantitative target is stated, the natural criterion is an unconditional proof of infinitude of such consecutive pairs.
why: It concerns how multiplicative structure behaves under the additive shift $n \mapsto n+1$, a concrete test case for the interplay between additive and multiplicative number theory outside the standard problem lists.

title: When does the converse to Schur's Lemma hold
open: Schur's Lemma tells us that a simple module $M$ over an $R$-algebra $A$ has a division ring as its endomorphism ring End$_{A\text{-}mod}(M)$ — and when $R = \mathbb{C}$ with finite-dimensional endomorphism ring, that ring is just $\mathbb{C}$ itself. Under what conditions on $R$ and/or $A$ does the converse hold, so that End$_{A\text{-}mod}(M)$ being a division ring, or being $R$ itself, forces $M$ to be simple?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 26, 3 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/2328/when-does-the-converse-to-schurs-lemma-hold.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the circumstances (on the commutative base ring $R$ and/or the $R$-algebra $A$) under which End$_{A\text{-}mod}(M)$ being a division ring — or being exactly $R$ — implies that $M$ is simple.
why: A clean answer would tell representation theorists exactly when endomorphism-ring computations can substitute for direct simplicity checks, a shortcut used constantly over $\mathbb{C}$ but of uncertain validity over general base rings.

title: A simple group with 3 generators
open: Every finite simple group is generated by two elements, though the known proof spans tens of thousands of pages. Does there exist a finitely presentable simple group that requires 3 generators — that is, one generated by 3 elements but not by 2?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question has score 26 and 1 answer.
solved_when: An explicit example is given of a finitely presentable simple group that is generated by 3 elements but not by 2.
why: It would separate finite from finitely presented infinite simple groups on a basic invariant — minimal generator number — and show that 2-generation is not a universal feature of simple groups.

title: Periodic Automorphism Towers
open: Does there exist a finite group $G$ with $Aut(G) \not\cong G$ such that $Aut^{(n)}(G) \cong G$ for some $n \geq 2$, where $Aut^{(2)}(G) = Aut(Aut(G))$ and so on? More broadly, Scott's textbook asks whether the sequence of isomorphism types of $Aut^{(n)}(G)$ is eventually periodic — equivalently, whether $|Aut^{(n)}(G)|$ is always bounded above — and it apparently remains open whether the sequence is always eventually constant; as Joel David Hamkins pointed out, the stated question is perhaps even open for infinite groups.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 26, 3 answers); a wonderful theorem of Wielandt says that if $G$ is a finite centerless group, then the sequence is eventually constant. Key works: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/27861/periodic-automorphism-towers
solved_when: Either a finite group $G$ is exhibited with $Aut(G) \not\cong G$ and $Aut^{(n)}(G) \cong G$ for some $n \geq 2$, or it is proved that no such group exists; the broader eventual-periodicity question is settled by determining whether the sequence $|Aut^{(n)}(G)|$ is always bounded above.
why: A positive example would show the automorphism tower of a finite group can be genuinely periodic rather than eventually constant, and settling the boundedness question would complete the picture left open in Scott's classic textbook beyond Wielandt's theorem for finite centerless groups.

title: Given a lattice L with n elements, are there finite groups H < G such that L $\cong$ the lattice
open: Is every finite lattice isomorphic to an interval $[H,G]=\{K: H \leq K \leq G\}$ in the subgroup lattice of some finite group $G$? For small sizes — specifically lattices with $n = 7$ or $n = 8$ elements — can one decide this, and in particular does a group exist realizing the one remaining exceptional $7$-element lattice, or can one prove existence without constructing the group or derive structural restrictions on any such $G$?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where the post (score 26) received 0 answers. The question is believed answered positively for $n = 6$ by Watatani (1996) MR1409040 and Aschbacher (2008) MR2393428. The poster believes the case $n = 7$ can be handled with one possible exception, the lattice shown in the record, for which no realizing group is known; partial restrictions on such a group were claimed by the poster. No recent work on the cases $n = 7$ or $n = 8$ was identified in the thread.
solved_when: A finite group $G$ with a subgroup $H$ is exhibited whose interval $[H,G]$ is the exceptional $7$-element lattice shown in the record, or a proof is given that no such group exists; more broadly, the realizability question is settled for all lattices with $n = 7$ and $n = 8$.
why: The unrestricted version is a famous open problem; settling the small cases (with one candidate exception at $n = 7$) would push the frontier past the known $n = 6$ result and sharpen our understanding of which subgroup-lattice intervals finite groups can realize.

title: Are all primes in a PAP-3
open: Is every odd prime contained in some 3-term arithmetic progression of primes? That is, for every prime $p>2$, does there exist a $k$ such that $p+k$ and $p+2k$ are both prime?
status: Van der Corput [1] proved infinitely many 3-term arithmetic progressions of primes, and Green & Tao [2] extended this to progressions of length $k$. The question, community-curated on MathOverflow (score 25, 1 answers), remains open. Computationally, the first 100,000 primes all lie in a PAP-3, with the largest $k$ needed just 1584 (see [4], and [5] where this is greatly extended). Heuristically each prime should lie in $\int_2^\infty \frac{a\,dx}{\log(x\log x)} = +\infty$ different PAP-3s, and no small prime obstructions exist, so the conclusion seems reasonable. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/34197/are-all-primes-in-a-pap-3
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every prime $p>2$ there is a positive integer $k$ with $p$, $p+k$, $p+2k$ all prime.
why: It asks for a Goldbach-like (or Sophie Germain-like) additive pattern in the primes — for a fixed odd $n$, primes $q$ with $2q-n$ also prime — so a solution would be a major advance in understanding additive patterns beyond van der Corput's and Green–Tao's infinitude results.

title: Why is it so hard to prove Toeplitz' conjecture
open: Does every simple closed curve in the plane contain four points that are the vertices of a square? This is the inscribed-square (Toeplitz) conjecture, asking for a proof that no Jordan curve can avoid hosting an inscribed square.
status: Asked and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 25, 1 answer). The questioner reports the problem appears as "Squaring the Lake" on p. 143 of Winkler's *Mathematical Puzzles: A Connoisseur's Collection*, with comments and sources at p. 148, and that the author notes it is "a little embarrassing that mathematicians cannot" solve it; the asker could only verify it for triangles.
solved_when: A proof — or disproof — that every simple closed curve in the plane contains four points forming the vertices of a square.
why: It is a basic, natural-sounding question about Jordan curves that has resisted solution for decades; settling it would resolve a long-standing embarrassment at the heart of elementary plane geometry.

title: Decidability of equality of elementary expressions
open: In the following definition the term expression is to be understood as a finite tree built from formal symbols without any predefined meaning assigned to them. Define the set $\mathcal{E}$ of elementary expressions as the minimal set such that: the expression $i$ is in $\mathcal{E}$ if $x\in\mathcal{E}$, then the expression $\exp(x)\in\mathcal{E}$, if $x\in\mathcal{E}$, then the expression $\ln(x)\in\mathcal{E}$, if $x,y\in\mathcal{E}$, then the expression $(x\cdot y)\in\mathcal{E}.$ Now we can assign meaning (a numeric value) to expressions in $\mathcal{E}$ as follows: $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\exp(x)$ is the exponent of $x$, $\ln(x)$ is the principal branch of the natural logarithm of $x$ (unless the value of $x$ is zero), $(x\cdot y)$ is the product of $x$ and $y$. These rules do not assign a value to an expression if it contains a logarithm of an expression whose value is zero, e.
status: community-curated on MathOverflow (score 25, 1 answers)
why: high community interest; long-tail problems outside standard lists

title: Is there a 7-regular graph on 50 vertices with girth 5? What about 57-regular on 3250 vertices
open: Does there exist a $d$-regular graph of girth 5 on exactly $d^2+1$ vertices — the Moore graph extremal case — for the degrees $d = 7$ and $d = 57$, the only values beyond $d = 2, 3$ not ruled out by the standard lower bound?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 24, 2 answers). Easy constructions exist for $d=2$ and $d=3$; eigenvalue methods rule out $d=4,5,6,8,9,10$ (posed as Problem 2 in a companion problem set), and a further argument shows the only possible values are $d \in \{2,3,7,57\}$, written up in a handout for a graph theory course. The existence questions for $d=7$ (50 vertices) and $d=57$ (3250 vertices) remain unresolved. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/43923/is-there-a-7-regular-graph-on-50-vertices-with-girth-5-what-about-57-regular-on
solved_when: A construction (or a nonexistence proof) is given for a 7-regular graph on 50 vertices with girth 5, and likewise for a 57-regular graph on 3250 vertices with girth 5.
why: It completes the classification of when the Moore bound $d^2+1$ on the order of a $d$-regular graph with no loops, multiple edges, 3-cycles, or 4-cycles is attained, closing a classic textbook exercise of Van Lint and Wilson (Problem 1.F).

title: Integer-distance sets
open: Does there exist an infinite integer-distance set of noncollinear points in the plane — that is, a set of points not all on one line such that every pair is separated by an integer Euclidean distance? Beyond existence, what are examples of maximal integer-distance sets, where no further point can be added while preserving the property?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 24, 3 answers), see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/136925/integer-distance-sets. Known constructions: lattice points along any one line parallel to a coordinate axis in $\mathbb{R}^d$ form a countably infinite integer-distance set; Euler established that every circle contains a dense rational-distance set, and scaling such a circle by a large common denominator yields rich finite integer-distance sets (e.g., five points on a circle including $(1221025, 0)$, $(781456, 586092)$, $(439569, \ldots)$, all at integer mutual distances). No infinite noncollinear example is recorded.
solved_when: An explicit infinite integer-distance set of noncollinear points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (especially $d=2$) is exhibited, or it is proved none exists; descriptions of maximal integer-distance sets would further resolve the question.
why: It would settle a long-standing community-vetted question about the rigidity of integer-distance constraints: collinear constructions (e.g., lattice points along a coordinate-parallel line) are trivial, but nothing noncollinear and infinite is known.

title: Smooth proper schemes over Z with points everywhere locally
open: Does there exist a smooth proper scheme $X\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ that has points everywhere locally, i.e. $X(\mathbb{Q}_v)\neq\emptyset$ for every place $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ including $v=\infty$, yet has no rational point, $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$? The questioner conjectures the answer is No; it is a variation on Poonen's question, taking Buzzard's example into account.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 24, 0 answers). The evidence against existence is described as flimsy: $X$ cannot be a curve or a torsor under an abelian variety (Abrashkin–Fontaine), nor a twisted form of $\mathbb{P}_n$; the questioner has not systematically checked known Hasse-principle-counterexample smooth projective $\mathbb{Q}$-varieties for everywhere good reduction, but considers the chances slim. Colliot-Thélène and Xu give a systematic treatment of many known examples of quasi-projective $\mathbb{Z}$-schemes $Y$ with $Y(\mathbb{Z}_p)\neq\emptyset$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/11316/smooth-proper-schemes-over-z-with-points-everywhere-locally
solved_when: A proof that no such scheme exists — or an explicit example of a smooth proper $\mathbb{Z}$-scheme with local points at every place but no rational point — is given.
why: It would settle whether an integral Hasse principle holds for smooth proper schemes over $\mathbb{Z}$, extending known restrictions (curves, torsors under abelian varieties, twisted forms of projective space) to the general case.

title: unboundedness of number of integral points on elliptic curves
open: Is the number of integral points on an elliptic curve over $\mathbf{Q}$, counted on a minimal Weierstrass model, unbounded as the curve varies? Siegel's theorem makes $n(E)$ finite (effectively so), and it is a well-defined invariant since minimal models give the same count; the question is whether this invariant takes arbitrarily large values, noting that without minimality the question is trivial by rescaling coordinates on a rank-1 curve.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 23, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/50661/unboundedness-of-number-of-integral-points-on-elliptic-curves.
solved_when: A proof that $n(E)$ is unbounded over all elliptic curves $E/\mathbf{Q}$, or a proof that it is bounded; either resolves the problem.
why: It probes how Siegel finiteness interacts with the arithmetic complexity of elliptic curves, a basic quantitative question about integral points that sits outside the standard problem lists.

title: Current state of the Komlos conjecture on vector balancing
open: Is there an absolute constant $K>0$ such that, for every dimension $d$ and any collection of unit vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\lVert v_i\rVert_2=1$, one can choose signs $w_i\in\{-1,1\}$ making $\lVert w_1v_1+\cdots+w_nv_n\rVert_\infty<K$? In particular, is the best known result still that for fixed $d$ the statement holds with $K=K(n)\approx\log n$?
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 23, 4 answers) asking for the current state of the Komlós conjecture and whether the best known result is $K=K(n)\approx\log n$ for fixed $d$; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/275169/current-state-of-the-komlos-conjecture-on-vector-balancing.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the existence of the absolute constant $K$ as stated; along the way, a characterization of the best dependence $K(n)$ achievable for fixed $d$ relative to the known $\approx\log n$ bound.
why: A uniform bound would settle the Komlós conjecture, a central question in vector balancing at the intersection of discrepancy theory, convex geometry, and combinatorics, and would resolve the natural quantitative gap between constant and logarithmic discrepancy.

title: Ramsey multiplicity
open: How many monochromatic copies of $K_a$ must appear in every two-coloring of the edges of $K_{R(a)}$? Formally, the Ramsey multiplicity $m(a)$ is the largest $m$ such that every 2-coloring of $K_{R(a)}$ contains at least $m$ monochromatic copies of $K_a$; determine $m(a)$ in general.
status: Community-curated problem on MathOverflow (score 23, 2 answers). It is known that $m(3)=2$ (any 2-coloring of $K_6$ contains 2 monochromatic triangles), and Piwakowski and Radziszowski showed around 1999 that $m(4)=9$. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/26040/ramsey-multiplicity
solved_when: A formula or effective procedure giving $m(a)$ for arbitrary $a$; in particular, values beyond the known $m(3)=2$ and $m(4)=9$.
why: It sharpens Ramsey's theorem from a guarantee of one monochromatic clique to a quantitative count, testing how much structure any coloring near the Ramsey threshold is forced to have.

title: What is known about the relationship between Fermat's last theorem and Peano Arithmetic
open: Is Fermat's Last Theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic, or is it independent of PA? Equivalently, what can be said about the theories $PA + \text{Fermat's Last Theorem}$ and $PA + \lnot \text{Fermat's Last Theorem}$ — noting that if $PA \vdash \text{FLT}$ the first collapses to $PA$ and the second is inconsistent, while if FLT is independent of PA both are consistent extensions distinct from $PA$ (and $PA \vdash \lnot \text{FLT}$ is impossible, since both PA and FLT are true in $\mathbb{N}$)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 22, 1 answer); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/293005/what-is-known-about-the-relationship-between-fermats-last-theorem-and-peano-ari. To the asker's knowledge, whether FLT is provable in PA remains open.
solved_when: A determination of whether $PA \vdash \text{Fermat's Last Theorem}$, or a proof that FLT is independent of PA.
why: It would locate Wiles's theorem relative to the standard finitistic base theory, telling us whether its proof can in principle be carried out with elementary arithmetic reasoning alone.

title: What is Chern-Simons theory expected to assign to a point
open: What should Chern-Simons theory assign to a point? Formally, given a compact, connected, (simply connected?) Lie group $G$ and a class $k \in H^4(BG, \mathbb{Z})$, one expects a fully extended $3$-dimensional topological quantum field theory extending the theory Witten constructed at a physical level of rigor (going down to surfaces), which Reshetikhin-Turaev and others later extended to $1$-manifolds; such a theory is determined by its value on $S^1$, a modular tensor category describable via loop group $LG$ representations at level $k$ or via quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ representations for suitable $q$ — but what invariant of a point completes this picture remains open.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 22, 3 answers); the question reflects high community interest in long-tail problems outside standard lists.
solved_when: A construction is given of the value Chern-Simons theory assigns to a point, completing the data of the theory on all manifolds of dimension $3$ and below (surfaces, $1$-manifolds, and a point).
why: A fully extended Chern-Simons theory would complete one of the central examples of functorial field theory at all codimensions, clarifying the relation between the loop group and quantum group descriptions of the modular tensor category assigned to the circle.

title: Splitting Pythagorean triples
open: Can the positive integers be partitioned into finitely many subsets, none of which contains a Pythagorean triple? If so, what is the minimum number of subsets needed — with a plausible guess being 3?
status: Open and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 22, 4 answers). A heuristic candidate exists: partitioning integers by the parity of the highest power of 5 dividing them splits most primitive triples and all their multiples. Schur proved the positive integers cannot be split into finitely many sum-free subsets (i.e. no finite partition splits all power-of-1 Fermat triples), while Fermat's Last Theorem shows all power-n triples for n>2 are split by the trivial partition into one set. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/1051/splitting-pythagorean-triples
solved_when: A finite partition of the positive integers into Pythagorean-triple-free subsets is exhibited, together with the exact minimum number of subsets required (or a proof that no finite partition exists).
why: A solution would settle whether Pythagorean triples behave like sum-free sets, which by Schur's theorem admit no finite partition of the integers, or like power-n triples for n>2, which Fermat's theorem shows are split by the trivial one-set partition.

title: Curves of constant curvature on S^2
open: Given a Riemannian metric on $S^2$, what is known about the structure of the set of simple closed curves of constant geodesic curvature? Formally: does such a curve pass through every point, and if not, can one estimate from below the area proportion covered; are there at least two such curves for each curvature value (perhaps more); and what is the topology of the surface formed by taking the union of all these curves, naturally mapping to $S^2$, on a generic $S^2$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 22 and 3 answers; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/31920/curves-of-constant-curvature-on-s2
solved_when: Answers are given to these questions: an existence statement (or a lower bound on the area proportion covered) for a simple closed constant-geodesic-curvature curve through each point of $S^2$; a lower bound (at least 2, or more) on the number of simple closed curves for each curvature value; and a description of the topology of the surface obtained as the union of all such closed curves on a generic $S^2$.
why: These curves form a natural bridge between the metric geometry of $S^2$ and the topology of an associated covering surface, and settling them would clarify the global incidence structure of constant-curvature curves on a general Riemannian 2-sphere.

title: Equilaterally triangulated surfaces with prescribed boundary
open: Does every closed polygonal path in $\mathbb{R}^3$ made of unit segments bound an immersed polygonal surface whose faces are unit equilateral triangles? Formally, can such a spanning surface be parametrized by a continuous locally one-to-one map from a compact connected 2-dimensional manifold with boundary, so that at most two triangles share an edge, the triangles around any vertex form an embedded topological disk, and only triangles sharing neither an edge nor a vertex may intersect?
status: The problem originates from Richard Kenyon's list (preserved via the Wayback Machine) and was posted on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with a score of 22 and 3 answers; no solution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every unit-segment closed polygonal path in $\mathbb{R}^3$ admits — or does not admit — such an immersed equilateral-triangulated spanning surface.
why: This is a problem from Richard Kenyon's list on which no progress has been reported even in special cases; a solution would clarify how much rigidity the unit equilateral constraint imposes on which polygonal boundaries are spannable.

title: Coiling Rope in a Box
open: What is the longest length L of rope of radius r that can be packed into a given box, where the rope is a smooth curve carrying a non-self-penetrating tubular neighborhood of radius r (and each endpoint of an open curve is surrounded by a ball of radius r)? The asker is more interested in general coiling strategies than exact values, noting for instance that in a $1{\times}1{\times}\frac{1}{2}$ box with $r=\frac{1}{4}$ a 'U' shape plausibly achieves $L=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\approx 1.3$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 21, 1 answers); record at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/26525/coiling-rope-in-a-box. The asker observes that if r is large relative to the box dimensions (as in the example above), no "penny-packing" cross-sectional approach applies.
solved_when: A characterization of the maximal rope length (or effective general coiling strategies) is available; a concrete instance is the $1{\times}1{\times}\frac{1}{2}$ box with $r=\frac{1}{4}$, where the candidate value is $L=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\approx 1.3$.
why: It concerns high community interest in long-tail problems outside standard lists; while circle packing in a square is notoriously difficult, the continuity of the rope curve may constrain the options enough to make packing a rope easier.

title: Generating random finite groups
open: Is there an efficient method to generate a random finite group of a given order $n$ uniformly at random, in the sense that each of the $g(n)$ non-isomorphic groups of order $n$ occurs with probability exactly $1/g(n)$ — for instance, producing each of the $267$ groups of order $64$ with equal probability? Groups of order $n = 2^k$ are of particular interest.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 21, 2 answers); the comments indicate this appears to be an open problem with little chance of resolution in the near future. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/164983/generating-random-finite-groups
solved_when: A procedure (presumably practical, not just theoretical) exists that, given $n$, outputs a group of order $n$ with each isomorphism class occurring with probability exactly $1/g(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the number of non-isomorphic groups of order $n$ (OEIS A000001); at minimum, this should be achieved for orders $n = 2^k$.
why: It would give access to typical finite groups — especially $2$-groups, which dominate the count of small groups — enabling experimentation and conjecture-testing on representative examples rather than the special families currently available.

title: In a Banach algebra, do ab and ba have almost the same exponential spectrum
open: In a complex unital Banach algebra, must the exponential spectra of $ab$ and $ba$ agree up to zero? Formally, where $e(x)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}: x-\lambda 1\notin G_1(A)\}$ and $G_1(A)$ is the identity component of the invertible group, is $e(ab)\cup\{0\} = e(ba)\cup\{0\}$ for all $a,b\in A$ — equivalently, is $1-ab\in G_1(A)$ if and only if $1-ba\in G_1(A)$? (The usual spectrum has this property.) Known cases: the identity holds if the invertible group $G(A)$ is connected (then exponential spectrum equals usual spectrum), and also whenever $Z(A)G(A)=\{ab: a\in Z(A), b\in G(A)\}$ is dense in $A$, where $Z(A)$ is the center.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 21, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/2369/in-a-banach-algebra-do-ab-and-ba-have-almost-the-same-exponential-spectrum.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that $e(ab)\cup\{0\} = e(ba)\cup\{0\}$ holds for all $a,b$ in every complex unital Banach algebra — equivalently, that $1-ab\in G_1(A)$ iff $1-ba\in G_1(A)$ for all $a,b$.
why: The usual spectrum is well known to satisfy $\sigma(ab)\cup\{0\}=\sigma(ba)\cup\{0\}$; settling whether the exponential spectrum, a topologically defined refinement, retains this property clarifies how invertibility-component structure interacts with products, and would resolve a long-standing community-vetted question in Banach algebra theory.

title: Avoidable words
open: Is there a word that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable? Here, a word $u(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is $k$-avoidable if some infinite word over a $k$-letter alphabet contains no value of $u$ (no subword of the form $u(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ with each $v_i$ nonempty) as a subword.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 21, 0 answers). All avoidable words have been described by Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty and Zimin (see slides of George McNulty's talk). Ronald Clark proved in his PhD thesis that $abubawacxbcycdazdcd$ is 5-avoidable. Source: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/93997/avoidable-words
solved_when: An explicit word is exhibited that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable, or equivalently a proof that every 5-avoidable-word threshold claim fails — concretely: a word $u$ together with an infinite word over $\{a_1,\dots,a_6\}$ avoiding all values of $u$, and a proof that no infinite word over 5 letters does so.
why: It would extend the known hierarchy of avoidability indices — $x^3$ is 2-avoidable but not 1-avoidable, $x^2$ is 3-avoidable but not 2-avoidable (infinite words of Thue and Morse), Walter's word $abwbcxcayba$ is 4-avoidable but not 3-avoidable, and Clark's word $abubawacxbcycdazdcd$ is 5-avoidable — by one more level, showing the hierarchy does not collapse.

title: Axiom of choice and bases of vector spaces over a fixed field
open: Let $k$ be a fixed field. Does the axiom "every vector space over $k$ has a basis" imply the full axiom of choice? More precisely, in 1984 Andreas Blass proved that the axiom "for every extension $K|k$, every vector space over $K$ has a basis" implies the axiom of choice, and he raised the question of whether restricting to vector spaces over the single field $k$ still suffices.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it has a score of 21 and 0 answers, indicating no recorded progress beyond Blass's 1984 result. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/68950/axiom-of-choice-and-bases-of-vector-spaces-over-a-fixed-field
solved_when: A proof (in ZF) that, for every field $k$, the statement "every vector space over $k$ has a basis" implies the axiom of choice; or a model of ZF in which every vector space over some fixed field $k$ has a basis but the axiom of choice fails.
why: It would pin down exactly how much choice is needed for the most basic theorem of linear algebra, separating the single-field case from Blass's all-extensions case.

title: Cutting convex sets
open: Can every bounded convex set in the Euclidean plane be cut into an arbitrary number $n$ of convex pieces with equal area and equal circumference? For $n=2$ this is possible and generically unique; one asks for which other $n$ (if any) uniqueness persists, and more generally, for which pairs $(n,d)$ a $d$-dimensional bounded convex set can be cut into $n$ convex pieces of equal volume and equal $(d-1)$-dimensional boundary area — and whether solutions exist generically uniquely, or at least generically finitely.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem has score 20 and 3 answers; the case $n=2$ in the plane is solved and generically unique, while for $d>2$ the $n=2$ solution is no longer generically unique. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/24352/cutting-convex-sets
solved_when: A characterization of the values of $n$ for which every bounded planar convex set admits an equal-area, equal-circumference convex partition into $n$ pieces; and, in the general case, a characterization of the pairs $(n,d)$ for which such partitions of any bounded convex set in $\mathbf E^d$ exist, together with a determination of when solutions are generically unique or generically finite in number.
why: Equal-volume, equal-surface partitions of convex bodies sit at the interface of convex geometry, measure partitioning, and equivariant topology; settling existence and uniqueness would clarify how rigid the fairness constraints are, and the $d>2$ case already shows uniqueness can fail, making the boundary of that phenomenon the heart of the question.

title: All compact surfaces $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ are rigid
open: Is every smooth, compact, boundaryless, connected surface $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ rigid? Formally, if $f:S\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a differentiable deformation with each $f_t:S\to S_t$ an isometry and $f_0\equiv\mathrm{Id}_S$, must each $f_t(S)$ be the image of $S$ under a rigid motion $A_t:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$?
status: The problem is stated as open, at least as of 2014, per a lecture in differential geometry by Fernando Codá. It is known for the sphere $S^2$ (Liebmann's Theorem) and for ovaloids, i.e. surfaces with Gaussian curvature $K$ strictly positive (Cohn-Vossen's rigidity theorem), where isometric embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are exactly restrictions of rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^3$. The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 20, 3 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/224711/all-compact-surfaces-s-subseteq-mathbbr3-are-rigid
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every isometric deformation of such a surface arises from rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^3$, covering the general compact boundaryless case beyond the known special cases.
why: Rigidity in the general compact case would extend the classical rigidity theorems (Liebmann's Theorem for the sphere, Cohn-Vossen's rigidity theorem for ovaloids with strictly positive Gaussian curvature) to all compact surfaces, answering a long-standing question in differential geometry.

title: Floors of rationals to powers: Infinite number of primes
open: If $r=a/b>1$ is a rational number in lowest terms that is not an integer (so $b>1$), must the sequence $\lfloor r \rfloor, \lfloor r^2 \rfloor, \lfloor r^3 \rfloor, \ldots$ contain infinitely many primes? For $r=13/4$ the floors begin $3, 10, 34, 111, 362, \ldots$, with the next prime after $3$ appearing only at $\lfloor r^{34} \rfloor = 253532870351270971$, and only four primes found up to $\lfloor r^{1000} \rfloor$.
status: Community-curated open problem on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 20 and 2 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/153426/floors-of-rationals-to-powers-infinite-number-of-primes); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit rational $r$) that for every non-integer rational $r>1$ in lowest terms, the sequence $\{\lfloor r^n \rfloor\}_{n\ge 1}$ contains infinitely many primes.
why: It asks whether a purely multiplicative sequence convolved with the floor function still reflects the primes — a basic and stubborn question about how primes interact with fractional powers, with no standard tools currently reaching it.

title: А generalization of Gromov's theorem on polynomial growth
open: Suppose a group $G$ admits a polynomial $P$ such that for every $n$ there exists a symmetric generating set $S=S^{-1}$ with $|S^n|\le P(n)\cdot|S|$ (or the stronger condition $|S^k|\le P(k)\cdot|S|$ for all $k\le n$). Must $G$ then be virtually nilpotent, i.e. have polynomial growth? Typically $|S|\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, since otherwise the conclusion follows easily from Gromov's original theorem.
status: Posted on MathOverflow, where it was believed known but was identified as open in an answer by Terry Tao (question score 20, 1 answer); the record indicates it has since been resolved, with a solution available on arXiv, though the reference is truncated. Key works: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/11091/%d0%90-generalization-of-gromovs-theorem-on-polynomial-growth
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that the above growth condition on some sequence of generating sets forces $G$ to be virtually nilpotent, under either the weaker condition $|S^n|\le P(n)\cdot|S|$ or the stronger uniform version $|S^k|\le P(k)\cdot|S|$ for all $k\le n$.
why: An affirmative answer would give a purely group-theoretic proof that manifolds with almost non-negative Ricci curvature have virtually nilpotent fundamental group (see Kapovitch--Wilking, "Structure of fundamental groups..."), using only one result from differential geometry: the Bishop--Gromov inequality.

title: Deligne-Simpson problem in the symmetric group
open: Which $k$-tuples of conjugacy classes in the symmetric group $S_n$ admit representatives whose product is the identity? That is, given conjugacy classes $C_1,\dots,C_k$, each specified by a partition of $n$, give a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of permutations $\sigma_i \in C_i$ with $\prod \sigma_i = 1$. A stronger variant asks for such $\sigma_i$ that are irreducible, in the sense that they have no common invariant proper subset $S \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$.
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow (question 12758, community score 20, with 2 answers); the poser was unable to find references in the literature and stated uncertainty about its difficulty. The question is inspired by Jonah Sinick's question via a simple geometric interpretation involving the Riemann sphere with $k$ punctures.
solved_when: A characterization — necessary and sufficient conditions on the conjugacy classes $C_1,\dots,C_k$ (given by partitions of $n$) — is proved for the existence of $\sigma_i \in C_i$ with product $1$, and ideally also for the irreducible variant where the $\sigma_i$ share no common invariant proper subset.
why: This is the finite-group analogue of the Deligne-Simpson problem, so a solution would connect the combinatorics of factorizations in $S_n$ to the classical multiplicative-eigenvalue problem, and would settle when a genus-zero branched cover (or an irreducible one) with prescribed branch cycle types exists.

title: Is every projective space curve a set-theoretic intersection of two surfaces? What is known about th
open: Is every irreducible curve in $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{C})$ the set-theoretic intersection of two surfaces in $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{C})$? More precisely, can such a curve always be realized as the common zero locus of two algebraic surfaces?
status: This is a long-standing open problem over $\mathbb{C}$; results are known in characteristic $p > 0$. The problem was posed and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 20, 1 answers), with the discussion at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/190938/is-every-projective-space-curve-a-set-theoretic-intersection-of-two-surfaces-wh.
solved_when: A proof that every irreducible curve in $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{C})$ arises as the set-theoretic intersection of two surfaces, or a counterexample exhibiting one that does not.
why: It is a long-standing test case for how loosely the set-theoretic structure of varieties determines their ideal-theoretic complexity; a resolution would sharpen our understanding of equations cutting out projective curves.

title: Minimal graphs with a prescribed number of spanning trees
open: Let $\alpha(n)$ denote the least integer $k$ such that there exists a simple graph on $k$ vertices having precisely $n$ spanning trees; what is the asymptotic behaviour of $\alpha$?
status: The question was posed in 1970 by the Czech graph theorist J. Sedlacek (On the minimal graph with a given number of spanning trees, Canad. Math. Bull. 13 (1970) 515–517), who showed the upper bounds above. The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 20, 4 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/93656/minimal-graphs-with-a-prescribed-number-of-spanning-trees, and drew further attention through a post on Dick Lipton's blog.
solved_when: An answer determining the asymptotic growth of $\alpha(n)$ as $n \to \infty$, improving on Sedlacek's bounds $\alpha(n) \leq \frac{n+6}{3}$ for $n \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ and $\alpha(n) \leq \frac{n+4}{3}$ (as stated for large $n$).
why: It resolves a long-standing extremal question connecting the complexity measure "number of spanning trees" to graph size, a natural inverse problem linking the Tutte polynomial to graph construction.

title: Irreducible polynomials with constrained coefficients
open: How many polynomials of degree $d$ with all coefficients in $\{\pm 1\}$ are irreducible? More precisely, what is the asymptotic count or density of irreducible polynomials among the $2^{d+1}$ such polynomials as $d$ grows?
status: Asked on MathOverflow (score 19, 4 answers), community-curated. The asker's initial no-go analysis: since a reducible polynomial is reduducible mod $3$, the number of reducible such polynomials is $O(\frac{d-1}{d}3^d)$, which is too large to help; reducing mod $2$ cannot distinguish these polynomials at all, since all coefficients become $1$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/7969/irreducible-polynomials-with-constrained-coefficients
solved_when: An asymptotic formula (or tight bounds) for the number of irreducible polynomials of degree $d$ with coefficients in $\{\pm 1\}$, valid as $d \to \infty$.
why: A solution would reveal how arithmetic structure survives severe coefficient constraints, informing the general theory of height-bounded and Littlewood-type polynomials.

title: What's the Kirby Diagram of a universal $\mathbb{R}^4$
open: What is an explicit Kirby diagram for the universal smoothing $U$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ constructed by Freedman and Taylor? Formally, writing $\mathcal{R}$ for the set of smoothings of $\mathbb{R}^4$ and end sum via proper rays $\gamma_i : [0,\infty) \to R_i$ (well defined up to diffeomorphism since $\gamma_i$ is unique up to ambient isotopy), one seeks a handle decomposition of the element $U \in \mathcal{R}$ such that $U \natural R \cong U$ for every $R \in \mathcal{R}$, whose existence was proved in "A universal smoothing of four-space."
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 19, 1 answers) with high community interest as a long-tail problem outside standard lists; Freedman and Taylor proved the existence of $U$ in "A universal smoothing of four-space," but no explicit Kirby diagram is known. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/54143/whats-the-kirby-diagram-of-a-universal-mathbbr4
solved_when: A Kirby diagram (explicit handle decomposition) is produced whose corresponding smoothing is diffeomorphic to the Freedman–Taylor universal $U$.
why: The universal $\mathbb{R}^4$ is known to exist only abstractly; an explicit diagram would make it computable and enable hands-on study of the end-sum structure of exotic smoothings of $\mathbb{R}^4$.

title: Meromorphic 1-form and Picard's theorem
open: If a punctured disk is covered by open sets carrying injective holomorphic functions whose differentials agree on every overlap, must these differentials glue to a meromorphic 1-form on the full disk? Formally, given the open unit disk $D$, the punctured disk $D^* = D\setminus\{0\}$, and an open cover $U_1,\ldots,U_n$ of $D^*$ with injective holomorphic $f_j$ on $U_j$ satisfying $df_j = df_k$ on $U_j\cap U_k$, is there a meromorphic 1-form on $D$ restricting to the glued differential?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 19 and 4 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/61882/meromorphic-1-form-and-picards-theorem). It is noted that the answer is yes when the residue is zero, with help of Picard's theorem; the general case remains open.
solved_when: A proof that the glued differential on $D^*$ extends meromorphically across $0$ (or an explicit counterexample) is given.
why: The case of vanishing residue already follows via Picard's theorem, so a general answer would settle the one remaining obstruction to gluing local primitives into a global meromorphic form — a natural sheaf-theoretic extension of Picard-type removability questions.

title: Free subgroups vs law
open: If a profinite group satisfies no nontrivial group law, must it contain a non-abelian free subgroup? Equivalently-by-analogy with the Tits alternative: does failure to satisfy a law force a free subgroup in the profinite (or residually finite) setting, e.g. does the profinite completion of a residually finite group obeying no law contain a non-abelian free subgroup?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 19, 2 answers). It is easy to construct torsion groups satisfying no law (e.g., the direct product of all finite groups), so in general the absence of a law does not imply a free subgroup, but the question for profinite groups remains open. The second question is known to have a positive answer for finitely generated p-groups, following from [Wilson, Zelmanov, Identities for Lie algebras of pro-p groups, JPAA 81(192), 103-109]. Source: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/52913/free-subgroups-vs-law
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for profinite groups the absence of a nontrivial law is equivalent to containing a non-abelian free subgroup, and likewise a resolution of whether the profinite completion of every residually finite, lawless group contains a non-abelian free subgroup.
why: These questions extend the Tits alternative from linears groups to residually finite and profinite groups, and a solution would delineate exactly when "large" profinite behavior is witnessed by a free subgroup; the second question is already answered positively for finitely generated p-groups, so the general case is the natural frontier.

title: The oriented homeomorphism problem for Haken 3-manifolds
open: Is there an algorithm, written down in the literature, that decides whether two oriented Haken 3-manifolds are homeomorphic by an orientation-preserving homeomorphism? Haken's algorithm reduces this to deciding whether a given orientable Haken 3-manifold admits an orientation-reversing self-homeomorphism, so the question is equally: does the literature contain such an algorithm?
status: Haken famously described an algorithm solving the homeomorphism problem for Haken 3-manifolds, fleshed out by many others, including Hemion and Matveev, who fixed some gaps. Whether an oriented version appears in the literature is posed as a community-vetted question on MathOverflow (score 19, 1 answer): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/107573/the-oriented-homeomorphism-problem-for-haken-3-manifolds.
solved_when: An algorithm appears in the literature that determines whether a pair of oriented Haken 3-manifolds M and N are orientedly homeomorphic, or equivalently whether an orientable Haken 3-manifold M admits an orientation-reversing self-homeomorphism.
why: The ordinary (unoriented) homeomorphism problem for Haken 3-manifolds is settled, but oriented manifolds arise naturally, and the existence of the oriented version — with its details — has not been spelled out anywhere, leaving a gap for anyone needing it in practice.

title: Undecidable easy arithmetical statement
open: Does there exist a natural, easy-to-state arithmetical proposition — of the flavor of the Collatz conjecture — that is provably undecidable in a standard formal system such as PA or ZFC? And is there any principled reason to expect that the Collatz conjecture itself might be undecidable?
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 18, 4 answers) raising the question of an easy arithmetical statement known to be undecidable, in the spirit of the Collatz conjecture, and whether there is reason to believe Collatz itself is undecidable. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/284921/undecidable-easy-arithmetical-statement
solved_when: An explicit arithmetical statement, recognizable as "easy" in the Collatz-like sense, is proved independent of a standard system like PA or ZFC (or, for the second part, a concrete argument is given for or against the undecidability of Collatz).
why: Current independence results (Gödel sentences, Goodstein, Paris–Harrington) either are metamathematical in flavor or combinatorial but not "elementary arithmetic" to a casual reader; a Collatz-like undecidable statement would show that undecidability already infects the simplest kind of schoolroom arithmetic.

title: Totally rational polytopes
open: Beyond boxes and hypercubes, do nontrivial families of totally rational polytopes exist in every dimension — polytopes whose vertex coordinates are rational and in which every face of each dimension has rational measure, along with positive rational volume? In particular, do totally rational simplices exist in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for arbitrarily large $d$, given that Pythagorean triples already give totally rational triangles?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 18, 1 answers); the question notes that hypercubes $\{0,1\}^d$ and axis-aligned boxes with integral vertex coordinates are totally rational, and that Pythagorean triples yield totally rational triangles. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/71949/totally-rational-polytopes
solved_when: Either a family of totally rational polytopes (defined for all $d$) other than hypercubes and axis-aligned boxes is exhibited, or it is shown that no such family exists; in particular, a resolution of whether totally rational simplices exist in arbitrarily large dimension.
why: Rational coordinates with all face measures rational is exactly the condition under which scaling converts every face measure into integers, so a positive answer would supply integral-geometry building blocks beyond orthogonal boxes.

title: Characterisation of bell-shaped functions
open: Which smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}$ are bell-shaped — that is, infinitely smooth, tending to zero at $\pm\infty$, with $f^{(n)}$ having exactly $n$ zeroes (counted with multiplicity) for every $n$? More sharply, can bell-shaped functions be characterised in terms of the interlacing condition, namely that for every $n \geqslant 0$ the zeroes of $f^{(n)}$ and $f^{(n+1)}$ interlace (counting multiplicity)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 18, 2 answers); the problem was publicised there as learned from Thomas Simon, with the aim of popularising it. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/282596/characterisation-of-bell-shaped-functions.
solved_when: A complete characterisation of the class of bell-shaped functions on $\mathbb{R}$ is given — equivalently, a proof or counterexample relating bell-shapedness to the interlacing-derivative property defined above.
why: A solution is expected to yield nice, publishable mathematics and would settle a natural structural question about higher derivatives that the standard literature leaves open.

title: Determine or estimate the number of maximal triangle-free graphs on $n$ vertices
open: How many maximal triangle-free graphs are there on $n$ vertices, exactly or asymptotically? This is one of Paul Erdős's open problems ("number of triangle-free graphs") listed on Fan Chung's website of Erdős problems.
status: The problem appears on MathOverflow (score 18, 2 answers) as a community-vetted open problem, with no known resolution recorded there; the asker also proposed a heuristic "connection game" approach (players choose edges and delete one of two edges whenever a triangle would form) and asked for comments or related results. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/159494/determine-or-estimate-the-number-of-maximal-triangle-free-graphs-on-n-vertices
solved_when: An exact formula or an asymptotic estimate for the number of maximal triangle-free graphs on $n$ vertices is determined.
why: It resolves a long-standing Erdős problem on enumerating a fundamental extremal graph class, and any answer would sharpen our understanding of how triangle-freeness and maximality interact at the counting level.

title: Why Donaldson's Four-Six Conjecture
open: What is the origin and motivation of Donaldson's "four-six" conjecture, asserting that two closed symplectic 4-manifolds $(X_1,\omega_1)$ and $(X_2,\omega_2)$ are diffeomorphic if and only if $(X_1\times S^2,\omega_1\oplus\omega)$ is deformation-equivalent to $(X_2\times S^2,\omega_2\oplus\omega)$, where $\omega$ is a symplectic structure on $S^2$ and deformation-equivalence means a diffeomorphism $\phi:X_1\times S^2\to X_2\times S^2$ such that $\omega_1\oplus\omega$ and $\phi^*(\omega_2\oplus\omega)$ can be joined by a path of symplectic forms? In particular, where did Donaldson make this claim, what motivated it, and are there good examples where it holds?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 2 answers). The question notes that the reference where the asker read the conjecture contained no background or original source, and that Ivan Smith's examples show failure of the analogous statement with $\mathbb{T}^2$ in place of $S^2$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/112417/why-donaldsons-four-six-conjecture
solved_when: The original source where Donaldson stated the conjecture is identified, together with a clear account of his motivation and examples supporting it (or, beyond the sourcing question, a proof or counterexample to the conjecture itself).
why: Understanding the source and motivation would clarify why stabilization by $S^2$ should be special: Ivan Smith showed through examples that the conjecture fails when $S^2$ is replaced by $\mathbb{T}^2$, so the statement is quite rigid.

title: Randomly switching street lights, in a square city
open: In an $N\times N$ city of streets with a light at each crossroads, initially lit according to a given subset $E\subset(1,\ldots,N)\times(1,\ldots,N)$, $2N$ kids each flip one on/off switch placed at the end of a street: what is the distribution of the number $K$ of lit lights, over all $4^N$ switch configurations, as a probability measure on $(1,2,\ldots,N^2)$ depending on $E$? A further target, flagged in an edit, is to compute the upper edge of this distribution.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 1 answers); an edit dated Jan 20 notes that Joseph O'Rourke, in his answer below, signaled the sub-question of computing the upper edge of the distribution.
solved_when: An explicit description (exact law, or sharp asymptotics) of $K$ as a probability measure on $\{1,\ldots,N^2\}$ is given for arbitrary initial sets $E$, together with a determination of the upper edge of the distribution.
why: The answer characterizes how local toggle operations aggregate into a global occupancy statistic, a prototype for similar combinatorics-probability questions; it is also a long-tail problem with demonstrated community interest.

title: Minimizing the excursion of a sum of unit vectors
open: Given $n$ unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ summing to zero, placed head to tail to form a closed polygon, how small can the maximum distance of any vertex from the origin be made by reordering the vectors? Formally: does there exist a constant $r_{\min}$, independent of $n$, such that every zero-sum sequence of unit vectors admits a permutation whose partial sums all lie within the origin-centered ball of radius $r_{\min}$, or must the optimal radius grow with $n$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 1 answer), where the problem is posed with the example of 12 cuboctahedron-derived vectors whose wanderings range from $\sqrt{10}$ down to $\sqrt{3}$ depending on ordering. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/105065/minimizing-the-excursion-of-a-sum-of-unit-vectors
solved_when: Either a universal constant $r_{\min}$ is proved to suffice for all $n$, or a construction is given of zero-sum unit-vector families in $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose every ordering forces an excursion growing without bound (e.g., at least some explicit function of $n$); the natural criterion absent stated quantitative targets is a sharp bound or a separation between the constant and growing cases.
why: It asks whether a closed unit-step polygon can always be reassembled to stay near its starting point — a basic combinatorial-geometric control question; a positive answer gives a universal rerouting tool, while a negative answer exhibits configurations that force unavoidable drift.

title: Covering the primes by arithmetic progressions
open: What is the largest integer $L$ such that the odd primes can be written as an exact union of arithmetic progressions, each of length at least $L$? Formally, with length defined as $\min_i |A_i|$ over the covering family and $L_{\max}$ the maximum over all exact covers of $P'$, the question is to determine $L_{\max}$, given that $L_{\max} \ge 2$ via the pairing of twin primes such as $\{3,5\}, \{521,523\}, \ldots$, while covers with all progressions of length $\ge 3$ (e.g. $\{3,11,19\} \cup \{5,17,29,41,53\} \cup \cdots$) remain out of reach.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 1 answers). The record notes $L_{\max} \ge 2$ via an exact cover of the primes excluding 2 by pairs such as $\{3,5\}, \{7,11\}, \ldots, \{521,523\}, \ldots$, that progressions of length $\ge 3$ cannot be gotten far with, and that Green–Tao establishes the existence of arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of primes.
solved_when: The exact value of $L_{\max}$ is determined, or equivalently a proof or disproof that the primes excluding 2 admit an exact cover by arithmetic progressions all of length at least 3.
why: It probes how finely the additive structure of the primes can be decomposed; a cover with long progressions would go beyond what pairwise (twin-prime-style) coverings give, while a negative answer would show such structure cannot exist.

title: Topological version of Bogomolov’s question
open: Does every closed oriented $n$-manifold $X_0$ admit a closed oriented $n$-manifold $X$ mapping to $X_0$ by a map of positive degree, where $X$ can be smoothly fibered over some $Y$ with $\dim(Y) = n - 2$? This is Gromov's topological analogue (posed on p. 753 of his paper *Singularities, Expanders and Topology of Maps*) of Bogomolov's original question on parametrizing complex algebraic manifolds by algebraic manifolds fibred by surfaces.
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow (score 17, 1 answer); Gromov states it without a reference, Bogomolov's original question lacks an easily located source, and the asker reports a possible proof for 3-manifolds. Key link: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/8724/topological-version-of-bogomolov-s-question
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the existence of such an $X$ and map $X \to X_0$ of positive degree for every closed oriented $n$-manifold $X_0$, together with a smooth fibration of $X$ over some base $Y$ of dimension $n - 2$; at minimum, resolution of the cases beyond the 3-manifolds the asker reports handling.
why: A positive answer would let arbitrary manifolds be "modeled," up to positive degree, by manifolds with a rich fibration structure — a topological route to the parametrization phenomena Bogomolov sought for algebraic manifolds; a negative answer would exhibit obstructions to such topological parametrization.

title: Convex bodies with constant maximal section function in odd dimensions
open: Must every convex body in $\mathbb R^n$, for odd $n\ge 3$, whose hyperplane sections of maximal volume have the same volume in every direction be a ball? Formally: if the maximal section function is constant over all directions, is the body necessarily a Euclidean ball in odd dimensions?
status: The counterexample in $\mathbb R^4$ is trivial: for any continuous strictly concave $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ with $f(-1)=f(1)=0$, the body of revolution $Q_f$ given by $y^2+z^2+t^2\le f(x)^2$ has $Q_f$ and $Q_g$ sharing the same maximal sections in every direction if and only if $f$ and $g$ are equimeasurable ($|\{f>t\}|=|\{g>t\}|$ for all $t>0$); since many concave functions are equimeasurable with $\sqrt{1-x^2}$, non-ball examples exist. With extra work similar constructions work in $\mathbb R^n$ for even $n$, though no similarly nice geometric description is known for $n\ge 6$. The problem record is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 1 answer): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/70391/convex-bodies-with-constant-maximal-section-function-in-odd-dimensions.
solved_when: A proof that in every odd dimension $n\ge 3$ any convex body with direction-independent maximal hyperplane section volume is a ball, or an explicit counterexample in some odd dimension.
why: Klee's question (circa 1970) is answered negatively in even dimensions by bodies of revolution, so settling the odd-dimensional case would complete the classification; counterexamples would reveal new non-uniqueness phenomena in convex geometry.

title: Optimal monotone families for the discrete isoperimetric inequality
open: Which monotone family of subsets of an $n$-element set minimizes the edge-boundary $I^p(F)$ under the product measure $\mu_p$, making the discrete isoperimetric inequality $I^p(F) \ge (1/p)\,\mu_p(F)(-\log \mu_p(F))$ tight? Formally, identify the monotone families for which equality (or near-equality) in (IR) is achieved for each $p$ and $n$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem is stated with full background on the edge-boundary $I^p(F)$ and the inequality (IR), which holds for every family $F$ and every $p$ (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/10799/optimal-monotone-families-for-the-discrete-isoperimetric-inequality, score 17, 1 answers).
solved_when: A characterization of the monotone families attaining equality — or the correct extremal value of $I^p(F)$ — is proved for all $n$ and all $p \in (0,1)$.
why: It would complete the discrete analogue of the classical sharp isoperimetric theorem on the cube, pinpointing the exact structure of extremal sets rather than just a lower bound, and would sharpen a tool used throughout Boolean analysis and combinatorics.

title: Normal curvature of Veronese embedding
open: Does the Veronese embedding minimize the maximal normal curvature among all smooth embeddings $\mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{S}^N$? Formally, is the constant $\kappa_n = \sqrt{\tfrac{n-1}{n+1}}$, attained by the Veronese embedding, the smallest possible worst-case normal curvature for any such embedding? The same question can be asked for $\mathbb{C}\mathrm{P}^n$ and $\mathbb{H}\mathrm{P}^n$.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 0 answers); no answer is known. The record notes that $\kappa_n$ can be visualized via the spherical distance $d_n$ between vertices of an inscribed equilateral $n$-simplex in $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$: $\kappa_n$ is the curvature of a spherical (statement truncated in the record). Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/445819/normal-curvature-of-veronese-embedding
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that no smooth embedding $\mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{S}^N$ has maximal normal curvature below $\kappa_n = \sqrt{\tfrac{n-1}{n+1}}$ — the value realized by the Veronese embedding $\mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{S}^{(n+3)\cdot n/2}$, whose induced metric is $2\times$ the canonical metric and which sends geodesics to circles of curvature $\kappa_n$.
why: It would establish a sharp curvature-optimality property for the most classical embedding of projective space, akin to extremal results for the round sphere. The analogous questions for $\mathbb{C}\mathrm{P}^n$ and $\mathbb{H}\mathrm{P}^n$ would extend the picture to the other compact rank-one symmetric spaces.

title: Does $S^4$ have a "symplecto-homeomorphic" structure
open: Does the 4-sphere admit a "symplecto-homeomorphic" structure — charts on $S^4$ equipped with the standard symplectic form on $\mathbb{R}^4$, whose transition maps are homeomorphisms that are $C^0$-limits of symplectomorphisms $(\mathbb{R}^4,\omega_\text{std})\to(\mathbb{R}^4,\omega_\text{std})$? Since $S^4$ cannot be a symplectic manifold (it admits no atlas whose transition maps are symplectomorphisms), and Eliashberg–Gromov showed that a $C^0$-limit of symplectomorphisms that is a diffeomorphism must be a symplectomorphism, this asks for the next best thing where the limiting transition maps are merely homeomorphisms.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 0 answers); the question may have originated from Alan Weinstein, who told it to the poster after conversations concerning symplectic rigidity. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/179898/does-s4-have-a-symplecto-homeomorphic-structure.
solved_when: An explicit construction of such an atlas on $S^4$ is given, or a proof that no such structure exists.
why: It probes the precise boundary of symplectic rigidity: Eliashberg–Gromov rigidity controls $C^0$-limits only when the limit is smooth, so this question tests whether rigidity still constrains topological structures on a manifold that admits no symplectic form at all.

title: Actions on ℍⁿ generated by torsion elements
open: Does there exist, for large $n$, a cocompact properly discontinuous isometric action on $n$-dimensional Lobachevsky space that is generated by elements of finite order? Equivalently, is there a cocompact properly discontinuous action $\Gamma\curvearrowright\mathbb{H}^n$ such that the quotient space $\mathbb{H}^n/\Gamma$ (the quotient space, not the orbifold) is simply connected?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 0 answers). The record notes that for large $n$ there is no cocompact action generated by reflections (Vinberg, 1984). A candidate source of actions is the group of integer-coefficient matrices over $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{5}]$ preserving the quadratic form $\tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\cdot x_0^2-x_1^2-\cdots-x_n^2$, which yields a cocompact properly discontinuous isometric action $\Gamma\curvearrowright\mathbb{H}^n$; for $n=2$ this $\Gamma$ contains the Coxeter group of the regular right-angled pentagon. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/102644/actions-on-%e2%84%8d%e2%81%bf-generated-by-torsion-elements
solved_when: A construction is given of a cocompact properly discontinuous isometric action $\Gamma\curvearrowright\mathbb{H}^n$ for large $n$ whose group $\Gamma$ is generated by torsion elements (equivalently, with $\mathbb{H}^n/\Gamma$ simply connected as a quotient space), or a proof that no such action exists.
why: It probes how far torsion can generate arithmetic hyperbolic lattices beyond the classical reflection case, which is known to fail in large dimensions; an answer would clarify the structural limits of torsion in cocompact hyperbolic group actions.

title: Special values of Artin L-functions
open: Should Stark's conjectural interpretation of the leading coefficient of an Artin L-function at $s=0$ as a regulator admit a formulation that genuinely "picks out the $\rho$-isotypical bit" of the units $\mathcal{O}_F^\times$ in the best possible way? Formally, for a Galois extension $F/K$ of number fields and an Artin representation $\rho$ factoring through $\operatorname{Gal}(F/K)$, can one find a natural and correct incarnation of Tate's formulation, given that the intuitive $\rho$-isotypical interpretation of units runs into various problems?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 17, 0 answers); the question is posed with the self-acknowledged caveat that it may push the "best possible world" heuristic too far. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/41358/special-values-of-artin-l-functions
solved_when: A formulation is given that realizes the leading coefficient $c(\rho)$ of the Taylor expansion of $L(F/K,\rho,s)$ at $s=0$ as the volume of a canonical $\rho$-isotypical component of $\mathcal{O}_F^\times$, overcoming the known obstructions to the naive intuition.
