why: It would sharpen Stark's conjecture into a precise structural statement about units, potentially unlocking refinements (such as Stark units and explicit class field theory) that the current formulation only suggests heuristically.

title: Smallest area shape that covers all unit length curve
open: In the Euclidean plane, what is the minimum-area region S such that every curve of unit length can be covered by some rigid motion (translation and rotation) of S? If the exact value remains out of reach, what are the best upper and lower bounds on this area?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 16 and 6 answers (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/32477/smallest-area-shape-that-covers-all-unit-length-curve); the original asker reports being told years earlier that the problem is open and could find no reference, and did not know which branch of mathematics it belongs to.
solved_when: The minimal area of such a universal cover S is determined (or tight matching upper and lower bounds are established).
why: This is a planar analogue of the universal cover / Kakeya-type covering problem; settling it would give a sharp answer to how much area is necessary to contain every unit-length curve up to rigid motion.

title: A conjecture by Euler about $8n+3$
open: Is every integer of the form $8n+3$ expressible as $(2k-1)^2 + 2p$ for some positive integer $k$ and prime $p$, as Euler conjectured? In other words, does every $8n+3$ equal an odd square plus twice a prime?
status: The problem appears as a community-vetted open problem on MathOverflow (score 16, 2 answers), where it was asked whether any progress or references exist; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/135608/a-conjecture-by-euler-about-8n3. No resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof or disproof is given that for every positive integer $n$ there exist a positive integer $k$ and a prime $p$ with $8n+3=(2k-1)^2+2p$.
why: It is a natural Euler-type additive prime problem lying outside the standard lists of open questions, and resolving it would clarify how primes distribute relative to odd squares in a specific quadratic residue class.

title: Kaplansky's 6th conjecture: dim(Irrep) | dim(algebra) - for semi-simple Hopf algebras
open: Let $H$ be a semisimple Hopf algebra. Must the dimension of every irreducible $H$-module divide the dimension of $H$, as Kaplansky's sixth conjecture asserts, and for which classes of Hopf algebras is this divisibility already known to hold?
status: The problem is community-curated and vetted on MathOverflow, where it has score 16 and 3 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/108404/kaplanskys-6th-conjecture-dimirrep-dimalgebra-for-semi-simple-hopf-alg); no resolution is recorded there.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the conjecture: for every semisimple Hopf algebra $H$, the dimension of any irreducible $H$-module divides $\dim(H)$.
why: The conjecture is a basic structural constraint on representation theory of semisimple Hopf algebras, analogous to familiar divisibility phenomena for finite groups; settling it would clarify how group-like the representation theory of such algebras must be.

title: Is the Steiner ratio Gilbert–Pollak conjecture still open
open: Is the Gilbert–Pollak conjecture on the Steiner ratio in the Euclidean plane still open — namely, is the infimum of the ratio between the length of a Steiner minimum tree and that of a minimum spanning tree over all finite point sets equal to $\sqrt{3}/2$?
status: Gilbert and Pollak conjectured $\rho = \sqrt{3}/2$. A proof by D. Z. Du and F. K. Hwang in 1990 was reportedly disproved by N. Innami et al. ("The Steiner Ratio Conjecture of Gilbert..."), leaving the conjecture unresolved; the question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 2 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/144081/is-the-steiner-ratio-gilbert-pollak-conjecture-still-open
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\rho = \inf_P L_s(P)/L_m(P) = \sqrt{3}/2$ for all finite point sets $P$ in the Euclidean plane, where $L_s(P)$ and $L_m(P)$ are the lengths of the Steiner minimum tree and minimum spanning tree on $P$, respectively.
why: Resolving it settles the fundamental gap between optimal Steiner-tree networks and ordinary spanning trees in the plane, a benchmark question in combinatorial optimization and geometric network design.

title: Does the image of the exponential map generate the group
open: Let $G$ be a connected Fréchet-Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Does the image $\exp(\mathfrak g) \subset G$ of the exponential map generate $G$ as a group?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 1 answer); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/281356/does-the-image-of-the-exponential-map-generate-the-group.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that for every connected Fréchet-Lie group $G$, the subgroup generated by $\exp(\mathfrak g)$ equals $G$; or an explicit connected Fréchet-Lie group where it does not.
why: For finite-dimensional Lie groups the analogous statement is classical, so this pins down how far the standard Lie theory survives in infinite dimensions, where diffeomorphism groups and other Fréchet-Lie groups arise naturally.

title: Is it known how the Sigma Algebra generated by Jordan measurable sets compares to universally measur
open: Where does the sigma algebra $\sigma(J)$ generated by the Jordan measurable sets sit relative to the analytic sets and, relatedly, relative to the universally measurable sets? Formally, does every analytic set belong to $\sigma(J)$, and does every set in $\sigma(J)$ belong to the class of universally measurable sets?
status: In a 1993 journal paper, K.G. Johnson showed that the Borel sigma algebra is a proper subset of $\sigma(J)$, which is a proper subset of the Lebesgue sigma algebra, and that a set is in $\sigma(J)$ if and only if it can be written as a union of a Borel set and a subset of a measure $0$ $F_\sigma$ set. Johnson stated he did not know where $\sigma(J)$ stands relative to the analytic sets or relative to the universally measurable sets. The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 2 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/315051/is-it-known-how-the-sigma-algebra-generated-by-jordan-measurable-sets-compares-t.
solved_when: The inclusion relations between $\sigma(J)$, the analytic sets, and the universally measurable sets are determined (in both directions, as applicable).
why: It would complete Johnson's picture of $\sigma(J)$, which already places it strictly between the Borel and Lebesgue sigma algebras, and settle whether the Jordan-generated sigma algebra captures any of the descriptive-set-theoretic hierarchy beyond Borel.

title: Is the Gromov conjecture still open
open: Is Gromov's conjecture on minimal volume still open — namely, that every closed simply connected odd-dimensional manifold has minimal volume $\min{\rm Vol}(M)=0$, where $\min{\rm Vol}(M):=\inf_{|K_g|\leq1}\{{\rm Vol}(M,g)\}$? An answer might also provide an illustrative example for the conjecture or explain whether Ricci flow methods can be brought to bear on it.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 2 answers). Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/251996/is-the-gromov-conjecture-still-open
solved_when: The conjecture is settled (proved or disproved) for all closed simply connected odd-dimensional manifolds, or a concrete example illustrating the conjecture / an explanation of how Ricci flow applies is supplied.
why: It concerns a long-tail, community-vetted problem of high interest that sits outside standard problem lists; settling it would advance understanding of the relationship between curvature bounds, volume, and the topology of odd-dimensional simply connected manifolds.

title: Diameter of universal cover
open: How much can the universal cover of a compact Riemannian manifold stretch in diameter? Formally, for a Riemannian manifold $M$ with universal cover $\tilde M$ (given the induced metric), what upper bounds can be given for $k=\mathop{diam}\tilde M/\mathop{diam} M$ in terms of $m=|\pi_1(M)|$ (or in terms of the group $\pi_1(M)$ itself)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 5 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/8534/diameter-of-universal-cover. The cover question for non-universal covers has been answered, but the universal-cover case remains open; constructions in the answers give $k\sim n$ for $\pi_1=\mathbb Z_{3\cdot 2^n}$ and $k$ of order $n^2$ for $\pi_1=S_n$, still $o(\log^2 m)$.
solved_when: A sharp bound on $k$ in terms of $m$ (or $\pi_1(M)$) is established. The naive bound $k\leqslant m$ is known, while $k\ll m$ is expected; the problem is open even for $\pi_1=\mathbb Z_m$, where even the correct asymptotics of $\sup k$ are unknown. Known constructions: $k\sim n$ (i.e. $k=O(\log m)$) for $\pi_1=\mathbb Z_{3\cdot 2^n}$, and $k$ of order $n^2$ for $\pi_1=S_n$ — much larger than $\log m$ but still $k=o(\log^2 m)$. Even the question of whether $\sup k$ for a given finite group $\Gamma=\pi_1(M)$ is an interesting group invariant is unresolved.
why: The ratio $k$ measures how geometrically inefficient a manifold's fundamental group is at "folding" its cover, and its asymptotics separate candidate bounds like $\log m$ from $\log^2 m$; determining them would also decide whether $\sup k$ is a meaningful invariant of finite groups.

title: Tiling the square with rectangles of small diagonals
open: For a given integer $k\ge3$, can the unit square always be tiled with $k$ rectangles so that the longest rectangle diagonal is as short as possible? Formally, in such an optimal tiling, must the sides of all rectangles be rational and their diagonals all equal? The analogous question for tiling the $n$-dimensional cube with rectangular boxes can be asked for every $n\ge3$.
status: Community-curated problem on MathOverflow (score 16, 2 answers); the solved cases consist of squares $k$ and a few small values, all unpublished. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/137287/tiling-the-square-with-rectangles-of-small-diagonals
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that in every optimal tiling of the unit square with $k$ rectangles, all rectangle sides are rational and all diagonals are equal — for general $k\ge3$, or analogously for tilings of the $n$-cube with rectangular boxes for $n\ge3$.
why: The solutions are obvious only in the easy cases when $k$ is the square of an integer and a few small values of $k$ (unpublished), and in each solved case the rational-sides, equal-diagonals pattern holds; confirming this pattern would give a complete structural characterization of optimal tilings, while a counterexample would reveal genuinely new geometry.

title: $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ Casson invariant
open: Is there a Casson-type invariant of a homology 3-sphere defined by counting representations of the fundamental group into $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$, analogous to Casson's original invariant counting $\operatorname{SU}(2)$ representations? Formally, such an invariant would be built from a Heegaard splitting, intersecting the representation varieties of the two handlebodies inside the representation variety of the Heegaard surface, perturbed to transversality.
status: Asked on MathOverflow (community-curated, score 16, 2 answers). Casson's original invariant counts $\operatorname{SU}(2)$ representations after perturbing to transversality; Curtis has an analogous invariant counting representations into $\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, counting only the finite points of intersection, using algebraic geometry to resolve singularities and ignoring higher-dimensional components; both must then show independence of choices. No analogous $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ invariant is established in the record. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/16410/operatornamesl-2-mathbb-r-casson-invariant
solved_when: A well-defined invariant of homology 3-spheres is constructed via the Heegaard-splitting intersection count of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ representation varieties, with the construction handling non-transverse and higher-dimensional components of the intersection and proving invariance under the choices involved (Heegaard splitting, perturbation).
why: It would extend the Casson program to a real Lie group where the geometry of the representation varieties is harder to control, potentially yielding a new invariant sensitive to hyperbolic and $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$-related structure on 3-manifolds.

title: Who conjectured the Cartan determinant conjecture
open: Who first stated the Cartan determinant conjecture — that every finite dimensional algebra of finite global dimension has Cartan determinant equal to one — and how old is the conjecture? Here the Cartan matrix has entries $c_{i,j}$ given by the dimension of $\mathrm{Hom}_A(P_i, P_j)$ over the division ring $D_i = \mathrm{End}_A(S_i)$, where $P_i$ are the indecomposable projective modules and $S_i$ the simple modules occurring as their tops.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question has a score of 16 and 1 answer (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/279920/who-conjectured-the-cartan-determinant-conjecture).
solved_when: A source identifying the originator of the Cartan determinant conjecture and the date of its first statement is produced and verified.
why: The problem concerns attribution and history rather than mathematics, but resolving it gives the community accurate provenance for a widely referenced conjecture in the representation theory of finite dimensional algebras.

title: Is it true that every f.g. infinite simple group has exponential growth
open: Must every finitely generated infinite simple group have exponential word-growth? Equivalently, can such a group have subexponential (in particular intermediate) growth? As Mark Sapir has pointed out, the analogous question of whether every finitely generated group of subexponential growth is residually finite was answered negatively in Anna Erschler, Not residually finite groups of intermediate growth, commensurability and non-geometricity, J. Algebra 272 (2004), no. 1, 154–172, http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021869303006410 — so the residual-finiteness obstruction cannot rule out a simple counterexample here.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 1 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/122199/is-it-true-that-every-f-g-infinite-simple-group-has-exponential-growth . The record notes the related negative result of Anna Erschler, Not residually finite groups of intermediate growth, commensurability and non-geometricity, J. Algebra 272 (2004), no. 1, 154–172, http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021869303006410 , which rules out one route to a positive answer.
solved_when: A proof that every finitely generated infinite simple group has exponential word-growth, or an explicit example of a finitely generated infinite simple group of subexponential growth.
why: A simple group of subexponential growth would be a striking counterexample to the intuition tying simplicity to exponential growth, while a positive answer would sharply delimit the growth spectrum available to infinite simple groups; either outcome advances the theory of groups of intermediate growth.

title: The Sylvester Gallai Theorem and Sections of Varieties with "Simple Topology".
open: Does a Sylvester–Gallai-type phenomenon survive when points are replaced by algebraic varieties? Given a k-dimensional real algebraic variety V (perhaps of some restricted class) embedded in n-dimensional affine space and spanning it, is there an affine r-dimensional linear space L such that V ∩ L spans L and is topologically "simple"?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 16 and 3 answers. The questioner notes that for smooth complex varieties the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem describes something like the opposite phenomenon: the homology of a hyperplane section is, more or less, as complicated as the homology of the original manifold in low degrees. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/4661/the-sylvester-gallai-theorem-and-sections-of-varieties-with-simple-topology
solved_when: A proof (or construction, for suitable classes of varieties) exhibiting, for such a spanning k-dimensional real algebraic variety V in affine n-space, an affine r-plane L with V ∩ L spanning L and having the specified "simple" topology; or a counterexample showing no such section need exist.
why: A positive answer would give a genuinely geometric higher-dimensional analogue of the Sylvester–Gallai theorem and reveal which varieties admit sections that are simultaneously spanning and topologically trivial, informing how topological complexity of a variety constrains its linear projections and sections.

title: An open problem in convex geometry
open: Do there exist four norms on the plane such that no three-dimensional normed space contains subspaces isometric to all four of these normed planes? Equivalently, are there four $0$-symmetric convex planar bodies for which no three-dimensional $0$-symmetric convex body has four central sections, each linearly equivalent to one of them?
status: The problem was posted on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated (score 16, 0 answers); the poster reports it seems old but is unsure of its origin, with the earliest reference found being Rolewicz, S., Plane sections of centrally symmetric convex bodies. Israel J. Math. 4 1966 135–138, and notes that Bessaga proved (C. Bessaga, A note on universal Banach spaces of a finite dimension, Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. 6 (1958), 97–101.) a related result for $n > 2$. No answer resolving the problem is recorded.
solved_when: Either an explicit example of four planar norms (or four $0$-symmetric planar convex bodies) with the stated property is given, or it is proved that for any four planar norms there is a three-dimensional normed space containing isometric copies of all four.
why: A solution would clarify how strongly finite-dimensional normed spaces can be universal for lower-dimensional ones, a basic question at the interface of convex geometry and the isometric theory of Banach spaces.

title: Comparing the Kazhdan-Lusztig and Steinberg pre-orders
open: Do the Kazhdan–Lusztig pre-orders on the symmetric group $S_n$ coincide with Steinberg's geometric pre-orders? Formally, Kazhdan and Lusztig define $x\leq_L y$ if any left ideal spanned by K-L basis vectors which contains $C_y$ also contains $C_x$ (and dually $x\leq_R y$ for right ideals, with $x\leq_L y$ iff $x^{-1}\leq_R y^{-1}$), while Steinberg's geometric version, with $\mathfrak{n}$ the strictly upper-triangular matrices in $\mathfrak{sl}_n$, sets $x\leq_l y$ if $B\cdot(\mathfrak{n}\cap\mathfrak{n}^y)\subset B\cdot(\mathfrak{n}\cap\mathfrak{n}^x)$ and $x\leq_r y$ if $x^{-1}\leq_l y^{-1}$: the question is whether $\leq_L$ and $\leq_l$ (equivalently $\leq_R$ and $\leq_r$) define the same pre-orders.
status: Community-curated question on MathOverflow (score 16) with 0 answers; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/53534/comparing-the-kazhdan-lusztig-and-steinberg-pre-orders.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that the Kazhdan–Lusztig pre-order $\leq_L$ and the Steinberg geometric pre-order $\leq_l$ coincide or differ on $S_n$.
why: A positive answer would connect the algebraic structure of the Hecke-algebra basis directly to the orbit geometry of the nilradical, tying representation-theoretic and geometric orderings of the symmetric group into one framework.

title: Finite Rank Commutators
open: Is there an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ on which every finite-rank commutator in $L(X)$ has zero trace? Equivalently, does there exist such an $X$ for which no nonzero-trace finite-rank operator $T$ can be written as $T = AB - BA$ with $A, B \in L(X)$, even though all zero-trace finite-rank operators are classically known to be commutators? A companion question asks for conditions on $X$ that guarantee every finite-rank operator in $L(X)$ is a commutator.
status: Posed by the asker with his former student Detelin Dosev, who have a joint paper (available on the asker's home page and the ArXiv) on classifying commutators in $L(X)$. It is classical that every zero-trace finite-rank operator in $L(X)$ is a commutator, and the converse holds trivially in finite dimensions; whether the conjectured infinite-dimensional example exists is open, with the asker noting it would be very hard to prove but might be known to be false. The record is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 16, 0 answers).
solved_when: An infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ is exhibited in which all finite-rank commutators in $L(X)$ have zero trace (or the conjecture is refuted); progress may alternatively consist of characterizing those $X$ for which all finite-rank operators in $L(X)$ are commutators.
why: It would separate the finite-dimensional intuition — where commutators are exactly the zero-trace operators — from the infinite-dimensional setting, giving the first classification of finite-rank commutators on a genuinely infinite-dimensional space.

title: Do torsion-free groups give projectionless group ($C^\ast$) algebras
open: If $G$ is a torsion-free group, must the reduced group $C^\ast$-algebra $C_r^\ast(G)$ be projectionless? Formally: is it the case that $C_r^\ast(G)$ has no projections other than $0$ and $1$ whenever $G$ is torsion-free, and correspondingly, is the group algebra $C[G]$ projectionless?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow with a score of 15 and 2 answers. Known examples support the question: $C_r^\ast(\mathbb{Z}) \cong C(S^1)$ is projectionless by the Gelfand transform, and for free groups $F_n$ with $n \geq 2$ a proof exists but is fairly complicated (see Davidson's book for $n = 2$). Torsion-free is a necessary hypothesis, since torsion elements produce projections.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that for every torsion-free group $G$, the reduced group $C^\ast$-algebra $C_r^\ast(G)$ — or at least the group algebra $C[G]$ — is projectionless, with torsion-freeness known to be necessary since groups with torsion yield projections.
why: Many projectionless $C^\ast$-algebras exist, but knowing exactly which group $C^\ast$-algebras are projectionless would clarify a fundamental structural divide between $C^\ast$-algebras and the von Neumann algebras they generate, which always contain nontrivial projections.

title: Does listing the prime factors always stop
open: Take a natural number, list its prime factors in increasing order with repetition according to multiplicity, concatenate their decimal (or any-base) representations to form a new number, and repeat. Does this process always terminate at a prime, regardless of the starting value?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 3 answers); the record gives no resolution. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/31406/does-listing-the-prime-factors-always-stop
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every natural number input, and in any base, the iterative concatenation of the ordered prime factorization eventually reaches a prime number.
why: This is a natural, easy-to-state question about integer dynamics whose behavior is completely uncharacterized; an answer would illuminate how multiplicative structure interacts with decimal (and other base) representation.

title: What is known about Ulam's problem of metric spaces with isometric squares
open: If the Cartesian squares of two metric spaces are isometric (under the Euclidean product metric), must the spaces themselves be isometric? In general no — but for which restricted classes of metric spaces does this implication hold?
status: The general question has a negative answer: $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}\sqrt{2}$ (rational multiples of $\sqrt{2}$) are not isometric, yet their squares are, via rotation by $\frac{\pi}{4}$ (proof at http://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1971-029-03/S0002-9939-1971-0278262-5/S0002-9939-1971-0278262-5.pdf). The question was posed as a community-curated MathOverflow thread (score 15, 2 answers) asking for the status on less general metric spaces (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/77446/what-is-known-about-ulams-problem-of-metric-spaces-with-isometric-squares); the record states no further partial results.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the metric spaces $A$ and $B$ for which isometry of $A^2$ and $B^2$ (with $d((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)) = \sqrt{d(x_1,x_2)^2 + d(y_1,y_2)^2}$) forces $A$ and $B$ to be isometric, including answers for the restricted cases raised in the question.
why: It would resolve Ulam's question from *Problems in Modern Mathematics* beyond the known counterexamples, clarifying when a metric space is determined by its squares.

title: The determinant of the sum of normal matrices
open: Given two normal matrices $A,B\in M_n({\mathbb C})$ with spectra $(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n})$ and $(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{n})$, must $\det(A+B)$ always lie in the convex hull of the numbers $\prod_{i=1}^n(\alpha_i+\beta_{\sigma(i)})$ as $\sigma$ ranges over all permutations in ${\mathfrak S}_n$? The analogous statement for traces is known: $\mathrm{tr}(AB)$ belongs to the convex hull of the numbers $\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_{j}\beta_{\sigma(j)}$, $\sigma\in{\mathfrak S}_n$.
status: Community-curated open problem on MathOverflow (score 15, 1 answer). The trace analogue is known (Exercise 101). No solution is recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/42902/the-determinant-of-the-sum-of-normal-matrices
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) settles, for all $n$ and all pairs of normal matrices, whether $\det(A+B)$ lies in the convex hull of $\{\prod_{i=1}^n(\alpha_i+\beta_{\sigma(i)}) : \sigma\in{\mathfrak S}_n\}$.
why: A positive answer would extend the classical majorization-type relation between spectra and traces of products of normal matrices to determinants, giving a sharp description of how eigenvalues constrain the determinant of a sum.

title: Optimal inspection path on a sphere
open: Suppose you must inspect every point of a unit sphere $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ by walking along a path $\gamma$ on $S$, but you can only see a distance $d$ from where you stand: for a given $d \in (0,\pi]$, what are the shortest such paths $\gamma(d)$? Formally, this asks for the shortest curve $\gamma$ on $S$ such that every point of $S$ lies within distance $d$ of some point of $\gamma$ — equivalently, the union of disks of radius $d$ centered on $\gamma$ covers $S$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 3 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/130255/optimal-inspection-path-on-a-sphere. The case $d \in [\pi/2,\pi]$ is settled, and it is suggested that as $d$ approaches zero the optimal path may be a type of spiral, but the small-$d$ regime remains open.
solved_when: The shortest covering path $\gamma(d)$ is determined (explicitly described) for every $d \in (0,\pi]$, including its precise length. For $d \in [\pi/2,\pi]$, $\gamma(d)$ is known to be an arc of a great circle of length $2\pi - 2d$ (a single point for $d = \pi$, an arc of length $\pi/2$ for $d = 3\pi/4$, a semicircle for $d = \pi/2$); the remaining regime $d \in (0, \pi/2)$ — conjecturally some type of spiral as $d$ approaches zero — must also be settled.
why: This is a natural geometric optimization question about covering a sphere by a tubular neighborhood of a curve, with high community interest as a long-tail problem outside standard problem lists; a solution would complete the picture of how the optimal inspection path transitions from great-circle arcs to spiraling curves.

title: Card game / options pricing / Brownian bridge question
open: In the classic red–black card-stopping game (a shuffled deck is dealt face up; you may stop at any time and receive one dollar per red card dealt minus one dollar per black card dealt), what is the optimal stopping strategy and the fair price of the game? Formally, with $r$ red and $b$ black cards remaining and value function $f_{r,b}$, determine the optimal policy and $f_{r,b}$ — and, per the original question, its connection to options pricing and Brownian-bridge analogues.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question has score 15 and 3 answers.
solved_when: A complete characterization of the optimal stopping rule and the exact expected value $f_{r,b}$ for the game (equivalently, a closed-form or effectively computable answer to the posted question) is given.
why: The game is a canonical discrete optimal-stopping problem bridging combinatorics, options pricing, and Brownian bridge limits; a clean solution would illuminate all three.

title: Is a smooth closed surface in Euclidean 3-space rigid
open: Is every smooth closed surface in Euclidean 3-space rigid under isometric deformations? A classical theorem of Cohn-Vossen shows this for closed convex surfaces, and Robert Connelly exhibited a polyhedral surface that can be deformed isometrically — the question is whether an arbitrary not-necessarily-convex smooth closed surface is necessarily rigid, or whether a smooth version of Connelly's flexible example can be constructed. It's easy to make smooth "hinges"; the real challenge is finding a smooth model of the vertices, where two or more hinges meet.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/1975/is-a-smooth-closed-surface-in-euclidean-3-space-rigid.
solved_when: Either a proof that every smooth closed surface in Euclidean 3-space is rigid (admits no nontrivial isometric deformation) is given, or an explicit smooth closed surface in Euclidean 3-space is constructed that admits a nontrivial isometric deformation.
why: It would settle whether flexibility, known for polyhedral surfaces since Connelly's example (a metal hinged model of which can be found at IHES), survives smoothing — the natural bridge between the polyhedral and smooth rigidity theories.

title: An infinite, amenable, finitely presentable group with no non-trivial finite quotients
open: Does there exist an infinite, amenable, finitely presentable group with no non-trivial finite quotients? Formally: is there a group that is simultaneously infinite, amenable, and finitely presentable, yet admits no surjection onto any non-trivial finite group?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 1 answers). Without finite presentability, Juschenko–Monod's construction gives a finitely generated, infinite, simple, amenable group. The asker notes that all standard known examples of finitely presentable groups without finite quotients appear to be non-amenable, and conjectures the question is open. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/156076/an-infinite-amenable-finitely-presentable-group-with-no-non-trivial-finite-quo
solved_when: An explicit example of an infinite, amenable, finitely presentable group with no non-trivial finite quotients is given; alternatively, a proof that no such group exists.
why: It would be the first finitely presentable amenable "monster" of its kind, showing finite presentability is compatible with amenability and trivial profinite completion; non-existence would reveal a deep structural obstruction linking finite presentability, amenability, and residual finiteness.

title: Strengthening of Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture: An algebraic approach
open: Is there a weighted strengthening of Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture of the following algebraic form? Given a union-closed family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ and real numbers $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\geq 1$, does there exist some $k\in[n]$ (possibly depending on the choice of the $x_i$) such that $$\sum_{k\in A,\,A\in \mathcal F}\prod_{i\in A}x_i\;\ge\;x_k\sum_{k\notin A,\,A\in \mathcal F}\prod_{i\in A}x_i?$$ For $x_i=1$ for all $i$, this asserts that some element $k$ is contained in at least as many sets of $\mathcal F$ as it is omitted from, which is exactly Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture; the conjecture is trivially true for the full power set of $[n]$, where both sides equal $x_k\prod_{i\neq k}(x_i+1)$ for every $k$. An analogous intersection-closed formulation can also be considered.
status: This problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 2 answers) and originates from the post "Strengthening of Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture: An algebraic approach" at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/481791/strengthening-of-frankls-union-closed-sets-conjecture-an-algebraic-approach; it remains open as stated there.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) of the stated weighted inequality for every union-closed family $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ and every choice of real weights $x_1,\dots,x_n\geq 1$; in the unweighted case $x_i=1$, this reduces to proving Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture itself.
why: A proof would yield a strictly stronger, algebraic form of one of the most famous open problems in extremal combinatorics, with Frankl's conjecture as an immediate corollary; a disproof would delimit exactly how far the union-closed principle can be pushed beyond counting arguments.

title: Amenability of groups in terms of a perturbation condition
open: If a countable group $G$ satisfies a quantitative commutant-approximation inequality — namely, there is a constant $C>0$ such that for every bounded operator $T \in B(\ell^2 G)$ the distance from $T$ to the commutant $\lambda(G)'$ is bounded by $C$ times $\sup_{g\in G}\|\lambda(g)T - T\lambda(g)\|$, where $\lambda\colon G \to U(\ell^2 G)$ is the left-regular representation — must $G$ be amenable?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 1 answers). The question notes the forward implication is fairly easy — amenability yields the inequality via a conjugation fixed point — and asks for the converse; the asker also clarified its relation to a version of the derivation problem raised in the comments. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/51680/amenability-of-groups-in-terms-of-a-perturbation-condition
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that the stated inequality for some constant $C>0$ holds if and only if $G$ is amenable. The amenability direction is already known: a fixed point of the conjugation action on $\overline{\rm conv}\{\lambda(g)T\lambda(g)^* \mid g \in G\}$ witnesses the inequality; the open part is the converse.
why: It would give a purely operator-algebraic, quantitative characterization of amenability via the left-regular representation, and it is closely tied to the derivation problem (the inequality holds for some $C$ if and only if the first bounded c... as noted in the original discussion).

title: Open bilinear maps that are not uniformly open
open: Does there exist a continuous, surjective bilinear map between Banach spaces that is open but not uniformly open? Here a map $f\colon X\to Y$ is uniformly open when for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $B_Y(f(x),\delta)\subseteq f(B_X(x,\varepsilon))$ for all $x\in X$ — a strictly stronger condition than mere openness.
status: This is a community-curated MathOverflow question (score 15, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/270616/open-bilinear-maps-that-are-not-uniformly-open. Known background from the record: uniformly open maps are surjective whenever the codomain is connected; the exponential function is open but not uniformly open; continuous surjective bilinear maps between Banach spaces need not be open — matrix multiplication gives an example, and Fremlin showed multiplication in $C[0,1]$ over the real scalars is another. Whether a continuous, surjective, open-but-not-uniformly-open bilinear map exists remains unanswered.
solved_when: An explicit example of a continuous, surjective, bilinear map between Banach spaces is produced that is open but not uniformly open, or a proof is given that every continuous, surjective, open bilinear map between Banach spaces is uniformly open.
why: Uniformly open maps are automatically surjective when the codomain is connected, so separating openness from uniform openness for bilinear maps clarifies how far the strong linearity-based openness theory extends to multilinear settings, where it already fails (continuous surjective bilinear maps need not be open at all).

title: Prime divisors of numbers 2^n + 3
open: Do infinitely many primes $p$ exist for which $p^2$ divides $2^n + 3$ for some natural number $n$? The question is a natural test case beyond the polynomial setting, since for any non-constant $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ the analogous statement follows from Hensel's lemma, and a similar result holds for the Fibonacci sequence despite its more complicated closed form.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 2 answers); the problem is community-vetted as open there.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the set of primes $p$ with $p^2 \mid 2^n + 3$ for some natural $n$ is infinite is exhibited.
why: It probes whether Hensel-type lifting of prime divisors extends to non-polynomial sequences; the sequence $a_n = 2^n + 3$ satisfies the recurrence $a_{n+2} = 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n$, and the case of Fibonacci suggests "good" identities may be decisive, so resolving this example clarifies what structures make such results true.

title: Razborov's response to Almost Natural Proofs
open: Has there been any progress on the idea Alexander Razborov proposed for responding to the Natural Proofs barrier by making the largeness condition relative? This was raised in connection with the papers "Amplifying lower bounds by means of self-reducibility" by Eric Allender and Michal Koucký and "Almost-natural proofs" by Timothy Chow, which Razborov mentioned at the end of his talk at the first Barriers Workshop at IAS in 2009.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 0 answers); no answers or progress are recorded there. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/33396/razborovs-response-to-almost-natural-proofs
solved_when: A published development (theoretical or survey-level) directly addressing the relativized largeness condition as a response to the two cited papers is identified and documented.
why: The Natural Proofs barrier blocks the standard routes to circuit lower bounds, and a viable relativized largeness condition would outline a concrete way around it.

title: On Polynomials dividing Exponentials
open: Find all positive integer pairs $(m, n)$ such that $m^2 - 1 \mid 3^m + (n! - 2)^m$, a corrected version (the book's second edition fixed a single mistyped number) of the originally posed $3^m + (n!-1)^m$ variant. More broadly, the question asks whether there exist general techniques for problems in which a polynomial divides an exponential expression, such as the original motivating instance of finding all positive integers $m$ with $m^2 - 1 \mid 3^m + 5^m$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question scored 14 and received 6 answers. No answer to the divisibility question is known: the authors of the book in which it appears confirmed (noted in a 2010 edit by Will Jagy) that they do not know how to solve it. A May 2015 edit records that the book's second edition corrected the problem, a single number having been mistyped, changing the target to $3^m + (n!-2)^m$.
solved_when: A complete characterization of the positive integer pairs $(m,n)$ satisfying $m^2 - 1 \mid 3^m + (n! - 2)^m$ (equivalently, a resolution of the general question for polynomial-versus-exponential divisibility of this type) is given.
why: Resolving it would supply the first general machinery for a whole class of divisibility problems in which polynomials divide exponentials — problems that are plentiful but currently lack any systematic attack.

title: Is there a non-zero ghost map between finite suspension spectra
open: Can a nonzero phantom — a map of spectra that induces the zero map on every stable homotopy group — exist between suspension spectra of finite CW-complexes? Formally, if $f=\Sigma^\infty f'$ is a ghost map between $X=\Sigma^\infty A$ and $Y=\Sigma^\infty B$ with $A,B$ finite CW-complexes, must its image $\bar f$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{SH}(X,Y)$ be zero?
status: Community-curated as an open question on MathOverflow (score 14, 1 answer); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof that every ghost map between suspension spectra of finite CW-complexes is zero in the stable homotopy category, or an explicit example of a nonzero one.
why: Ghost maps obstruct the intuition that stable homotopy groups see maps between finite complexes; settling this determines whether finite suspension spectra behave like compact objects with no phantom phenomena.

title: Are acyclic subcomplexes of finite contractible 2-complexes contractible
open: Is every acyclic subcomplex of a finite contractible simplicial 2-complex itself contractible — that is, if $Y$ is a contractible finite simplicial 2-complex and $X \subseteq Y$ is connected with $H_1(X)=0$ and $H_2(X)=0$, must $\pi_1(X)$ be trivial? Equivalently: if $m < n$, $G = \langle a_1,\dotsc,a_m \mid r_1 = \dotsb = r_m = 1\rangle$ is a balanced sub-presentation of $J = \langle a_1,\dotsc,a_n \mid r_1 = \dotsb = r_n = 1\rangle$ and $J$ is trivial, is $G$ trivial (given that the abelianization of $G$ is trivial)?
status: The question was asked on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated (score 14) with 2 answers, but remains unanswered.
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, is given for the contractibility of every acyclic subcomplex $X$ (connected, $H_1(X)=0$, $H_2(X)=0$) of any finite contractible simplicial 2-complex $Y$; equivalently, for the triviality of every group $G$ with a balanced presentation extending to a trivial balanced presentation $J$ as above.
why: A positive answer would give a powerful inheritance property for contractibility of 2-complexes, directly constraining which balanced presentations can hide nontrivial groups inside trivial ones; a counterexample would exhibit subtle torsion-free acyclicity in combinatorial group theory.

title: On cubic reciprocity for $x^3+y^3+z^3 = 996$
open: Does the Diophantine equation $x^3+y^3+z^3=3w^3$ with $x\geq y\geq z$ and $w=1$ have any integer solutions beyond the two known ones $(1,1,1)$ and $(4,4,-5)$? Formally, are there larger solutions satisfying the congruence restrictions $x\equiv y\equiv z \bmod 9$ (forced for $w=1$ by Cassels), and analogously, does $x^3+y^3+z^3=996$ — another $N<1000$ observed to obey the same congruence behavior, with known solutions such as $(11,2,-7)$ and $(216936450544, \dots)$ — admit further large solutions?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 14, 1 answer). As Noam Elkies points out in the linked post, Cassels in a 1985 paper showed $w=1$ forces $x\equiv y\equiv z \bmod 9$, and for general $w$, Heath-Brown in a 1992 paper showed either $x\equiv y\equiv z \bmod 9$ or one of $x,y,z$ equals $9m$. Checking the Elsenhans–Jahnel list for $N<1000$ finds large solutions for $w=2,3,4$; the list covers only $10^{14}$, so raising it might reveal a large solution for $w=1$. The asker reports at least two other $N<1000$ obeying $(2)$, including $N=996$ with solutions $(11,2,-7)$ and $(216936450544,\dots)$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/225572/on-cubic-reciprocity-for-x3y3z3-996
solved_when: A larger integer solution of $x^3+y^3+z^3=3$ (i.e. $w=1$) beyond $(1,1,1)$ and $(4,4,-5)$ is exhibited, or it is proved none exists; or, for the related search, a solution of $x^3+y^3+z^3=996$ beyond the listed ones is found, for example by extending the Elsenhans–Jahnel list, which currently covers $|x^3+y^3+z^3|$ searches only up to $10^{14}$.
why: Resolving the existence of larger solutions would clarify how congruence obstructions from cubic reciprocity shape the solution set of $x^3+y^3+z^3=N$, a problem of long-standing interest for which large solutions exist for $w=2,3,4$ but none is yet known for $w=1$.

title: Normal numbers, Liouville function, and the Riemann Hypothesis
open: Is the real number $\lambda^*$, defined via the Liouville function $\lambda(k)=(-1)^{\Omega(k)}$, normal in base 2 — or, more plausibly, is it not normal? Its normality would imply the Riemann Hypothesis, but the question is whether the binary digits of $\lambda^*$ are nonetheless random enough for RH to hold, and it may amount to a tractable probability-theory question.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 14, 1 answer), with the problem statement noting that proving normality of $\lambda^*$ is believed harder than proving RH, since normality already implies RH. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/391736/normal-numbers-liouville-function-and-the-riemann-hypothesis.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\lambda^*$ is normal in base 2 is given; equivalently for the stated intent, a proof that $\lambda^*$ is not normal, ideally with an analysis of how random its binary digits nonetheless are.
why: Normality of $\lambda^*$ would imply RH, so the problem sits directly between probability theory of digit expansions and the Riemann Hypothesis; resolving it would clarify how much pseudorandomness of the Liouville function is needed for RH.

title: Is there any o-minimal expansion of the real field with functions of growth higher than exponential
open: Does there exist an o-minimal expansion of the real field in which a function of super-exponential growth is definable? Formally, letting $\bar{\mathbb{R}} = (\mathbb{R},0,1,+,-,*,<)$ and calling $f$ of growth higher than exponential if for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $r\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\exp^N(x) < f(x)$ for all $x>r$ (where $\exp^N$ denotes the $N$-fold iterate of $\exp$), can one find an o-minimal expansion of $\bar{\mathbb{R}}$ in which such an $f$ is definable?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 14, 1 answer). The record cites the MathOverflow thread at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/121010/is-there-any-o-minimal-expansion-of-the-real-field-with-functions-of-growth-high.
solved_when: An explicit o-minimal expansion of $\bar{\mathbb{R}}$ is given in which some definable $f$ eventually dominates every finite iterate $\exp^N$; or, conversely, a proof is given that no o-minimal expansion of the real field can define such a function.
why: It probes the structural limits of o-minimality itself: all standard o-minimal structures (like $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an,exp}}$) define only functions of at most exponential growth, and the question is whether that is an accident of current constructions or a theorem.

title: Do there exist polynomials of degree and height $M$ taking prime values at $1, 2, \dots, M$
open: For every positive integer $M$, must there exist a nonconstant integer polynomial of degree at most $M$, constant term $1$, and all nonconstant coefficients in $\{0,1,\dots,M\}$, which takes prime values at all of $1,2,\dots,M$? Equivalently, writing $f(x)=1+\sum_{i=1}^M a_i x^i$ with $a_i\in\{0,1,\dots,M\}$ not all zero, is there always such an $f$ with $f(1),f(2),\dots,f(M)\in\mathbb P$? Weaker or asymptotic versions, such as existence for all sufficiently large $M$, are also of interest.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow with a score of 14 and 0 answers; no answer or resolution is recorded. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/512119/do-there-exist-polynomials-of-degree-and-height-m-taking-prime-values-at-1-2
solved_when: For every positive integer $M$ (or, for the asymptotic version, for all sufficiently large $M$), one exhibits a polynomial $f(x)=1+\sum_{i=1}^M a_i x^i$ with $a_i\in\{0,1,\dots,M\}$ not all zero such that $f(1),f(2),\dots,f(M)$ are all prime.
why: A solution would show that severely height-restricted polynomials can still interpolate prime values on arbitrarily long initial segments, a phenomenon lying outside standard prime-producing polynomial constructions.

title: Is it an open problem whether fast-growing hierarchies can be defined without fundamental sequences
open: Can an ordinal hierarchy of fast-growing functions exist without any underlying choice of fundamental sequences? Formally: is there a model of ZF containing a function $F : \omega_1 \rightarrow (\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N})$ such that $F(\alpha)$ eventually outgrows $F(\beta)$ whenever $\alpha > \beta$, yet containing no function $S: \omega_1 \cap \text{Lim} \rightarrow (\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \omega_1)$ assigning to each countable limit ordinal a sequence with supremum $\alpha$?
status: The question, sourced from the Googology Wiki's statement that it is open whether an ordinal hierarchy can be defined without fundamental sequences, was posted on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/345913/is-it-an-open-problem-whether-fast-growing-hierarchies-can-be-defined-without-fu), where it received a score of 14 and no answers.
solved_when: A model of ZF is exhibited (or proved impossible) in which such a strictly increasing hierarchy $F$ on $\omega_1$ exists while no such fundamental-sequence system $S$ exists; the source question additionally asks whether the openness of this problem itself can be confirmed.
why: It probes whether the standard construction of fast-growing hierarchies genuinely depends on fundamental sequences, separating the growth-rate structure from the choice of cofinal approximations.

title: Torsion-freeness of two groups with 2 generators and 3 relators and Kaplansky Zero Divisor Conjectur
open: Are the two groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ given by the presentations $\langle a,b \mid (ab)^2=a^{-1}ba^{-1},\ (a^{-1}ba^{-1})^2=b^{-2}a,\ (ba^{-1})^2=a^{-2}b^2 \rangle$ and $\langle a,b \mid ab=(a^{-1}ba^{-1})^2,\ (b^{-1}ab^{-1})^2=a^{-2}b,\ (ba^{-1})^2=a^{-2}b^2 \rangle$ torsion-free? In both groups, $1+a+b$ is a zero divisor in the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[G_i]$, so a proof that either group is torsion-free would yield a counterexample to the Kaplansky zero divisor conjecture.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/231922/torsion-freeness-of-two-groups-with-2-generators-and-3-relators-and-kaplansky-ze
solved_when: One either proves that $G_1$ or $G_2$ is torsion-free — producing a counterexample to the Kaplansky zero divisor conjecture — or proves that both groups contain torsion, with the explicit zero-divisor relations $(1+a+b)\cdot(\text{the exhibited sums})=0$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[G_i]$ verified.
why: Either outcome is significant: torsion-freeness would refute Kaplansky's zero divisor conjecture, a foundational conjecture in group rings, while exhibiting torsion would close off this concrete family of candidate counterexamples.

title: Pillai's arithmetical function and primality
open: Is it true that $1+P(n)\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ holds exactly when $n$ is prime, where $P(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n \gcd(k,n)$ is Pillai's arithmetical function? In particular, the case of squarefree composite $n$ with more than 3 prime factors remains completely open, and a proof or reference for that case is sought.
status: The equivalence was stated without proof in 2014 on OEIS A018804 and has since been reverted to a conjecture. A recent MathOverflow question (score 13, 1 answer) did not obtain a full proof; the case of squarefree composites with more than 3 factors is completely open. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/496298/pillais-arithmetical-function-and-primality
solved_when: A proof (or refutation, via counterexample) of the equivalence $1+P(n)\equiv 0 \pmod{n} \iff n$ is prime, covering at minimum the open case of squarefree composites with more than 3 factors.
why: It would give a clean, purely gcd-based characterization of primality for Pillai's arithmetical function, resolving a conjecture stated on OEIS A018804 that was later reverted for lack of proof.

title: Kronecker's Jugendtraum for real quadratic fields
open: Kronecker's Jugendtraum (Hilbert's 12th problem) asks for explicit generation of the abelian extensions of an arbitrary number field by adjoining special values of transcendental functions — realized for $\mathbb{Q}$ by Kronecker–Weber ($\mathbb{Q}^{ab}=\mathbb{Q}^{cycl}=\mathbb{Q}(e^{2\pi i \mathbb{Q}})$) and for imaginary quadratic fields by complex multiplication, where roughly $K^{ab}=K(j(\tau), \wp(\tau,z))$ with $\tau$ corresponding to an elliptic curve with complex multiplication by the ring of integers of $K$ and $z \in \Lambda \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ (i.e. adjoining $j(E)$ and the $x$-coordinates of torsion points of $E$). Is there, for real quadratic fields, some class of special analytic functions and some special kind of objects which conjecturally play the role that the $j$-function plays in the imaginary quadratic case?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question is recorded with score 13 and 3 answers.
solved_when: A construction is given that, for real quadratic fields $K$, generates $K^{ab}$ by adjoining special values of an explicit analytic construction, in analogy with the complex-multiplication description for imaginary quadratic fields.
why: It would complete Hilbert's 12th problem for the next natural class of fields beyond $\mathbb{Q}$ and imaginary quadratic fields, giving explicit class field theory where none is currently known.

title: A maximal element, where Schur gives a minimal element
open: Among the functions $d_\chi(S)=\frac{1}{\chi(e)}\sum_{g\in H}\chi(g)\prod_{i=1}^n s_{ig(i)}$ built from a subgroup $H\subseteq\frak S_n$ and an irreducible complex character $\chi$ — a family in which Schur's inequality makes the determinant the smallest element (with the signature character giving the determinant and the trivial character giving the permanent) — is there a natural characterization of the maximal one, i.e., is there a largest element of this family of upper bounds for $\det(S)$ over all $S\in SPD_n$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 1 answers); the question recalls Schur's result as presented in F. Goldberg's answer, which establishes $\det(S)\le d_\chi(S)$ for all $S\in SPD_n$. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/108530/a-maximal-element-where-schur-gives-a-minimal-element
solved_when: A description (or characterization) is given of the maximal element of the family $\{d_\chi\}$ for a given $n$, taking into account that several pairs $(H,\chi)$ yield the same function (for instance, only $11$ distinct functions arise for $n=3$).
why: It would complete the picture of Schur-type determinant upper bounds, of which Hadamard's inequality ($H=(e)$) and the permanent are special cases, identifying the best possible bound in this family.

title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic geometry of convex surfaces
open: Does the intrinsic metric of a convex surface in Euclidean 3-space determine its extrinsic geometry in a usable way — can quantities not invariant under local isometric deformations, such as mean curvature, principal directions, principal curvatures, or umbilic points, be computed, recognized, or characterized intrinsically? Alexandrov's isometric embedding theorem and Pogorelov's rigidity result guarantee such an intrinsic characterization exists in principle, but the known proof is non-constructive and offers no hint of how to carry it out.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/283568/intrinsic-vs-extrinsic-geometry-of-convex-surfaces.
solved_when: A method is given to compute, recognize, or characterize at least one of the non-intrinsic-invariant geometric quantities or features listed (mean curvature, principal directions, principal curvatures, or umbilic points) purely in terms of the intrinsic metric of the convex surface.
why: It would turn the existence statement of Alexandrov and the uniqueness of Pogorelov into an effective dictionary between intrinsic and extrinsic geometry, making curvature data of convex surfaces accessible from the metric alone.

title: Which knot invariants have no known diagram-independent descriptions
open: Which knot invariants, currently defined via properties of knot diagrams invariant under the three Reidemeister moves, still lack a diagram-independent description — that is, a formulation as a property of the three-dimensional knot itself, with no reference to diagrams?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 1 answer); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/341313/which-knot-invariants-have-no-known-diagram-independent-descriptions.
solved_when: A list is produced identifying those knot invariants for which no diagram-independent description is known, each entry accompanied (where possible) by evidence of the gap; conversely, any invariant on the list is removed once such a description is found.
why: In principle every knot invariant admits a diagram-independent description, yet in practice years can pass between an invariant's discovery and such a formulation, so a census of the gap directs effort toward invariants whose intrinsic geometric meaning remains hidden.

title: Is $\varliminf_{n \rightarrow +\infty} |n \sin n| = 0$ correct, where $n$ is an integer
open: Is it true that $\varliminf_{n \rightarrow +\infty} |n \sin n| = 0$, where $n$ runs over the integers? The existence of the limes inferior follows from Dirichlet's approximation theorem, but the problem is to prove that it is $0$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 1 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/144080/is-varliminf-n-rightarrow-infty-n-sin-n-0-correct-where-n-is-an.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\varliminf_{n \rightarrow +\infty} |n \sin n| = 0$ for integer $n$.
why: Resolving it would settle a natural question at the interface of Diophantine approximation and the arithmetic nature of $\pi$, a long-tail problem of high community interest outside standard lists.

title: What is the status of this conjecture on symplectic forms "standard-at-infinity" on $\math
open: If a symplectic form on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, $n \ge 3$, agrees with the standard form $\omega_0$ outside a compact set, must the manifold be symplectomorphic to the standard $(\mathbb{R}^{2n}, \omega_0)$?
status: This is Problem 50 (Standard-at-infinity) in McDuff and Salamon's *Introduction to Symplectic Topology*. In dimension four the analogous question has a positive answer by a celebrated theorem of Gromov [287]. A theorem of Floer–Eliashberg–McDuff [451] asserts that if $(M, \omega)$ is a symplectic manifold with $\pi_2(M) = 0$ that is symplectomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}^{2n}, \omega_0)$ outside of a compact set, then $M$ is necessarily diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. Mark McLean and others constructed many examples of symplecti (record truncated). The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 0 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/483874/what-is-the-status-of-this-conjecture-on-symplectic-forms-standard-at-infinity
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every symplectic form on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, $n \ge 3$, coinciding with $\omega_0$ on the complement of a compact set, is (or is not) symplectomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}^{2n}, \omega_0)$.
why: It is the natural higher-dimensional analogue of Gromov's celebrated four-dimensional theorem; an answer would settle whether exotic standard-at-infinity symplectic structures can exist on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ for $n \ge 3$.

title: How can an approach to $P$ vs $NP$ based on descriptive complexity avoid being a natural proof in th
open: Can a descriptive-complexity approach to separating $P$ from $NP$ sidestep the Razborov–Rudich natural proofs barrier by exploiting the uniformity of $P$? More precisely: is the uniformity of $P$ used in such an essential way in such a proof that the barrier cannot apply to it — or does the argument extend to nonuniform circuit lower bounds, where natural proofs would block it?
status: The question arose from Vinay Deolalikar's paper and Richard Lipton's first post about it, with discussions summarized on a polymath wiki page; Lipton remarked that the approach "exploits a uniform characterization of P that may not extend to give lower bounds against circuits." It is community-curated on MathOverflow with score 13 and 0 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/34980/how-can-an-approach-to-p-vs-np-based-on-descriptive-complexity-avoid-being-a).
solved_when: A rigorous account is given of whether a descriptive-complexity proof (in the style of Deolalikar's approach) can avoid being a natural proof, i.e., either a proof that the uniformity of $P$ is essential so that the natural proofs barrier does not apply, or a demonstration that the approach necessarily yields a natural proof and is thus blocked.
why: The natural proofs barrier is one of the fundamental obstructions to any $P$ vs $NP$ separation, so knowing whether uniformity provides a genuine escape route determines whether an entire family of descriptive-complexity attacks on $P$ vs $NP$ is viable or doomed.

title: Is the fundamental group of any compact hyperbolic 3-manifold embeddable into a p-adic group
open: Does every compact hyperbolic $3$-manifold $M$ admit, for some prime $p$ and some finite extension $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$, an injective homomorphism $\tau \colon \pi_1(M) \to \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathcal{O}_K)$, where $\mathcal{O}_K$ is the ring of integers of $K$? The question is tied to the existence of faithful low-dimensional representations of hyperbolic groups (see the survey by Aschenbrenner, Friedl, and Wilton), an affirmative answer would partially confirm Conjecture 1 of a paper by Luo, and such homomorphisms $\tau$ are also discussed in a paper by Calegari and Emerton. The answer is obviously "yes" when $M$ is arithmetic.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 2 answers), where it is noted that the answer is obviously "yes" for arithmetic $M$, that it connects to faithful low-dimensional representations of hyperbolic groups via the survey by Aschenbrenner, Friedl, and Wilton, that an affirmative solution would partially confirm Conjecture 1 of a paper by Luo, and that group homomorphisms of this kind are also discussed in a paper by Calegari and Emerton. Key record: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/267936/is-the-fundamental-group-of-any-compact-hyperbolic-3-manifold-embeddable-into-a
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every compact hyperbolic $3$-manifold $M$ there exists a prime $p$, a finite field extension $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$, and an injective group homomorphism $\tau \colon \pi_1(M) \to \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathcal{O}_K)$, where $\mathcal{O}_K$ is the ring of integers of $K$.
why: An affirmative solution would partially confirm Conjecture 1 of Luo's paper and advance the broader study of faithful low-dimensional representations of hyperbolic groups.

title: Zero divisor conjecture for finite fields
open: Is the zero-divisor conjecture true over finite fields — that is, for a torsion-free group $G$ and a finite field $K$, does the group ring $K[G]$ have no non-trivial zero divisors? More specifically, over $K = \mathbb{F}_2$, is there a constant $R > 0$ such that every zero divisor $a \in K[G]$, written as $a = \sum g_i$ with $g_i \in G$, has rank (the minimal number of elements in such an expression) exceeding $R$?
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 12, 4 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/62548/zero-divisor-conjecture-for-finite-fields. The classical attractive conjecture concerns non-trivial zero-divisors in $\mathbb{C}[G]$ for torsion-free $G$; the finite-field variant and the rank-bounded $\mathbb{F}_2$ variant are posed as open, with a related question "Group ring and left zero divisor."
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $K[G]$ is a domain for every torsion-free group $G$ and finite field $K$; or, in the refined $\mathbb{F}_2$ formulation, determination of whether some constant $R > 0$ bounds from below the rank of all zero divisors.
why: It tests whether the classical complex zero-divisor conjecture extends to positive characteristic, where the usual analytic and embedding tools over $\mathbb{C}$ are unavailable; the rank-bounded version would give a concrete finitary handle on potential counterexamples.

title: level sets of multivariate polynomials
open: How large can the boundary of a sublevel set of a multivariate polynomial be? Given a polynomial $p:\mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R$ of degree at most $d$ restricted to the unit cube $Q=[0,1]^n$, with mean value zero ($\int_Q p(x)\,dx = 0$), consider for $\alpha>0$ the sublevel set $E_\alpha = \{x\in Q: |p(x)|\leq \alpha\}$; the question asks for estimates on the induced Lebesgue measure of its boundary, $|\partial E_\alpha| = |\{x\in Q: |P(x)|=\alpha\}|$, uniform over classes of polynomials, analogous to known bounds for $|E_\alpha|$ such as the Carbery–Wright estimate $|E_\alpha| \lesssim \min(pd,n) \frac{\alpha^{1/d}}{\|p\|_{L^p(Q)}^{1/d}}$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 12 and 3 answers; the one-dimensional case ($n=1$, where $E_\alpha$ is a finite union of closed intervals) is described as easy, while the multivariate boundary-measure question is posed as open. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/4672/level-sets-of-multivariate-polynomials
solved_when: A bound on $|\partial E_\alpha|$ is established that is uniform over the class of degree-$d$ polynomials with mean value zero on $Q$, in the spirit of the known uniform estimates for $|E_\alpha|$.
why: Bounds on the measure of level sets would extend the classical Carbery–Wright-type sublevel-set estimates from volumes to boundaries, giving control on the size of nodal-type hypersurfaces $\{|p|=\alpha\}$ uniformly across polynomial classes.

title: Transcendentality of all irrationals in the Cantor set
open: Are all irrational numbers in the Cantor set transcendental? Equivalently, must every irrational algebraic number have at least one digit equal to 1 in its ternary expansion — indeed, if it has one such digit, must it have infinitely many?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 1 answers); posed by a student researcher who reduced it to whether every irrational algebraic number has a 1 in its ternary expansion, noting that such a number with one 1 must have infinitely many. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/114758/transcendentality-of-all-irrationals-in-the-cantor-set
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit irrational algebraic number whose ternary expansion uses only 0s and 2s) of the statement that every irrational element of the Cantor set is transcendental.
why: The heuristic is that Cantor set members are non-normal while algebraic irrationals are widely believed to be normal; a resolution either way would be the first concrete instance separating algebraic numbers from a simply described non-normal set.

title: No real roots of $\frac{1}{2^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{3^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{5^{1+it}}$
open: Is it true that $\frac{1}{2^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{3^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{5^{1+it}} \neq 0$ for every real number $t$? In other words, can this three-term exponential sum with prime bases never vanish along the critical line $\operatorname{Re}(s)=1$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question scored 12 and received 1 answer; discussion and context are at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/503219/no-real-roots-of-frac121it-frac131it-frac151it.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of the nonvanishing of $\frac{1}{2^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{3^{1+it}} + \frac{1}{5^{1+it}}$ for all real $t$; a counterexample is an explicit $t$ for which the sum equals zero.
why: It is a striking example of how simple-looking equations involving complex exponentials can resist standard techniques, and a resolution would illuminate the behavior of Dirichlet-type sums with few prime terms on the line $\operatorname{Re}(s)=1$.

title: Gerstenhaber conjecture for free loop space
open: Is Gerstenhaber's conjecture still open — namely, that for a simply connected compact oriented smooth $d$-manifold $M$, the Hochschild cohomology $HH^{\ast}(C^{\ast}(M))$ is isomorphic as a Gerstenhaber algebra to the $d$-shifted homology $H_{\ast+d}(LM)$ of the free loop space of $M$? In particular, what are the recent advances toward the conjecture, and is there a short proof that the two agree even just as graded vector spaces?
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 2 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/219344/gerstenhaber-conjecture-for-free-loop-space; no resolution is recorded there.
solved_when: An answer either establishes or refutes the Gerstenhaber algebra isomorphism $HH^{\ast}(C^{\ast}(M)) \cong H_{\ast+d}(LM)$ for every simply connected compact oriented smooth $d$-manifold $M$, or supplies a short proof of the weaker graded-vector-space isomorphism $HH^{\ast}(C^{\ast}(M)) \cong H_{\ast+d}(LM)$, together with an account of the current state of the conjecture.
why: Resolving it would settle a basic structural bridge between the algebra of Hochschild cohomology and the topology of free loop spaces, a central theme in string topology.

title: distance regular metric spaces
open: Must there be, up to equality of intersection numbers, essentially only one "fully rich" distance regular metric space on nonnegative real distances — namely the Euclidean plane? Formally, a metric space (V,d) is distance regular if for all nonnegative reals a>0, b, c there is an integer p(a,b,c) counting the points A with d(A,B)=c and d(A,C)=b whenever d(B,C)=a; the conjecture is that if additionally p(a,b,c)>0 whenever the triangle inequality for a,b,c is strict (i.e., does not fail), then the parameters p(a,b,c) are exactly those of the Euclidean plane (which are 0, 1, or 2 according as the triangle inequality fails, is tight, or is strict), even though non-isomorphic examples may exist. Has this conjecture been formulated, proved, or refuted before?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 12 and 3 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/9957/distance-regular-metric-spaces); the record states no resolution of the conjecture.
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for the conjecture: every distance regular metric space with distances ranging over all nonnegative reals, satisfying p(a,b,c)>0 whenever the triangle inequality for a,b,c does not fail, has the Euclidean plane's parameters p(a,b,c) ∈ {0,1,2} (0 when the triangle inequality fails, 1 at equality, 2 when strict); non-isomorphic examples with these same parameters do not refute the conjecture.
why: It would give a purely combinatorial, intersection-number characterization of Euclidean geometry among all metric spaces, and connect the classical theory of distance regular graphs to the continuous-distance setting; a counterexample would reveal a fundamentally new family of highly regular metric geometries.

title: Die-rolling Hamiltonian cycles
open: If a labeled rectangular region of the integer lattice admits a die-rolling Hamiltonian cycle — a Hamiltonian cycle obtained by rolling a unit die cube over edges so it lands on each square exactly once with the top face matching that square's label — must that cycle be unique? Formally: can a labeled region ever admit two distinct die-rolling Hamiltonian cycles?
status: The problem arose out of one posed in 2005 and was largely solved two years later in a paper entitled "On rolling cube puzzles"; the open record is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 2 answers), where a $4 \times 4$ rollable board is given as an example. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/87437/die-rolling-hamiltonian-cycles
solved_when: A proof that die-rolling Hamiltonian cycles are always unique, or an explicit labeled rectangular region of the integer lattice carrying two distinct die-rolling Hamiltonian cycles.
why: The question sits in the long tail of rolling-cube puzzles that fall outside standard open-problem lists but draw sustained community interest; resolving it completes the uniqueness picture left open after the original rollability question was largely settled.

title: Are Galois groups of Q with restricted ramification supposed to be finitely generated
open: Is the Galois group $G_{\mathbb Q,S}$ of the maximal extension of $\mathbb Q$ unramified outside a finite set $S$ of places supposed to be topologically finitely generated, i.e. to contain a dense finitely generated subgroup? More precisely, is there a standard conjecture or published opinion, including the stronger refinement suggested by JSE that $|S|$ generators suffice, with a distinguished set of generators labeled by the places of $S$ and inert at their labeling place, and possible weakenings such as restricting ramification at $S$ to be tame?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 1 answer); whether the group is finitely generated appears to be open, and the refined conjectures (JSE's $|S|$ generators labeled by $S$ and inert at the labeling place, and the tame variant) are raised as questions of whether they are standard rather than as published claims.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, e.g. by exhibiting a finite extension of $\mathbb Q$ unramified outside $S$ whose existence contradicts the hypothesis) of finite generation of $G_{\mathbb Q,S}$, or a definitive published account of the standard conjectural expectation, including whether the $|S|$-generator refinement with labeled inert generators is standard.
why: Settling it would determine the basic structure of the fundamental groups of Spec $\mathbb Z$ with restricted ramification, a cornerstone for arithmetic analogues of topological finiteness.

title: $\log n$ factor in Binomial empirical process
open: For the centered, normalized Binomial empirical process $\bar Y_j := n^{-1}Y_j - p_j$ with independent $Y_j \sim \operatorname{Binom}(n, p_j)$ and $1/2 \ge p_j \downarrow 0$, pin down whether the $\log n$ factor in the known characterization of $\Delta_n = \mathbb{E}\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}|\bar Y_j| \to 0$ is genuinely necessary.
status: CK'23 gave an exact characterization of the $p \in [0,\tfrac12]^{\mathbb{N}}_{\downarrow 0}$ for which $\Delta_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, via the functional $T(p)$; the remaining question, posted as a community-vetted open problem on MathOverflow (score 12, 1 answers; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/447472/open-problem-log-n-factor-in-binomial-empirical-process ), is the role of the $\log n$ factor in that characterization.
solved_when: The $\log n$ factor's role in the convergence $\Delta_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ is resolved: either it is shown to be removable (with the corresponding improvement to the characterization) or an example is given showing it cannot be removed.
why: The question, raised in Cohen and Kontorovich, "Local Glivenko-Cantelli", https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04054 , to appear in COLT 2023 (henceforth, CK'23), concerns the exact sharp condition — via the functional $T(p) := \sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{\log(j+1)}{\log(1/p_j)}$ — under which the uniform absolute deviation vanishes; resolving the $\log n$ factor yields the sharp form of this local Glivenko–Cantelli type result.

title: Detecting almost-primes quickly
open: Primality has fast deterministic and probabilistic tests, but is there a fast (possibly probabilistic) algorithm to decide whether a given number is the product of at most two primes? More concretely, is there a property satisfied by all or most products of two primes but by few other numbers that could serve as the basis of such a test — without explicitly using divisor sums or the Möbius function, which would make the task either trivial or of doubtful computational utility?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question scored 12 and received 2 answers; no resolution is recorded. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/36738/detecting-almost-primes-quickly
solved_when: A fast algorithm, probabilistic ones allowed, correctly decides whether a number is the product of at most two primes; or a usable distinguishing property fulfilled by all or most semiprimes but few other numbers is identified.
why: A solution would extend the practical toolkit of fast number-theoretic recognition tests beyond primality to semiprimes, a class central to factoring-based cryptography.

title: Second duals of Grothendieck spaces
open: Is the second dual of a Grothendieck space again a Grothendieck space? More precisely, does $X^{**}$ inherit the Grothendieck property whenever $X$ has it, or does a counterexample exist?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 0 answers). It is known that $\ell_\infty$ is a Grothendieck space and that its even duals $\ell_\infty^{**}$, $\ell_\infty^{(4)}$, \dots are Grothendieck spaces; a note proves this using the fact that these spaces are $C(K)$ spaces for large Stonian $K$'s. No general answer or counterexample is recorded. Original source: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/149326/second-duals-of-grothendieck-spaces
solved_when: A proof that $X^{**}$ is Grothendieck for every Grothendieck space $X$, or an explicit counterexample of a Grothendieck space whose second dual fails the property.
why: It resolves a question asked by J. Diestel on p. 105 in J. Diestel, "Grothendieck spaces and vector measures", Vector and Operator Valued Measures and Applications, Acad. Press (1973) pp. 97–108, and would clarify whether the Grothendieck property is stable under biduals beyond the classical $C(K)$ examples.

title: Once differentiable, piecewise degree three polynomials on triangulated planar domains
open: Is the dimension of the space $S$ of once differentiable functions on a planar triangulation — functions that restrict to a bivariate polynomial of degree 3 on each triangle — always equal to the Schumaker-style lower bound $3V_B + 2V_I + 1 + \sigma$, where $V_B$ counts boundary vertices, $V_I$ interior vertices, and $\sigma$ singular vertices? In other words, does every such triangulation attain the known lower bound, or is the dimension sometimes strictly larger?
status: Posted on MathOverflow (question 72189, score 12) with no answers; the problem is community-curated and described by the poser as easily stated but very difficult, wished to be solved within their lifetime. It is known that $\dim S \geq 3V_B + 2V_I + 1 + \sigma$. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/72189/once-differentiable-piecewise-degree-three-polynomials-on-triangulated-planar-d
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) determining the exact dimension of $S$ for arbitrary triangulations of polygonal planar domains, specifically deciding whether $\dim S = 3V_B + 2V_I + 1 + \sigma$ always holds, with $\sigma$ the number of singular interior vertices.
why: The dimension of this spline space governs whether one can build well-behaved $C^1$ finite elements and interpolation schemes on general triangulations, a basic tool in numerical analysis and geometric modeling.

title: Pencils with many completely decomposable fibers
open: Does there exist a rational function $F = G/H : \mathbb{P}^4 \to \mathbb{P}^1$ that does not, after any linear change of coordinates, belong to $\mathbb{C}(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)$, yet has three completely decomposable fibers — that is, three fibers over which every irreducible factor of $\mu G - \lambda H$ is linear?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 0 answers).
