status: The problem is posed as a community-curated question on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/344325/a-question-regarding-kadison-kaplansky-idempotent-conjecture-a-nearest-group-el), where it received 1 answer and comments, including an answer and comments by Prof. Valette that prompted a revision of the original question; the record states no further results.
solved_when: A precise characterization (or existence/nonexistence result) is given, for a discrete group $G$ and a self-adjoint unitary $u \in C^*_{\mathrm{red}}(G)$ with $u \neq \pm 1$, of the element $g \in G$ nearest to $u$ in the operator-norm distance, together with an analysis of what this implies about the presence of nontrivial projections and hence about the Kadison–Kaplansky conjecture for torsion-free groups.
why: Since a nontrivial projection $e$ yields a self-adjoint unitary $u = 1-2e \neq \pm 1$, understanding how close such an element can be to an actual group element offers a potential geometric route into the Kadison–Kaplansky and, more broadly, Baum–Connes conjectures.

title: Small quadrilaterals containing a given convex region
open: How small an area must a quadrilateral have if it is to contain every convex planar set of unit area? Chakerian (1973) and Kuperberg (1983) showed that the constant 2, which follows from a simple argument, can be improved to $\sqrt 2$ and even strictly below it; the challenge is to push the constant down further, perhaps all the way to the conjectured optimum attained by a regular pentagon — and any nice arguments giving bounds below 2 are welcome.
status: Community-curated as an open problem on MathOverflow (score 8, 1 answers), sourced from https://mathoverflow.net/questions/136351/small-quadrilaterals-containing-a-given-convex-region; the easy bound of 2 is classical, and improvements to $\sqrt 2$ and below are due to Chakerian (1973) and Kuperberg (1983).
solved_when: An explicit constant $c < \sqrt 2$ is proved such that every convex planar set of area 1 is contained in a quadrilateral of area $c$; the conjecture is fully settled by identifying the optimal constant and showing it is attained by a regular pentagon.
why: It resolves a natural extremal question about circumscribed polygons of convex bodies, and the conjectured pentagon extremal would reveal a sharp limit on how tightly a quadrilateral can enclose arbitrary convex shapes.

title: Poisson binomial conjecture
open: If two sums of independent Bernoulli random variables are built from coordinatewise ordered success probabilities, must the two sums be at least as distinguishable as the corresponding balanced pair? Formally, with $X_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i)$, $Y_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q_i)$ mutually independent, $p_i\ge q_i$, $n$ even, $\gamma:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(p_i-q_i)$, and $\bar X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,1/2+\gamma/2)$, $\bar Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,1/2-\gamma/2)$, the conjecture asserts $$\max_{k\ge 0}|\mathbb{P}(X\ge k)-\mathbb{P}(Y\ge k)| \ge \mathbb{P}(\bar X\ge n/2)-\mathbb{P}(\bar Y\ge n/2).$$ A positive resolution would in particular settle the conjecture in "Minimizing total variation under constraint."
status: Posed as a community-curated problem on MathOverflow (score 8, 2 answers), where it remains open; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/477402/poisson-binomial-conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the displayed inequality for all $n$ even, all $p_i\ge q_i$ in $[0,1]^n$, and all independent Bernoulli sums $X$, $Y$; equivalently, resolution of the implied conjecture in "Minimizing total variation under constraint."
why: It identifies the balanced Bernoulli pair as extremal for the Kolmogorov distance between sums with coordinatewise ordered parameters, giving a sharp baseline for distinguishability questions about Poisson-binomial distributions.

title: Base locus of divisors on blowings up of the projective space
open: Let $X$ be the blowing-up of $\mathbb{P}^n$ at $r$ general points, with standard basis $\{H, E_1,\dots,E_r\}$ of $Pic(X)$, and let $D = dH - \sum m_j E_j$ be an effective divisor with $m_j \in \mathbb{Z}$. Is it true that $m_1 \geq 0$ implies $E_1 \not\subseteq Bs(|D|)$? If all $m_i$ are non-negative, this amounts to asking whether $\dim |dH - m_1E_1 - \dots - m_rE_r| > \dim |dH - (m_1+1)E_1 - \dots - m_rE_r|$: equivalently, the hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{P}^n$ of degree $d$ passing through $r$ general points with multiplicities $m_1,\dots,m_r$ should not all pass through $p_1$ with multiplicity $m_1 + 1$. The statement is immediate for nonspecial linear systems, but special ones leave it genuinely open.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 8 and 2 answers; the poster reports the claim is obvious to intuition and trivial for nonspecial linear systems, but could not prove it in general, with special linear systems the potential obstruction.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that for every effective divisor $D = dH - \sum m_j E_j$ on the blowing-up of $\mathbb{P}^n$ at $r$ general points with $m_1 \geq 0$, the exceptional divisor $E_1$ is not contained in the base locus $Bs(|D|)$ — equivalently, that raising the imposed multiplicity at one point by one strictly drops the dimension of the corresponding linear system whenever all multiplicities are non-negative.
why: It would settle a basic expected-dimension phenomenon for linear systems on blowings-up of projective space, where special systems are the known source of pathologies; a counterexample would expose new special behaviour.

title: An inequality related to the unfair 0-1 polynomial conjecture
open: Let $x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $y_0,y_1,\dots,y_n$ be nonnegative reals, and let $z_k=\sum_{i+j=k}x_iy_j$ be the coefficients of the product polynomial, so that $P_x(t)P_y(t)=P_z(t)$. Defining $F(x_0,\dots,x_n)=\left(\sum_{k=0}^n x_k\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^n x_k^3\right)-\left(\sum_{k=0}^n x_k^2\right)^2=\sum_{k<l}x_kx_l(x_k-x_l)^2\ge 0$, does there exist a constant $C_n>0$ such that $C_n F(x_0,\dots,x_n)F(y_0,\dots,y_n)\le F(z_0,\dots,z_{2n})$ for all such $x,y$? Since $F(x)=0$ exactly when $P_x(t)$ is a scalar multiple of a 0-1 polynomial, such an inequality would imply that if a product $P_z(t)$ is a scalar multiple of a 0-1 polynomial, then both factors $P_x(t)$ and $P_y(t)$ are — the "unfair" 0-1 polynomial conjecture.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem has attracted moderate attention (score 8) and 1 answer; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A constant $C_n>0$ is exhibited (or shown not to exist) such that $C_n F(x)F(y)\le F(z)$ holds for all nonnegative $x_0,\dots,x_n$, $y_0,\dots,y_n$ with $z_k=\sum_{i+j=k}x_iy_j$; no quantitative lower bound on $C_n$ is specified.
why: The inequality would yield a proof of the unfair 0-1 polynomial conjecture — that factors of 0-1 polynomials are themselves 0-1 polynomials (up to scaling) — via the identity $F(x)=\sum_{k<l}x_kx_l(x_k-x_l)^2$, which detects exactly the 0-1 case.

title: Maximal class of simple graphs of order $n$ with mutually distinct numbers of spanning trees
open: How many distinct spanning-tree counts can connected simple graphs on $n$ vertices realize? Formally, if $A_n$ is the set of integers $x$ such that some connected simple graph of order $n$ has exactly $x$ spanning trees, determine the growth rate of $|A_n|$ — in particular whether $|A_n| = \omega(n^2)$.
status: The question was raised by J. Sedlacek in "On the number of spanning trees of finite graphs," Cas. Pro. Pest Mat., Vol. 94 (1969) 217-221, where he showed $|A_n| = \omega(n)$ and remarked that it is not known if $|A_n| = \omega(n^2)$. Known observations: $|A_n| \leq n^{n-2}$, $|A_n| \leq |A_{n+1}|$, and via prime partitions $|A_n| = \omega(\sqrt{n}e^{\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{n/\log n}})$. Values computed with sage+nauty include $|A_1|=1$, $|A_2|=1$, $|A_3|=2$, $|A_4|=5$. The record is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 1 answer). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/100816/maximal-class-of-simple-graphs-of-order-n-with-mutually-distinct-numbers-of-sp
solved_when: The asymptotic growth rate of $|A_n|$ is determined; a concrete sharpening would resolve Sedlacek's remark that it is not known if $|A_n| = \omega(n^2)$.
why: It measures how rich the possible spanning-tree counts of graphs are compared to the trivial bound $|A_n| \leq n^{n-2}$, the total number of labeled graphs on $n$ vertices via Cayley's formula.

title: Is the Collatz conjecture known to be true for interesting unbounded classes of numbers
open: Is there a concrete, unbounded family of integers on which the Collatz ($3n+1$) conjecture can be verified outright? In particular, does there exist a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]$ with unbounded range such that every integer of the form $|f(m)|$, $m\in\mathbb Z$, satisfies the Collatz conjecture, and do the numbers $3^x$ for $x\in\mathbb Z$ — the simplest non-trivial non-polynomial family — satisfy the conjecture?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 0 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/412276/is-the-collatz-conjecture-known-to-be-true-for-interesting-unbounded-classes-of. No answer or resolution is recorded.
solved_when: Either an explicit polynomial $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ with unbounded range is exhibited (and proved) such that every $|f(m)|$ satisfies the Collatz conjecture, or the conjecture is proved (or disproved) for all numbers of the form $3^x$, $x\in\mathbb Z$.
why: The Collatz conjecture itself is open, and establishing truth on natural unbounded families would be the first evidence of structure beyond direct computation, potentially revealing which classes of trajectories can be controlled analytically.

title: Does every model of $I\Delta_0$ has an end extension to a model of $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$
open: Does every model of $I\Delta_0$ admit an end extension to a model of $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$? Formally: for any $M \models I\Delta_0$, is there an end extension $N \supseteq_e M$ with $N \models I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$?
status: Posed as open in the paper "End extensions of models of linearly bounded arithmetic." Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 0 answers); no further progress recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/226580/does-every-model-of-i-delta-0-has-an-end-extension-to-a-model-of-i-delta-0-o
solved_when: A proof that every model of $I\Delta_0$ has an end extension satisfying $I\Delta_0+\Omega_1$, or a counterexample model of $I\Delta_0$ admitting no such end extension.
why: It probes whether the totality of the function $x^{\log x}$ (the $\Omega_1$ axiom) can always be gained by end extension — a basic question about how much closure end extensions can force in arithmetic.

title: Is there a finite-index finite-depth II$_1$ subfactor which is more than $7$-super-transitive
open: Does there exist a finite-index finite-depth II$_1$ subfactor of index greater than $4$ which is more than $7$-super-transitive? Formally, one seeks such a subfactor whose standard invariant goes beyond the known $7$-super-transitive example, the extended Haagerup subfactor.
status: Community-curated and vetted on MathOverflow, where the question (score 8) received 0 answers. Known examples include many $3$-super-transitive subfactors (Haagerup, $S_4 < S_5$, and others), exactly one $5$-super-transitive example (the Haagerup-Asaeda subfactor), and one $7$-super-transitive example (the extended Haagerup subfactor); below index $4$, the $A_n$ and $D_n$ families are arbitrarily super-transitive. Background discussion appears in Noah and Emily's posts on subfactors and planar algebras on the Secret Blogging Seminar (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/182/is-there-a-finite-index-finite-depth-ii-1-subfactor-which-is-more-than-7-sup).
solved_when: An explicit finite-index finite-depth II$_1$ subfactor (necessarily of index greater than $4$) is constructed or shown to exist whose super-transitivity exceeds $7$.
why: It would push past the current frontier of super-transitivity for subfactors above index $4$, where progress has stalled at $7$; a positive answer would yield a genuinely new kind of standard invariant, while a systematic obstruction would clarify what limits super-transitivity.

title: Must Mersenne numbers be divisible by arbitrary large primes with exponent one
open: As $n$ varies over the Mersenne numbers $M_n = 2^n - 1$, must $M_n$ be divisible by arbitrarily large primes $p$ with exponent one, i.e. $p \mid M_n$ but $p^2 \nmid M_n$? Equivalently, must the exponential diophantine equation $2^n - 1 = A x^2 y^3$, for constant $A$, have only finitely many solutions $(n, x, y)$ with $n > 1$? Unconditional results are sought; abc easily implies the claim.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow with score 7 and 2 answers. Ribenboim's paper "Remarks on Exponential Congruences and Powerful Numbers" states on p. 7 the conjecture (M') that infinitely many Mersenne numbers are not powerful. An easy partial construction: since 3 divides $M_{6n+2}$ with exponent one, every $M_{6n+2}$ is non-powerful, giving infinitely many non-powerful Mersenne numbers — but this does not address the exponent-one prime divisor growing arbitrarily large. abc implies the full statement.
solved_when: An unconditional proof that for arbitrarily large primes $p$ there exists $n$ with $p \mid M_n$ and $p^2 \nmid M_n$ (equivalently, that $2^n - 1 = A x^2 y^3$ has only finitely many solutions with $n > 1$).
why: The statement (M'), "there exist infinitely many Mersenne numbers which are not powerful," implies $B_2$, which in turn implies the infinitude of non-Wieferich primes — so a solution would settle a well-known related open question.

title: distribution of degree of minimum polynomial for eigenvalues of random matrix with elements in finit
open: What is the distribution of the degrees of the minimal polynomials of eigenvalues of a random $n \times n$ matrix $A_{n,p}$ with iid entries uniform over the finite field $F_p$? Formally, if $d(\lambda)$ denotes the degree of the minimal polynomial of an eigenvalue $\lambda$ (lying in some finite extension of $F_p$), does the distribution of $d(\lambda)$, suitably normalized, converge to a limiting law — perhaps Gaussian — as $n \to \infty$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 7 and 1 answer; the poster notes uncertainty about whether symmetry guarantees diagonalizability over $F_p$ (no counterexamples known) and asks whether the problem has been studied before.
solved_when: A limiting law for the normalized distribution of $d(\lambda)$ is identified and proved as $n \to \infty$, for iid uniform entries over $F_p$ (with the symmetric or antisymmetric variant as an optional variant to ensure diagonalizability, if it indeed does).
why: It would extend the well-developed theory of random matrices over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ to fields of positive characteristic, where eigenvalues live in extensions of the base field and classical spectral statistics do not directly apply.

title: Status of linearity of mapping class group
open: Is the mapping class group of a closed surface $\Sigma_g$ linear for every genus $g$? The question is sharpened by a conflicting literature: Bigelow and Budney (2001) establish linearity for $g=2$, and Nikolaev (2003) claims a positive resolution for all $g$, yet Farb (in a 2006 book, chapter 2) and Ozsvath, Lipshitz, and Thurston (2010) still list the problem as open — so, specifically, has a mistake been found in Nikolaev's proof, and why is there apparently little confidence in it?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answer). The question was posed as a followup noting that linearity for $g=2$ follows from Bigelow and Budney (2001), that Nikolaev (2003) claims the general case, and that Farb (2006, chapter 2) and Ozsvath, Lipshitz, and Thurston (2010) treat the problem as open; the asker reports the matter does not appear to have been satisfyingly answered.
solved_when: The linearity of the mapping class group of $\Sigma_g$ is either proved for arbitrary $g$ by an argument the community accepts, or the claimed proof by Nikolaev (2003) is definitively vindicated or refuted, resolving the discrepancy with Farb (2006) and Ozsvath, Lipshitz, and Thurston (2010).
why: It settles whether a basic structural property — linearity — holds for one of the central groups in low-dimensional topology and geometric group theory, and removes a genuine uncertainty in the literature, where published sources disagree on whether the problem is open.

title: Hyperbolic groups and spaces of negative curvature
open: Is every Gromov-hyperbolic group the fundamental group of a compact space of strictly negative curvature? More precisely, Gromov says he "tried for about 10 years to prove that every hyperbolic group is realizable by a space of negative curvature" in his interview with Martin Raussen and Christian Skau (page 6): https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/rtx100300391p.pdf
status: This question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answer): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/334951/hyperbolic-groups-and-spaces-of-negative-curvature. Gromov himself reports having tried for about 10 years to prove the conjecture without success; no resolution is recorded in the record.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation, via a hyperbolic group not realizable by any space of negative curvature) is established, resolving the conjecture Gromov describes.
why: A positive answer would give a geometric, curvature-based model for every hyperbolic group, tightly linking large-scale group theory to concrete negative-curvature geometry; a counterexample would reveal hyperbolicity phenomena invisible to Riemannian curvature.

title: about CMC hypersurfaces with symmetries
open: Beyond the rotationally symmetric tori, what other open problems govern constant-mean-curvature hypersurfaces with prescribed symmetries — for instance, which CMC tori in $S^3$ admit only an isometric circle action as their continuous symmetry group? Formally, given the Andrews–Li classification showing every CMC torus in $S^3$ is rotationally symmetric (confirming a conjecture of Pinkall and Sterling), the question is to characterize the possible symmetry groups of CMC surfaces and hypersurfaces in space forms and classify the corresponding surfaces.
status: This is a community-curated MathOverflow question (score 7, 1 answers). Andrews and Li announced a complete classification of CMC tori in $S^3$, confirming a conjecture of Pinkall and Sterling: any such torus is rotationally symmetric, reducing the problem to a previous classification due to Perdomo, also studied by Hynd, Park and McCuan. Related techniques appear in Brendle's solution of the Lawson Conjecture, which states that the only minimal ($H=0$) torus in $S^3$, up to congruences, is the Clifford torus $S^1(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\times S^1(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$. It is known that CMC tori in $S^3$ exist that are not congruent to the family $S^1(r)\times S^1(\sqrt{1-r^2})$ of Clifford tori, so in a certain sense their only continuous symmetries are encoded in an isometric circle action, as confirmed by Andrews' and Li's result.
solved_when: A classification of CMC tori in $S^3$ up to congruence is obtained (the record states no further quantitative targets), together with a determination of their symmetry groups, extending the Andrews–Li rotational-symmetry result and Perdomo's classification of the rotationally symmetric case.
why: It completes the symmetry picture for CMC surfaces in $S^3$ opened by the Lawson conjecture and the Pinkall–Sterling conjecture, and identifies which symmetric families are the full story rather than just examples.

title: What is the degree of a symmetric boolean function
open: Does there exist an $N\in\mathbb N$ and a sequence of non-constant functions $\{p_n:[n]\to\{1,-1\}\}_{n=N}^{\infty}$ such that for all $n>N$ we have $\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}p_n(i)\binom{n}{i}=0$? In other words, can the binomial coefficients of each row be signed (nontrivially, with alternating signs folded in) so that every row beyond some point sums to zero?
status: Asked on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answer), community-curated as an open problem. The asker notes an explicit construction for all odd $n$: $p_n(i)=(-1)^{i}$ for $i\le (n-1)/2$ and $(-1)^{i+1}$ for $i\ge (n+1)/2$, i.e., summing the first half of the binomial coefficients and subtracting the second half, which works because odd rows split evenly; the even case is unresolved, and the methods that solved the previous question (credited by the asker to darij grinberg and Mikael de la Salle) appear not to extend. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/74191/what-is-the-degree-of-a-symmetric-boolean-function.
solved_when: An explicit $N$ and a construction of non-constant sign functions $p_n$ for all $n>N$ satisfying the vanishing sum is given, or a proof that no such $N$ and sequence exist.
why: A positive answer yields a signed vanishing identity for binomial coefficients row by row, strengthening the previously solved version of the question; a negative answer shows the odd-$n$ symmetric construction is essentially all there is.

title: Artin's conjecture for $n=2$
open: Is $2$ a primitive root modulo $p$ for infinitely many primes $p$? This is the special case $n = 2$ of Artin's primitive root conjecture, and it remains open.
status: Community-curated and vetted on MathOverflow (score 7, 2 answers), reflecting high community interest as a long-tail problem outside standard problem lists; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/47974/artins-conjecture-for-n-2.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that there are infinitely many primes $p$ for which $2$ is a primitive root modulo $p$; equivalently, resolution of Artin's conjecture in the case $n = 2$.
why: It is the cleanest unsolved instance of Artin's conjecture, a foundational question in multiplicative number theory linking the order of $2$ mod $p$ to the structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$.

title: Upper bound of the expectation of sum of the absolute value pairs
open: Given two arrays $A,B$ of length $n$ with all entries i.i.d. from the same distribution on $[0,1]$, sort each and form $S=\sum_{i=1}^n|A_{(i)}-B_{(i)}|$ — what is the sharpest possible upper bound on $\mathbb{E}[S]$, uniformly over all distributions on $[0,1]$? The conjecture is that the supremum is attained when the distribution is uniform, though this remains unproven.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 4 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/301135/upper-bound-of-the-expectation-of-sum-of-the-absolute-value-pairs; the poster attempted an order-statistics derivation but found the expressions too complex to complete. No solved result is recorded.
solved_when: An explicit upper bound on $\mathbb{E}[S]$ is established for arbitrary distributions on $[0,1]$, ideally with proof (or disproof) that the uniform distribution maximizes it.
why: A clean bound would resolve a natural question about matched order statistics and likely follow from, or sharpen, known order-statistics estimates; without it, the conjectured extremal role of the uniform distribution stays unverified.

title: Congruence obstructions for three consecutive powerful numbers
open: Can modular arithmetic alone rule out Erdős's conjectured non-existent triples of three consecutive powerful numbers — that is, can we find a modulus $n$ for which the system $x_1^2 x_2^3 = A-1$, $y_1^2 y_2^3 = A+1$ has no solution modulo $n$ for every residue class $A \pmod{n}$, proving no such triple exists? More generally, can this congruence-obstruction method be pushed to establish non-existence for further naturally defined classes of triples?
status: Community-curated as a MathOverflow question (score 7, 1 answer), recorded at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/468771/congruence-obstructions-for-three-consecutive-powerful-numbers. Known square moduli with computed obstructions include $n = 4$ ($A \equiv 1, 3$), $n = 9$ ($A \equiv 2, 4, 5, 7$), $n = 16$ ($A \equiv 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15$), $n = 25$ ($A \equiv 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21$), $n = 36$ (25 listed classes), and $n = 49$ ($A \equiv 6, 8, 13, 15, 20, 22, 27, 29, 34, 36, 41, 43$).
solved_when: A modulus $n$ (or family of moduli) is exhibited whose congruence obstructions cover all residue classes $A \pmod{n}$, i.e. for which the above system is unsolvable modulo $n$ for every $A$, thereby proving that three consecutive powerful numbers do not exist; or, for the broader question, new naturally defined families of triples are shown impossible by such obstructions.
why: Erdős's conjecture that three consecutive powerful numbers never occur remains out of reach; a complete congruence obstruction would settle it by entirely elementary modular means, and any extension of the method gives unconditional non-existence results for classes of triples currently untouched.

title: Integral straight-line embeddings of planar graphs
open: Does every planar graph admit a straight-line drawing in which all edge lengths are integers? This is Harborth's question, and it remains open even though every n-vertex planar graph is known to have a straight-line grid drawing on an O(n) × O(n) grid — integer coordinates alone do not force integer edge lengths.
status: The question was raised by Heiko Harborth; per the Fáry's theorem article on Wikipedia, the answer remained unknown as of 2009. The cited reference is Kemnitz, Arnfried, and Heiko Harborth. "Plane integral drawings of planar graphs." Discrete Mathematics 236 .1 (2001): 191-195. The Kemnitz–Harborth article closes by noting it seems to be a very hard problem to prove that every pentagon with sides of integral length contains an inner point with rational distances to its vertices. The record is a community-curated MathOverflow post (score 7, 1 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/163845/integral-straight-line-embeddings-of-planar-graphs
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every planar graph has a planar straight-line drawing with all edge lengths integral; a natural stepping stone singled out by Kemnitz and Harborth is proving that every pentagon with integral side lengths contains an inner point with rational distances to its vertices.
why: It would resolve a long-standing, widely circulated question in combinatorial geometry; the rational-distances subproblem alone would be a significant advance, since even that special case is described by Kemnitz and Harborth as "a very hard problem."

title: Implication of Polignac's conjecture on prime distribution in models of PA
open: Does Polignac's conjecture — that for some natural number $d$ there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes at distance $d$, with the twin prime conjecture as the $d = 2$ instance — have consequences for how primes are distributed inside nonstandard models of Peano Arithmetic? In particular, since every model of PA has order type $\mathbb{N} + \mathbb{Z} \cdot A$ for some dense linear order without endpoints, with nonstandard numbers arranged in unbounded densely ordered $\mathbb{Z}$-blocks, one may ask whether the conjecture constrains the distribution of primes across those blocks.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem received score 7 and 1 answers; the asker observed the implication independently and requested references, noting someone else must have realized it as well.
solved_when: A precise characterization is given of which models of PA are compatible with Polignac's conjecture holding or failing — equivalently, a determination of whether the conjecture's truth forces, rules out, or leaves invariant the distribution of primes among the $\mathbb{Z}$-blocks of a nonstandard model.
why: It would connect a classical analytic number theory conjecture to the structural theory of nonstandard models of PA, revealing whether standard prime distribution facts have model-theoretic content.

title: Milnor's isotopy invariant using spectral sequence
open: Did Stalling's closing suggestion — that Milnor's link isotopy invariants admit an interpretation via spectral sequences — ever get developed further? In his final remark in "the augmented ideal in group ring" (Ann. Math. Studies 84, R. H. Fox memorial volume), he proposes such a connection to Milnor's "Isotopy of links" (Algebraic geometry and topology, Princeton press); what is known about carrying this program out?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answers); the record cites the MathOverflow thread https://mathoverflow.net/questions/41676/milnors-isotopy-invariant-using-spectral-sequence but reports no further advances beyond Stalling's remark.
solved_when: A reference or construction is identified that realizes Milnor's link isotopy invariants through a spectral sequence, in the sense suggested by Stalling's final remark, or it is shown that no such development exists beyond the original suggestion.
why: A spectral-sequence interpretation would give a homological, potentially computational route to Milnor's invariants, linking them to the augmented ideal machinery Stalling developed.

title: What is known about polyhedra nets that allow overlapping
open: Can every convex polyhedron be unfolded to a planar net in which at most some bounded number of faces overlap? Formally, the classical open question asks whether every convex polyhedron has a non-overlapping net; the relaxation studied here asks, for example, whether every convex polyhedron can be unfolded with a maximum of 2 faces overlapping, and how the question extends to polyhedra that are topologically convex, i.e. whose graph is isomorphic to the graph of a convex polyhedron.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 2 answers). The record cites an example of an open polyhedron without a net that is topologically convex, and notes the closed case is taken care of by a paper mentioned in an answer below. The poster reports being unable to increase the number of overlapping sides without bound without breaking the topologically convex property, but considers it a reasonable task. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/6690/what-is-known-about-polyhedra-nets-that-allow-overlapping
solved_when: A resolution of the overlapping variant: e.g. a proof (or refutation) that any convex polyhedron can be unfolded with at most 2 overlapping faces, together with an answer for the topologically convex case — where, per the record, one solution route is to find a procedure that modifies either polygon so the number of overlapping sides increases without bound while preserving topological convexity.
why: It quantifies how far the classical edge-unfolding conjecture can fail: even a small constant bound on overlaps would be a strong structural result, while the topologically convex case exhibits polyhedra with no net at all, separating the combinatorial from the geometric setting.

title: If $N = qn^2$ is an odd perfect number with $\gcd(q,n)=1$, is it possible to have $q + 1 = \sigma(n)
open: Can an odd perfect number $N = qn^2$ in Eulerian form (so $q$ is the Euler prime, $\gcd(q,n)=1$) satisfy $q + 1 = \sigma(n)$? The Descartes spoof $n_1 = 3003 < \sigma(n_1) = 5376 < q_1 = 22021$ (with quasi-Euler prime $q_1$) suggests heuristically that one might be able to prove $q + 1 \neq \sigma(n)$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answer). Known essential estimates include Acquaah and Konyagin's bound $q < n\sqrt{3}$, which can be used to obtain an upper bound for $\sigma(q)/n$, and Ochem and Rao's lower bound $N > 10^{1500}$ for odd perfect numbers, which combined with $n < q$ gives $I(q) < 1 + 10^{-500}$.
solved_when: A proof or disproof that $q + 1 = \sigma(n)$ is impossible (or possible) for an odd perfect number $N = qn^2$ with Euler prime $q$ and $\gcd(q,n)=1$ is established; the record's motivating target is the proposition: if $N = q^k n^2$ is an odd perfect number with Euler prime $q$, then $3 \nmid N$ implies $q < n$.
why: Resolving this would advance the broader study of the structure of odd perfect numbers in Eulerian form; the equality is tied to proving that $3 \nmid N$ forces $q < n$, a structural constraint on the Euler prime.

title: Is the square achievement game on the $n × n$ grid resolved for $6 \le n \le 14$
open: Is the square achievement game on the $n \times n$ grid settled for every $n$ with $6 \le n \le 14$? In this game two players alternately mark unoccupied cells of an $n \times n$ grid, and the first to own four cells at the vertices of an axis-parallel square wins; the middle of the range $6 \le n \le 14$ remains unresolved. The problem was posed by Martin Erickson in *Pearls of Discrete Mathematics* (CRC Press, 2010) and is listed as open at Open Problem Garden. Both ends of the range appear to be settled: Jenrich, *Guaranteed successful strategies for a square achievement game on an $n$ by $n$ grid*, gives explicit strategies showing a draw for $n = 3, 4$ and a first-player win for $n = 5$, while Bacher and Eliahou, *Extremal binary matrices without constant 2-squares* (J. Comb. 1 (2010), 77–100), prove $n_0 = 15$ — every $2$-colouring of $[n] \times [n]$ with $n \ge 15$ contains four points of one colour at the vertices of an axis-parallel square — so no draw is possible from $n = 15$ onward.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); no resolution for $6 \le n \le 14$ is recorded. Key works: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/514742/is-the-square-achievement-game-on-the-n-%c3%97-n-grid-resolved-for-6-le-n-le-14
solved_when: For each $n$ with $6 \le n \le 14$, it is determined whether the game on the $n \times n$ grid is a first-player win or a draw, with a proof (explicit strategy or otherwise).
why: Completing the full range $3 \le n \le 15$ closes a charming, explicitly finite combinatorial game left open in Erickson's book, and the middle range is where strategy and Ramsey-type structure interact without either endpoint's simplification.

title: A recursive overlap construction of finite Bernoulli‐sum laws and an entropy-concavity conjecture
open: Is the Shannon entropy of the recursively defined probability vectors $P_n$ concave as a function of $p$, when $P_1=(p,1-p)$ and $P_{n+1}=p\,L(P_n)+(1-p)\,R(P_n)$ embeds $P_n$ into the left and right ends of a strictly longer vector (with $a_1=2$)? Concavity is known for the non-overlapping case $a_n\ge 2^n$ and for $a_n=n+1$, but open for intermediate growth such as $a_n=n^2+1$ and Fibonacci-like sequences $a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{n-1}+1$.
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 7, 1 answer), available at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/514729/a-recursive-overlap-construction-of-finite-bernoulli-sum-laws-and-an-entropy-con. The asker proved the non-overlapping case $a_n\ge 2^n$ easily and $a_n=n+1$ fairly easily, but could not handle $a_n=n^2+1$ or the Fibonacci-like sequences $a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{n-1}+1$ of special interest; Mathematica code (requested from ChatGPT) verified the conjecture for tested sequences up to $n=30$, and some up to $n=100$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that the entropy of $P_n$ is concave in $p$ for every strictly increasing integer sequence $(a_n)$ with $a_1=2$ — in particular for $a_n=n^2+1$ and the Fibonacci-like case $a_{n+1}=a_n+a_{n-1}+1$.
why: It would establish concavity of entropy for a natural recursive family of finite Bernoulli-sum laws in the overlap regime, extending results currently limited to the sparse ($a_n\ge 2^n$) and minimal-growth ($a_n=n+1$) cases.

title: Polynomial identification of natural numbers
open: Is there a single polynomial $f(x,y,n)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,n]$ whose integer zeros characterize exactly the natural numbers — that is, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ if and only if there exist $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $f(x,y,n)=0$? This generalizes the Poonen Christmas problem, which corresponds to the special case $f(x,y,n)=cn+g(x,y)$ with nonzero $c\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $g\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/501564/polynomial-identification-of-natural-numbers
solved_when: An explicit polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,n]$ is exhibited with $n\in\mathbb{N}\Longleftrightarrow\exists x,y\in\mathbb{Z},\, f(x,y,n)=0$, or such a polynomial is proved not to exist. "Open Question A" in Prunescu's linked paper is exactly this question.
why: A formula of Raphael Robinson from *Arithmetical definitions in the ring of integers*, modified as by Zhi-Wei Sun in *A new relation-combining theorem and its applications* (and reiterated by Mihai Prunescu in this paper), already gives the near example $n\in\mathbb{N}\Longleftrightarrow\exists x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $(x^2-(4n+2)y^2-1=0)\land(y\neq 0)$; closing the remaining gap would settle a clean Diophantine definability question with high community interest outside standard problem lists.

title: The behaviour of $\mathsf{HOD}^{L[x]}$ on a cone
open: What is the behaviour of $\mathsf{HOD}^{L[x]}$ on a cone of reals, as it determines the ultraproduct $\prod_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \mathsf{HOD}^{L[d]} / \mu$ introduced in "Introduction to $Q$-Theory" by Kechris-Martin-Solovay (proceedings of the Cabal Seminar 1979–1981), where $\mu$ is the Martin (cone) measure on Turing degrees $\mathcal{D}$, an ultrafilter assuming AD? Formally, since the Martin measure is $\omega_1$-complete the ultraproduct is well-founded and its analysis reduces to $\mathsf{HOD}^{L[x]}$ on a cone (noting $x \in d \in \mathcal{D}$ implies $L[x] = L[d]$), but the authors write "this ultraproduct is understood as taken within $L(\mathbb{R})$" and it is unclear how to prove that every $f \in \prod_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \mathsf{HOD}^{L[d]}$ agrees with such an $f \in L(\mathbb{R})$.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); no answers or resolutions are recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/487645/the-behaviour-of-mathsfhodlx-on-a-cone.
solved_when: A description of $\mathsf{HOD}^{L[x]}$ for a cone of reals is given — in particular, a proof (or refutation) that every $f \in \prod_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \mathsf{HOD}^{L[d]}$ agrees with a function in $L(\mathbb{R})$, thereby justifying that the ultraproduct is taken within $L(\mathbb{R})$.
why: It clarifies a foundational construction from Q-theory, developed back when axioms up to $I_3$ were believed compatible with $\Delta^1_2$-nondeterminacy; without a proof, the ultraproduct's meaning "within $L(\mathbb{R})$" rests on an unverified claim.

title: What is the current status of research on the von Neumann's inequality for $n \ge 3$
open: Does there exist a constant $C_n \ge 1$ such that, for every tuple of commuting contractions $(T_1, \ldots, T_n)$ on a Hilbert space $H$, the polynomial functional calculus is uniformly bounded in the sense that $\|p(T_1, \ldots, T_n)\| \le C_n \sup_{(z_1,\ldots,z_n) \in \overline{\mathbb{D}^n}} |p(z_1,\ldots,z_n)|$ for all $p \in \mathbb{C}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$? In other words, does von Neumann's inequality admit a dimension-dependent constant extension to $n \ge 3$ commuting contractions?
status: This is a community-curated question on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). The asker reports anecdotal mention of more recent approaches — "using graph theory for $n \ge 3$" and "using spectral theory" — but could find nothing newer than Shalit's work, which they date to 2021 "if I remember correctly." Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/461473/what-is-the-current-status-of-research-on-the-von-neumanns-inequality-for-n-g
solved_when: An explicit constant $C_n \ge 1$ is shown to work for all commuting contraction tuples and all polynomials in $n$ variables (or, conversely, a counterexample tuple is constructed for which no finite $C_n$ suffices).
why: A positive answer would extend one of the foundational results of operator theory to higher dimensions, giving a uniform substitute for the lost von Neumann inequality in several variables; the currently scattered and anecdotal state of knowledge (e.g., rumored graph-theoretic and spectral-theoretic approaches) leaves the multivariable theory without a clear benchmark.

title: Is the unit-stick number of a knot equal to its stick number
open: Is the fewest number of unit-length sticks needed to realize a knot — its equilateral (unit) stick number $\sigma_1(K)$ — always equal to its ordinary stick number $\sigma(K)$? If not, exhibit a knot for which it is provable that $\sigma_1(K) > \sigma(K)$.
status: This is a community-vetted MathOverflow question (score 7, 0 answers). The trefoil is known to have stick number $6$, though not with all sticks of equal length; the poster believes, without formal proof, that its unit-stick number is also $6$. A comment by user @aorq shows the "unit-stick number" has been studied under the name "equilateral stick number" in work by Rawdon, Eric J., and Robert G. Scharein. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/394427/is-the-unit-stick-number-of-a-knot-equal-to-its-stick-number
solved_when: Either a proof is given that $\sigma_1(K) = \sigma(K)$ for every knot $K$, or a specific knot $K$ is identified with a proof that its unit-stick number strictly exceeds its stick number. A natural first benchmark noted in the record: confirming the conjectured $\sigma_1(K_{3_1}) = 6$ for the trefoil, whose stick number is $6$.
why: It asks whether allowing sticks of arbitrary length ever helps minimize the number of edges in a polygonal knot realization; a separating example would reveal a genuinely new gap between equilateral and general stick realizations.

title: Isometries on the unit sphere
open: If two Banach spaces have unit spheres that are isometric as metric spaces, must the spaces themselves be isometric? Formally: given an onto isometry $f:S_X \to S_Y$, does it follow that $X$ and $Y$ are isometric?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); no resolution recorded. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/355567/isometries-on-the-unit-sphere
solved_when: A proof that every onto isometry between the unit spheres of two Banach spaces extends to (or implies) an isometry between the spaces, or a counterexample: two non-isometric Banach spaces with isometric unit spheres.
why: It tests whether the metric geometry of the unit sphere alone determines the surrounding Banach space, a foundational question in the isometric theory of normed spaces.

title: When do two knots have isomorphic fundamental bikeis
open: Under what circumstances do two knots have isomorphic fundamental bikeis? More precisely, characterize (or give usable criteria for) the equivalence relation on knots induced by isomorphism of their fundamental bikeis, where a bikei is an involutive biquandle and the fundamental bikei is built from the semiarcs of an unoriented knot diagram, as defined in Elhamdadi and Nelson's book *Quandles: An Introduction to the Algebra of Knots*.
status: Posted on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); the question notes a thesis by Martina Vaváčková (record text truncated). No resolution recorded.
solved_when: A characterization (or effectively checkable criterion) is given for when the fundamental bikeis of two given knots are isomorphic, determining exactly which knot pairs the invariant fails to distinguish.
why: The fundamental bikei is a computable unoriented-diagram invariant of knots, and knowing exactly when two knots share it tells us both the discriminating power and the precise blind spots of this algebraic invariant.

title: Status of two Banach space theory open problems posted by Pełczyński
open: Do Pełczyński's two questions about separable infinite-dimensional Banach spaces not isomorphic to a Hilbert space admit answers — namely, must such a space contain an infinite-dimensional subspace with a Schauder basis that is not complemented in it, and must it contain two infinite-dimensional subspaces with Schauder bases that are not isomorphic to each other?
status: The questions originate from the book 'Open Problems in the Geometry and Analysis of Banach Spaces' and are attributed to A. Pełczyński; the record is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/298635/status-of-two-banach-space-theory-open-problems-posted-by-pe%c5%82czy%c5%84ski.
solved_when: Both questions are resolved, affirmatively or negatively, for every separable infinite-dimensional Banach space not isomorphic to a Hilbert space: either each such space is shown to contain an infinite-dimensional subspace with a Schauder basis not complemented in it, or a counterexample is produced; and likewise either each such space contains two non-isomorphic infinite-dimensional subspaces with Schauder bases, or a counterexample is produced.
why: These problems probe how strongly non-Hilbert structure forces richness in the lattice of subspaces, and settling them would sharpen the basic theory of subspace structure in separable Banach spaces, a foundational question outside standard problem lists with substantial community interest.

title: Limit cycles as closed geodesics(2)
open: Is the number of limit cycles of a quadratic polynomial vector field on the plane uniformly bounded — i.e., is Hilbert's constant $H(2)$ finite? Formally, for vector fields $P(x,y)\partial_x + Q(x,y)\partial_y$ with $P, Q \in \mathbb{R}[x,y]$ of degree 2 vanishing at the origin, the question asks whether there exists a uniform upper bound $H(2)$ on the number of limit cycles; the proposed approach is to realize limit cycles as closed geodesics of a Riemannian metric placed on the regular part of the phase space.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/277495/limit-cycles-as-closed-geodesics2. The record links an updated proof of the finiteness part of Hilbert's 16th problem at http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=im&paperid=8352&option_lang=eng.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $H(2)$ — the supremum of the number of limit cycles over all quadratic polynomial vector fields — is finite.
why: It is the first open case of the finiteness part of Hilbert's 16th problem, which asks for a uniform bound $H(n)$ for polynomial vector fields of degree $n$; even $n=2$ is unresolved.

title: Graphs with graphic imbalance sequences
open: Suppose every edge of a simple graph joins vertices of different degrees; must the multiset of edge imbalances then be a graphic sequence? Formally, if $imb(e)=|d(u)-d(v)|>0$ for all $e=uv\in E(G)$, is the imbalance sequence $M_G$ always graphic?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). The conjecture has been verified for all such graphs with at most 9 vertices by Vova Skochko. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/140819/graphs-with-graphic-imbalance-sequences
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the Imbalance Conjecture: graphs with $imb(e)>0$ on every edge have graphic imbalance sequences; equivalently, via Erdős–Gallai, that such graphs satisfy the corresponding inequality condition.
why: It would explain when irregularity data alone forces a graphic structure, extending the known fact that imbalance sequences of trees are graphic.

title: How many values a polynomial map misses
open: If a polynomial over an infinite field misses even one value, must it miss infinitely many? Formally: for an infinite field $F$ and $f \in F[x]$ with $M_f(F) = |F \setminus f(F)| > 0$, is $M_f(F)$ necessarily infinite?
status: Posted on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers), where it is community-curated as an open question; the asker knows the answer is positive when $F$ is algebraically closed (the record's statement is truncated at "algebra"), but no general answer is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that for every infinite field $F$ and every non-surjective univariate polynomial $f \in F[x]$, the set $F \setminus f(F)$ is infinite — or an explicit example where a polynomial misses at least one but only finitely many values.
why: It would settle whether the finite-field phenomenon — where a non-surjective $f \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ of degree $d > 0$ satisfies $M_f(\mathbb{F}_q) \geq (q-1)/d$, a bound tending to infinity with $q$ — extends to infinite fields.

title: Has n^2*|sin(n)| limit
open: Does $\lim_{n\to\infty} n^2|\sin(n)|$ equal infinity? Equivalently, does there exist a subsequence $n_k$ of the natural numbers with $\lim_{k\to\infty} n_k^2|\sin(n_k)| = 0$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); no answer is known. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/83550/has-n2sinn-limit.
solved_when: It is proved that either $n^2|\sin(n)| \to \infty$, or a subsequence $n_k$ with $n_k^2|\sin(n_k)| \to 0$ is exhibited.
why: The answer controls how well multiples of $\pi/2$ can be approximated by integers at the $n^2$ scale, a concrete test case for Diophantine approximation of $\pi$.

title: A Special Pair of Models for ZFC (New Version)
open: Can ZFC admit two models $M$ and $N$ with $M\subseteq N$, $\aleph_{1}^{N}=\aleph_{1}^{M}$, and $\aleph_{2}^{N}=\aleph_{\omega +1}^{M}$? Failing a full answer, what partial or analogous results are known for nearby choices of $\aleph$s?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 6, 4 answers); according to Peter's answer there, the problem is still open, and the poster solicits partial or similar results with references. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/146876/a-special-pair-of-models-for-zfc-new-version
solved_when: Two models of ZFC satisfying all three displayed conditions are exhibited (or the existence of such a pair is shown impossible); alternatively, substantive partial or similar results for different but not-too-different $\aleph$s are identified, with references.
why: It tests how much freedom forcing-style extensions have to manipulate the $\aleph$-structure while preserving cardinals, a basic lever in independence results.

title: A Hot Betting On HOD
open: Is the existence of a nontrivial elementary embedding from $HOD$ to $HOD$ an acceptable large cardinal axiom? Formally: whereas there is no nontrivial elementary embedding from $V$ to $V$, and a nontrivial elementary embedding from $L$ to $L$ is an acceptable large cardinal axiom, the question is whether the corresponding embedding on $HOD$ can consistently be taken as a large cardinal axiom.
status: Posed at the end of the paper "Generalizations of the Kunen Inconsistency" by Hamkins, Kirmayer, and Perlmutter (no year given in the record); the question is community-curated on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/145974/a-hot-betting-on-hod, score 6, 1 answers).
solved_when: A determination of whether a nontrivial elementary embedding $j:HOD\to HOD$ is consistent (relative to established large cardinal assumptions) and acceptable as a large cardinal axiom, or a proof that it is not.
why: HOD sits between $L$ and $V$ and exhibits a wide range of behavior between $L$-like and $V$-like, so settling this would clarify which inner-model embedding phenomena generalize beyond $L$ and $V$.

title: Arctangents of odd powers of the golden ratio
open: Do the arctangents of odd powers of the golden ratio $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ admit representations as rational linear combinations of arctangents of positive integers — and is $\arctan\varphi^{17}$ the first odd power for which no such representation exists? Computations give such identities for powers 1 through 15 (e.g. $\arctan\varphi^{7}=3\arctan1+\frac12\,\arctan2-\arctan5$), but none was found for $\arctan\varphi^{17}$, nor for any positive even power of $\varphi$.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 42, 2 answers), posed while attempting to answer a Math StackExchange question; the poster found identities for odd powers up to 15 but could not find one for $\arctan\varphi^{17}$ or for any positive even power. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/210167/arctangents-of-odd-powers-of-the-golden-ratio
solved_when: A proof that $\arctan\varphi^{17}$ has no rational linear combination of arctangents of positive integers equal to it, together with a resolution of the analogous non-existence question for positive even powers of $\varphi$; alternatively, an explicit representation for $\arctan\varphi^{17}$ or for some even power would settle the question in the other direction.
why: It probes the exact boundary of arctangent identities rooted in the golden ratio's algebraic structure, indicating which Fibonacci-related values lie in the rational span of arctangents of integers.

title: What is the status on this conjecture on arithmetic progressions of primes
open: Is it true that for every prime $p$, there is an arithmetic progression of $p$ primes whose least element is $p$ — that is, does $P(p) = p$ hold for all primes $p$, where $P(p)$ denotes the maximum length of an arithmetic progression of primes with least element $p$? This strengthens the Green-Tao theorem by asserting that long prime progressions appear "as soon as possible," and $P(p) \leq p$ is immediate by viewing the progression mod $p$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 26, 1 answers); the question appears at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/260783/what-is-the-status-on-this-conjecture-on-arithmetic-progressions-of-primes.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $P(p) = p$ for every prime $p$.
why: It shows prime arithmetic progressions of length $n$ exist at the smallest possible starting point, sharpening the qualitative Green-Tao theorem into an optimal, "as early as possible" statement.

title: An explicit series representation for the analytic tetration with complex height
open: Is there an explicit series representation for analytic tetration with complex height? More precisely, restricting to real bases in $1<a<e^{1/e}$, can the analytic tetration function (extending the recurrence ${^{-1}a}=0$, ${^{n+1}a}=a^{({^n a})}$, whose sequence of iterates is strictly increasing and converges) be written as an explicit series in the complex height variable?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 25, 3 answers). No explicit series representation is currently recorded; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/259278/an-explicit-series-representation-for-the-analytic-tetration-with-complex-height.
solved_when: An explicit series formula for the analytic tetration $({^z a})$ valid for complex heights $z$ is produced and verified for real bases $1<a<e^{1/e}$.
why: An explicit series would make analytic tetration computable and manipulable like classical special functions, unlocking concrete evaluation, analytic continuation, and asymptotic analysis beyond the current functional-equation constructions.

title: A conjecture based on Wilson's theorem
open: Do the "Wilson pairs" of a prime — the pairings of $\{2,\dots,p-2\}$ into products $\equiv 1 \pmod p$ — have asymptotically equidistributed pair-products, in the sense that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{k \in A_{p_n}}(k-1)}{(p_n)^3}$ exists and equals $\tfrac18$, where $A_{p_n}$ is the multiset of integer pair-products $(a\cdot b)$ with $ab \equiv 1 \pmod{p_n}$? (Lagrange's theorem gives the pairing; e.g. for $p=11$, $A_{p_5}=\{12,12,45,56\}$, and the claimed limit comes from the observed values such as $\frac{11+11+44+55}{11^3}=\frac{1}{11}$ and $\frac{123218233}{997^3}$ for $p=997$.)
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 24, 2 answers). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/225459/a-conjecture-based-on-wilsons-theorem
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $\frac{\sum_{k \in A_{p_n}}(k-1)}{(p_n)^3}$ is determined: either the limit as $n \to \infty$ is proved to be $\tfrac18$, or the conjecture is disproved/refined with the correct asymptotics.
why: A solution would reveal how the multiplicative inverses modulo $p$ are distributed as integers — a concrete bridge between Wilson's theorem and equidistribution questions about modular inverses, with the constant $\tfrac18$ suggesting a clean underlying structure.

title: Can an integer reciprocal series remain rational after a unit shift in the denominator
open: Does there exist an infinite sequence of positive integers $a_n$ (repetitions allowed) such that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and both $S(0)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n}$ and $S(1)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n+1}$ are rational — or can one prove this impossible? The positive integrality of the $a_n$ is the essential restriction: if arbitrary positive reals are allowed, such examples exist by construction, and if negative integers are allowed, telescoping series give examples.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 23, 2 answers). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/513215/can-an-integer-reciprocal-series-remain-rational-after-a-unit-shift-in-the-denom
solved_when: An explicit sequence of positive integers with convergent reciprocal series is produced for which both $S(0)$ and $S(1)$ are rational, or a proof is given that no such sequence exists.
why: It isolates exactly how much arithmetic rigidity integer denominators impose on Egyptian-style series; a resolution either way would sharpen our understanding of which rational values reciprocal series over the integers can attain.

title: Given any five points, we can always draw a pair of non-intersecting circles whose diame
open: Given any five coplanar points, can one always find two disjoint pairs among them such that the circles having those pairs as diameter endpoints do not intersect? Tangent circles count as non-intersecting; coincident circles count as intersecting.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 23, 1 answers); the question is posted at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/459295/conjecture-given-any-five-points-we-can-always-draw-a-pair-of-non-intersecting. The asker tested a generator of five pseudo-random points without finding a counterexample, and noted the analogous statement fails for four points: the vertices of an equilateral triangle plus its centre admit no such pair of non-intersecting circles.
solved_when: The conjecture is proved for all configurations of five coplanar points, or an explicit counterexample configuration is exhibited.
why: A proof or counterexample settles a simply stated extremal-geometry question that resisted attacks on Math SE and MathOverflow, clarifying how many points force a non-intersecting pair of diameter circles (four points do not suffice).

title: Distinct exponents in the factorization of the factorial, a problem of Erdős
open: Does the number of distinct exponents in the prime factorization of $n!$ admit an asymptotic formula — that is, is it true that $h(n) = (c + o(1))\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2}$ for some positive constant $c$, as Erdős conjectured with "no doubt" in 1982? In his paper Erdős proved $c_1\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2} < h(n) < c_2\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2}$ for all sufficiently large $n$, but stated that "we do not know enough about the difference of consecutive primes" to pass to an asymptotic; the question is whether our current knowledge of prime gaps suffices.
status: Erdős proved the two-sided bound with positive constants $c_1, c_2$ in P. Erdős, Miscellaneous problems in number theory, Congressus Numerantium 34 (1982), 25-45 (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1982-08.pdf). He expressed "no doubt" that the asymptotic $h(n) = (c + o(1))\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2}$ holds, attributing the obstacle to insufficient knowledge of the difference of consecutive primes. The question was posed on MathOverflow (score 20, 1 answers: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/413332/distinct-exponents-in-the-factorization-of-the-factorial-a-problem-of-erd%c5%91s) asking whether, after 40 years, enough is now known to prove the conjecture; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of Erdős's conjecture that $h(n) = (c + o(1))\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2}$ as $n \to \infty$ for some positive constant $c$, improving on the known bounds $c_1\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2} < h(n) < c_2\big(\frac{n}{\log n}\big)^{1/2}$ valid for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: Closing the gap between Erdős's two-sided bounds would likely require and reflect new control over the fine distribution of consecutive prime gaps, connecting a concrete multiplicative quantity to hard questions about primes.

title: Several conjectured identities for polylogarithms
open: Is a conjectured explicit linear identity for $\operatorname{Li}_4$ at rational arguments $z\in\{\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac14,\tfrac34,\tfrac19\}$ correct — namely that $720\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac12\right)-2160\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac13\right)+2160\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac23\right)+270\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac14\right)+540\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac34\right)+135\,\operatorname{Li}_4\!\left(\tfrac19\right)$ equals $19\pi^4+30\left(\pi^2-\beta^2\right)\left(10\alpha^2-12\alpha\beta+3\beta^2\right)-30\,\alpha^2\left(19\alpha^2-24\alpha\beta+8\beta^2\right)$, where $\alpha=\ln2$, $\beta=\ln3$? And are several similar conjectured identities for $\operatorname{Li}_5(z)$ involving powers of the golden ratio $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ likewise true?
status: The problem was originally asked at M.SE a couple of years ago with four linked posts; the asker put a bounty on it, but it remained unanswered and was re-posted on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 20 and 1 answer. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/261408/several-conjectured-identities-for-polylogarithms
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the stated $\operatorname{Li}_4$ identity and of the associated $\operatorname{Li}_5$ identities involving powers of $\phi$.
why: These identities probe the structure of polylogarithm values at rational arguments and their relation to $\pi$, logarithms, and algebraic constants such as the golden ratio; resolving them would clarify which weight-4 and weight-5 polylogarithmic combinations collapse to classical constants.

title: A seemingly simple inequality
open: For real numbers $a_i, b_i$ and $n>1$, must the inequality $\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2\ge \sqrt{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^4\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^4\right)}+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 b_i^2$ hold, where the $a_i$ and $b_i$ are not required to be non-negative? Extensive numerical simulations have produced no counterexample.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 19, 4 answers). The inequality is known to hold for $n=2$, and Fedor Petrov observed in his answer that it also follows by an argument used in one of his answers to the related question. The general case remains open, having received no answer on math.SE before being cross-posted. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/259637/a-seemingly-simple-inequality
solved_when: A proof of the inequality for all $n>1$ and all real $a_i, b_i$, or an explicit counterexample.
why: The conjecture was formulated by Fedor Petrov in an attempt to solve a particular case of a related question, so a resolution settles that case; it is also a natural Cauchy–Schwarz-type inequality with the twist that the variables may be negative.

title: The number of points modulo $p$ of certain elliptic curve is $p$ or $p+2$ for $p$ of for
open: Is it true that for primes of the form $p=27a^2+27a+7$, the curve $E_k/\mathbb{F}_p : y^2=x^3+2k^3$ (the quadratic twist of $y^2=x^3+2$, with $k$ a nonzero integer mod $p$) satisfies $\#E_k(\mathbb{F}_p)=p+1+(2k^3/p)$, where $(a/b)$ is the Kronecker symbol — i.e. the point count is always either $p$ or $p+2$? Numerical evidence, including a Sage check with a 200-bit prime $p$ ($a=2^{100}+8$, $p=27a^2+27a+7$, $k=3$), supports the conjecture.
status: This is a community-curated open problem on MathOverflow (score 18, 1 answer). The record gives no published resolution; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/283758/conjecture-the-number-of-points-modulo-p-of-certain-elliptic-curve-is-p-or
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, with counterexample) of Conjecture 1: for every prime $p=27a^2+27a+7$ and every integer $k$ nonzero modulo $p$, $\#E_k(\mathbb{F}_p)=p+1+(2k^3/p)$.
why: A proof would explain a striking rigidity in the traces of these cubic twists, tying point counts of $y^2=x^3+2k^3$ directly to the Kronecker symbol $(2k^3/p)$ for this family of primes; a disproof would expose the limits of the numerical evidence.

title: A curious series related to the asymptotic behavior of the tetration
open: Does the asymptotic behavior of the convergent tetration sequence ${^n a}$, for real bases $1<a<e^{1/e}$, admit a characterization through an explicit series (as posed in the linked MathOverflow question)? Formally, writing $\lambda = -W(-\ln a)$ with $W$ the principal branch of the Lambert W-function (so $0<\lambda<1$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}{^n a}=e^\lambda$), the question asks to analyze the "curious series" governing the approach of ${^n a}$ to its limit.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 18, 3 answers). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/260379/a-curious-series-related-to-the-asymptotic-behavior-of-the-tetration
solved_when: The series identified in the question is rigorously analyzed — its convergence established and its relation to the asymptotics of ${^n a} - e^\lambda$ (with $1<a<e^{1/e}$, $0<\lambda<1$) determined.
why: It would give exact asymptotic control over how finite power towers converge, a basic question about tetration for which the record indicates substantial community interest.

title: Which motivic cohomology groups of complex numbers are non-torsion
open: Which motivic cohomology groups of the complex numbers are non-zero, and better, non-torsion — that is, for which pairs $(i,j)$ is the $i$th cohomology of the motivic complex ${\mathbb{Q}}(j)$ over $\mathbb{C}$ non-zero? The question asks both for unconditional non-vanishing (and "largeness") results and for what should hold conjecturally, and it can be equivalently phrased in the language of $K$-theory.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 18, 1 answers). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/269354/which-motivic-cohomology-groups-of-complex-numbers-are-non-torsion
solved_when: A characterization is given of the pairs $(i,j)$ for which $H^i$ of the complex ${\mathbb{Q}}(j)$ over $\mathbb{C}$ is non-torsion, with unconditional lower bounds and conjectural predictions clearly separated.
why: These groups sit at the interface of motivic cohomology and $K$-theory of $\mathbb{C}$; knowing where they are non-torsion pins down the rank structure of algebraic $K$-groups of the complex numbers.

title: Is there a progress on a solution of the inequality $\pi (m+n) \leq \pi (m) + \pi (n)$
open: Is the prime-counting function subadditive — does $\pi(m+n) \leq \pi(m) + \pi(n)$ hold for all positive integers $m$ and $n$, as Hardy and Littlewood conjectured in 1923? What progress, if any, has been made toward resolving this conjecture?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where a question asking for progress on the inequality received a score of 17 and 5 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/30590/is-there-a-progress-on-a-solution-of-the-inequality-pi-mn-leq-pi-m-p).
solved_when: A proof or disproof of the conjectured inequality $\pi(m+n) \leq \pi(m) + \pi(n)$ for all positive integers $m, n$ is established.
why: Resolving it would settle a 1923 conjecture of Hardy and Littlewood about the distribution of primes, a long-standing question of high community interest that lies outside the standard lists of open problems.

title: Do primes of the form $4k+1$ ever lead the greatest prime factor race
open: Do the numbers whose greatest prime factor is a prime of the form $4k+1$ ever catch up to — or overtake — those whose greatest prime factor is of the form $4k+3$? Formally, with $f_1(n)$ and $f_3(n)$ counting natural numbers $\le n$ whose greatest prime factor is of the form $4k+1$ and $4k+3$ respectively, does $f_1(n) \ge f_3(n)$ ever hold?
status: This is a community-curated MathOverflow question (score 16, 0 answers). Computation up to $n \le 3 \times 10^{10}$ gives $14970975209$ numbers whose greatest prime factor is $4k+1$ versus $15029024755$ whose greatest prime factor is $4k+3$, with no instance of $4k+1$ equaling or taking the lead. In both races the overall proportions are roughly $50\%$ each. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/433862/do-primes-of-the-form-4k1-ever-lead-the-greatest-prime-factor-race
solved_when: Either an $n$ is exhibited with $f_1(n) \ge f_3(n)$, or a proof is given that $f_1(n) < f_3(n)$ for all $n$.
why: It is a natural analogue of Chebyshev's prime race that appears to behave differently: unlike the ordinary race, where the lead changes or ties occur (A038691, A096628), the greatest-prime-factor race shows persistent dominance by $4k+3$, and explaining this would reveal something about how residue classes distribute among large prime factors.

title: Numbers of the form $x^2(x-1) + y^2(y-1) + z^2(z-1)$ with $x,y,z\in\mathbb Z$
open: Is every even integer representable as $x^2(x-1) + y^2(y-1) + z^2(z-1)$ with $x,y,z\in\mathbb Z$, and if so, in infinitely many ways? This is an analogue of Heath-Brown's conjecture that every $k\not\equiv\pm4\pmod9$ has infinitely many representations as $x^3+y^3+z^3$, with the polynomial here being shifted so the cube terms partially cancel.
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow (score 16, 0 answers) with no resolution recorded; it is linked to OEIS sequences A336205 and A336240. A parametric identity $x^2(x-1) + y^2(y-1) + z^2(z-1) = 2a^2(a-1)$ was formulated by the asker based on a comment of Robert Israel at https://oeis.org/A336240. Original question: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/366273/numbers-of-the-form-x2x-1-y2y-1-z2z-1-with-x-y-z-in-mathbb-z
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every even integer admits at least one representation $x^2(x-1)+y^2(y-1)+z^2(z-1)$ with integer $x,y,z$, together with a proof that every such representation count is infinite.
why: The sums-of-three-cubes problem is famous for the difficulty of constructing even a single representation (e.g., of 33 and 42); a shifted form conjectured to represent all even integers infinitely often would give a tractable variant where infinitely many solutions are expected.

title: Maximum matching in a graph with no "shortcuts"
open: Does every directed acyclic graph with no shortcuts and with all indegrees and outdegrees at most 2 admit a large matching? Formally, if $G$ is such a shortcut-free DAG, must the underlying undirected graph $G^\star$ contain a matching of size at least $\frac{1}{4}e(G)$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 15, 3 answers). Small examples support the conjecture, though a general proof appears elusive. A lower bound of $\frac{1}{5}e(G)$ is almost trivial and holds even with shortcuts; with some effort the bound $\frac{2}{9}e(G)$ was proved. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/263982/maximum-matching-in-a-graph-with-no-shortcuts
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture: every DAG $G$ without shortcuts, with indegree and outdegree of every vertex at most 2, has a matching in $G^\star$ of size at least $\frac{1}{4}e(G)$.
why: Resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about how shortcut-freeness forces matchings in the underlying undirected graph; the gap between the trivial $\frac{1}{5}e(G)$ bound, the current $\frac{2}{9}e(G)$, and the conjectured $\frac{1}{4}e(G)$ is where the real difficulty lies.

title: Status of Grothendieck's conjecture on homomorphisms of abelian schemes
open: Is Grothendieck's conjecture on homomorphisms of abelian schemes still open — namely, that if a homomorphism $u_l: T_l(A) \rightarrow T_l(B)$ of $l$-adic Tate modules of abelian schemes over a reduced connected base $S$ (locally of finite type over Spec($\mathbf{Z}$) or a field $k$) specializes at some point $s\in S$ to a map induced by a homomorphism of abelian varieties, then some multiple $n u_l$ with $n>0$ is induced by a homomorphism $v: A \rightarrow B$? And if unresolved in general, what partial results are known in positive characteristic?
status: The question was posed as a community-curated MathOverflow post (score 15, 1 answer). The record states that Grothendieck notes the conjecture follows from Tate's conjectures on algebraic cycles and proves the characteristic-zero base field case (with $n=1$) using the Serre–Tate theorem; no further resolution is recorded. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/123317/status-of-grothendiecks-conjecture-on-homomorphisms-of-abelian-schemes
solved_when: The conjecture is proved (or disproved) in the stated generality: for every such $S$, $A$, $B$, prime $l$, and $u_l$ satisfying the specialization hypothesis, there exist an integer $n>0$ and a homomorphism $v: A \rightarrow B$ with $T_l(v) = n u_l$. Short of that, a satisfactory answer includes any partial results for positive characteristic.
why: The conjecture governs how far fiberwise homomorphisms of abelian varieties lift across a family, and a resolution would complete the picture beyond the characteristic-zero case, where Grothendieck proved the statement via the Serre–Tate theorem.

title: Arithmetic progressions in stopping time of Collatz sequences
open: Do the Collatz stopping times of numbers of the form $2^n+1$ follow a hidden arithmetic structure, as suggested by numerical data (e.g., long runs of consecutive values such as $480, 481, \dots, 483$ or $560, 561, \dots, 570$ in the observed sequence)? More formally, can one characterize or prove the occurrence of arithmetic progressions among the stopping times of the $3n+1$ sequences starting at $2^n+1$?
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow, inspired by simulations of numbers of specific forms and an earlier linked question; it is community-curated there with score 15 and 1 answer. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/348733/arithmetic-progressions-in-stopping-time-of-collatz-sequences
solved_when: A rigorous characterization or proof of the observed arithmetic-progression patterns in the stopping times of $2^n+1$ under the $3n+1$ map is given; absent quantitative targets in the record, this natural criterion applies.
why: It would reveal structure in Collatz stopping times for a natural sparse family of starting values, giving a rare rigorous foothold in a problem area where almost everything remains heuristic.

title: A cubic and six conics problem
open: Given a cubic curve and five conics where each conic meets the cubic in six points and consecutive conics share three points on the cubic, must six distinguished points of intersection (three on the first conic and cubic, three on the fifth conic and cubic) always lie on a single conic? A formal proof (or counterexample) of this asserted incidence theorem is sought.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 14, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/232342/a-cubic-and-six-conics-problem; the problem was posed by the original poster, who describes themselves as an electrical engineer rather than a mathematician, and states the configuration without a proof.
solved_when: A rigorous proof — or disproof by counterexample — of the stated conic membership claim for $P_1, \dots, P_6$ under the given incidence hypotheses is provided.
why: A proof would add a new incidence theorem to the classical toolkit of cubic–conic configurations; long-tail problems like this lie outside standard lists and attract substantial community interest.

title: A conjecture about $\lfloor n!\cdot q/e\rfloor-\,!n\cdot q$
open: For each rational $q$, is the sequence $s_n^{(q)}=\lfloor n!\cdot q/e\rfloor-\,!n\cdot q$ (where $!n$ is the subfactorial) periodic in $n$? Moreover, when $q$ is the reciprocal $1/m$ of a positive integer $m$, is the period exactly $m$ for even $m$ and $2m$ for odd $m$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/222478/a-conjecture-about-lfloor-n-cdot-q-e-rfloor-n-cdot-q.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $s_n^{(q)}$ is periodic for every rational $q$, together with a determination of the period in the case $q=1/m$, namely $p_{1/m}=m$ when $m$ is even and $p_{1/m}=2m$ when $m$ is odd.
why: It would clarify the interplay between the factorial growth of $n!$, the irrationality of $e$, and the subfactorial $!n$ through an explicit periodicity phenomenon accessible to elementary methods.

title: A probability involving areas in a random pentagram inscribed in a circle: Is it really just $\frac1
open: Choose five points uniformly at random on a circle and form the inscribed pentagram; the five triangular "petals" have areas which, taken consecutively (clockwise or anticlockwise), we call $a,b,c,d,e$. Is it exactly true that $P(a^2<bc)=\frac{1}{2}$? Simulations strongly suggest it, but note the curious feature that this near-half probability arises for the *non-symmetrical* triple of consecutive petals: for other pairings, simulations suggest $P(a^2<bd)\approx0.468$, $P(a^2<be)\approx0.505$, and $P(a^2<cd)\approx0.460$, so a proof must explain why only $a^2<bc$ hits exactly one half.
status: The question was posted at MSE and was not answered; it is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 13, 1 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/470132/a-probability-involving-areas-in-a-random-pentagram-inscribed-in-a-circle-is-it. Simulations of $10^7$ random pentagrams yielded a proportion $0.5000179$ satisfying $a^2<bc$, and related simulations suggest $P(a^2<bd)\approx0.468$, $P(a^2<be)\approx0.505$, $P(a^2<cd)\approx0.460$; for other random star polygons $\{n/2\}$ inscribed in a circle, simulations suggest further (truncated in the record). No proof or disproof is known.
solved_when: A rigorous proof (or disproof) that $P(a^2<bc)=\frac{1}{2}$ for three consecutive petals of a random inscribed pentagram; the record's simulation evidence is a proportion of $0.5000179$ over $10^7$ random pentagrams, alongside the simulated values $\approx0.468$, $\approx0.505$, $\approx0.460$ for the non-consecutive-symmetric pairings.
why: It would clarify a subtle exact-vs-coincidental half in a natural geometric probability model, and likely reveal a hidden structure in the joint distribution of consecutive petal areas of random star polygons.

title: What is the Status of Borel conjecture today
open: If two closed aspherical $n$-manifolds have isomorphic fundamental groups, must they be homeomorphic? Formally, this is the Borel conjecture: any homotopy equivalence between closed aspherical manifolds is homotopic to a homeomorphism.
status: Community-curated as an open problem on MathOverflow (question score 13, 1 answer); it remains a long-tail problem outside standard problem lists, with ongoing community interest. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/228595/what-is-the-status-of-borel-conjecture-today
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that any two closed aspherical $n$-manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups are homeomorphic, for all dimensions $n$.
why: It is the rigidity counterpart to the Borel–Novikov conjectures: a positive answer would reduce the topological classification of aspherical manifolds to algebra, namely their fundamental groups.

title: An analogue of the Bass-Quillen conjecture with power or Laurent series
