open: Do projective modules over power or Laurent series rings extend from the base ring, as they do for polynomial rings in the Bass–Quillen conjecture? Formally: if $R$ is regular and $P$ a projective module over $R[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ (or the Laurent-series analogue), is $P \cong Q \otimes_R R[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ for some projective $R$-module $Q$? The polynomial-variable version is the Quillen–Suslin theorem when $R = k$ is a field (every projective $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$-module is free), and the Bass–Quillen conjecture in general — known, e.g., for $R$ of Krull dimension $\leq 2$ and for $R$ a localization of an affine $k$-algebra — but the power and Laurent series analogues remain open.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem drew noticeable interest (score 12, 2 answers). The polynomial-variable case is settled in many cases: for $R$ of Krull dimension $\leq 2$, and when $R$ is a localization of an affine $k$-algebra over a field $k$. The power and Laurent series analogues are posed but unresolved. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/137381/an-analogue-of-the-bass-quillen-conjecture-with-power-or-laurent-series
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that for every regular ring $R$ and every projective $P$ over $R[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$, one has $P \cong Q \otimes_R R[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ for a projective $R$-module $Q$; likewise for the corresponding Laurent-series version.
why: It would extend the homotopy-invariance of projective modules from polynomial to completed variables, clarifying whether completion in the variables behaves like polynomial extension for $K$-theoretic and module-theoretic purposes; the completion step is where such invariance typically breaks.

title: Seeking proof of the Cuckoo Cycle Conjecture
open: Does the Cuckoo Cycle Conjecture about random bipartite graphs hold — that is, can the behavior of cycles in the Cuckoo graph arising from cuckoo hashing be characterized as conjectured? A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture as stated for the random graph model underlying the Cuckoo Cycle proof-of-work scheme would settle the question.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 1 answers). Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/327172/seeking-proof-of-the-cuckoo-cycle-conjecture
solved_when: A rigorous proof or counterexample for the Cuckoo Cycle Conjecture is given, formalizing the conjectured behavior of cycles in the random bipartite Cuckoo graph (with array locations as nodes and item location pairs as edges).
why: It would give a firm theoretical foundation for the Cuckoo Cycle proof-of-work scheme and settle the corresponding question about cycle structure in random bipartite graphs.

title: A conjecture about certain values of the Fabius function
open: Are the integers obtained by clearing denominators of the Fabius function's values at dyadic points $2^{-n}$ always integral — that is, is every term of the sequence $a_n = F(2^{-n})\, 2^{\binom{n-1}{2}} (2n)! \prod_{m=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(4^m-1)$ an integer? The Fabius function is the smooth monotone $F:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ satisfying $F(0)=0$, $F(1-x)=1-F(x)$ for all $x$, and $F'(x)=2F(2x)$ for $0<x<1/2$; it takes rational values at dyadic rational arguments, with $F(2^{-n}) = \frac{1}{n!\,2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}} \sum_{m\ge0}\binom{n}{2m} c_m$, where $c_0=1$ and $c_n = \frac{1}{(4^n-1)(2n+1)}\sum_{m\ge1}\binom{2n+1}{2m+1} c_{n-m}$ (only finitely many terms nonzero).
status: Posed on MathOverflow (score 11, 1 answer), where it is community-curated; the explicit formulas for $F(2^{-n})$ in terms of the recurrence for $c_m$ are known per the cited references. Key works: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/261649/a-conjecture-about-certain-values-of-the-fablius-function
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $a_n$ as defined above is an integer for every $n\ge1$; the conjectured sequence begins $1, 5, 15, 1001, 5985, 2853\ldots$, and the underlying values $F(2^{-n})$ appear as OEIS A272755 / A272757.
why: The Fabius function is a canonical example of a smooth nowhere-analytic function, and integrality of these normalized values would reveal hidden arithmetic structure in its dyadic values, where analysis alone gives only the explicit summation formula above.

title: An open triangle problem in plane geometry
open: Does every triangle $ABC$ contain a point $P$ that is the circumcenter of its own cevian triangle with respect to $ABC$? More precisely, if the cevians through $P$ meet the opposite sides to form a triangle, when is $P$ the circumcenter of that triangle — and can such a point be constructed?
status: The problem was posed in an advanced Plane Geometry forum to several experts, who answered negatively — the point cannot be constructed by ruler and compass, nor even found by computer calculation. The poster conjectures existence for an arbitrary triangle. The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 11, 3 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/408481/an-open-triangle-problem-in-plane-geometry, and remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the existence of such a point $P$ for an arbitrary triangle $ABC$, together with — in the affirmative case — a construction of $P$.
why: It settles a natural fixed-point-type question linking a point to the geometry of its own cevian triangle, extending the classical theory of cevian constructions beyond ruler-and-compass reach.

title: Does the interior of Pascal's triangle contain three consecutive integers
open: Does the interior of Pascal's triangle — the entries excluding $\binom{n}{0},\binom{n}{1},\binom{n}{n-1},\binom{n}{n}$ — contain three consecutive integers? Data from the OEIS list A006987, which enumerates the smallest $10000$ interior entries, shows $15$ pairs of consecutive integers and a single pair separated by $2$, but no triple, and Conjecture 3.1 of *Binomial Collisions and Near Collisions* (asserting a complete list of binomials differing by $1$) would imply no such triple exists — yet even that conjecture falls short of settling the question.
status: Community-curated and unresolved on MathOverflow (score 11, 0 answers), after having defeated Math SE; no answer is known.
solved_when: A proof or disproof that three consecutive integers all occur as interior binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}$ with $2 \le k \le n-2$; equivalently, resolution of whether the near-collision structure suggested by Conjecture 3.1 of *Binomial Collisions and Near Collisions* rules out such a triple.
why: It would settle a natural extremal question about how close binomial coefficients can cluster, sharpening our understanding of binomial collisions and near-collisions; a negative answer would follow from, and lend support to, the conjectured complete classification of binomials differing by $1$.

title: Is new $n$-conjecture as follows correct
open: Given a positive integer $P>1$ with prime factorization $P=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$, define $h(1)=+\infty$ and $h(P)=\min(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$. Is it true that for any pairwise coprime positive integers $P_1,\ldots,P_n$, we have $\min\{h(P_1),\ldots,h(P_n), h(P_1+\cdots+P_n)\}\leq n+1$? The case $n=2$ asserts $\min\{h(P_1), h(P_2), h(P_1+P_2)\}\leq 3$ for coprime $P_1,P_2$.
status: Posed on MathOverflow (community-curated, score 10, 1 answer); the proposer originally asked the $n=2$ case two years earlier in a linked question and reformulated it into the general $n$-conjecture, with $h(1)=+\infty$ set for consistency. Key record: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/365019/is-new-n-conjecture-as-follows-correct
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, by counterexample) of the stated inequality for general $n$, and in particular resolution of the $n=2$ case $\min\{h(P_1), h(P_2), h(P_1+P_2)\}\leq 3$ for coprime $P_1,P_2$.
why: A solution would give a new constraint on how prime powers can be distributed among coprime summands and their sum, in the spirit of the $abc$ conjecture; a counterexample would clarify the limits of such $n$-conjecture generalizations.

title: Why is $\sup f_- (n) \inf f_+ (m) = \frac{5}{4} $
open: Why does the identity $\sup_n f_-(n) \cdot \inf_m f_+(m) = \frac{5}{4}$ hold, where $f_-(n) = \prod_{i=0}^n (\sin(i) - \frac{5}{4})$ and $f_+(m) = \prod_{i=0}^m (\sin(i) + \frac{5}{4})$? A formal explanation is sought: the vanishing of the relevant logarithmic integrals (e.g., $\int_0^{2\pi} \ln(\sin(x) + \frac{5}{4})\,dx = 0$) shows the supremum and infimum are finite, but does not account for the value of their product.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 2 answers). The asker shows the relevant logarithmic integrals vanish or equal $2\pi^2 i$, which "almost" explains the finiteness of the supremum and infimum, and notes finiteness of both can be proven but the value of the product remains unexplained; it is also noted (as "not easy") that there exists a unique pair of entire functions $g_-(x), g_+(x)$. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/322240/why-is-sup-f-n-inf-f-m-frac54
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\sup f_-(n) \inf f_+(m) = \frac{5}{4}$, explaining the value of the product rather than merely the finiteness of both quantities.
why: It resolves a long-standing community puzzle from math.stackexchange/MathOverflow explaining a numerically observed constant; it is a high-interest long-tail problem lying outside standard problem lists.

title: $\sum_{i<j} x_{ij}^\alpha \ge \sum_{i<j} y_{ij}^\alpha $ for arbitrary cyclic polygons
open: Among all polygons inscribed in a given circle, does the regular one maximize the sum of the $\alpha$-th powers of its pairwise chord lengths for every exponent $1 \le \alpha \le 2$? Formally, if $A_1\ldots A_n$ is regular and $B_1\ldots B_n$ is any inscribed polygon, with $x_{ij}=A_iA_j$ and $y_{ij}=B_iB_j$, is $\sum_{i<j} x_{ij}^\alpha \ge \sum_{i<j} y_{ij}^\alpha$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 4 answers); the cases $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=2$ are proved in the asker's papers linked in the record. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/304819/sum-ij-x-ij-alpha-ge-sum-ij-y-ij-alpha-for-arbitrary-cyclic-po
solved_when: The inequality is proved for all $n \ge 3$ and all $\alpha$ with $1 \le \alpha \le 2$; the endpoints $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=2$ are already established in the asker's papers.
why: The inequality says the regular polygon is extremal for a whole family of chord-power sums, interpolating between perimeter-type ($\alpha=1$) and quadratic ($\alpha=2$) quantities; a full proof would unify and extend known triangle inequalities such as $a^\alpha+b^\alpha+c^\alpha \le 3\cdot 3^{\alpha/2}R^\alpha$.

title: A counterexample to a conjecture of Lawson
open: Is there an embedded minimal surface in $\mathbf{S}^3$ that divides the sphere into two domains of unequal volume, contradicting the conjecture Lawson formulated (as quoted by Yau)? The conjecture is known to hold for equatorial spheres and Clifford tori, and the analogous statement was known to fail in higher-dimensional spheres, so the question is whether a counterexample exists in $\mathbf{S}^3$ itself.
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 1 answers). The asker recalls reading that some surface contradicting the conjecture had been found but cannot remember the source, and searches are obscured by Lawson's other, more prominent conjecture. The original source is Shing-Tung Yau, Problem section, Seminar on Differential Geometry, 102 (1982.
solved_when: A specific embedded minimal surface in $\mathbf{S}^3$ dividing the sphere into two domains of unequal volume is identified (with reference), or the conjecture is proved for all embedded minimal surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^3$.
why: Settling this determines whether the equal-volume property is a genuine feature of embedded minimal surfaces in the 3-sphere, separating the 3-dimensional case from the known failures in higher dimensions.

title: Prove that there are no composite integers $n=am+1$ such that $m \ | \ \phi(n)$
open: Suppose $n = am + 1$ with $a$ and $m > 1$ positive integers, and let $p$ be the least prime divisor of $m$; if $a < p$ and $m \mid \phi(n)$, must $n$ be prime? For prime $n = am+1$ we automatically have $\phi(n) = n - 1 = am$, so the conjecture asserts the converse: the divisibility $m \mid \phi(n)$ forces primality.
status: A community-curated MathOverflow question (score 10, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/373497/prove-that-there-are-no-composite-integers-n-am1-such-that-m-phin. Two special cases are proven: when $m$ is a product of two distinct odd primes (see https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3843195/let-n-apq1-prove-that-if-pq-phin-then-n-is-prime ), and when $m$ is a prime power (see https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02327 ). The general case for arbitrary $m > 1$ remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for arbitrary $m > 1$ under the condition $a < p$, where $p$ is the least prime divisor of $m$. No counterexamples have been found so far.
why: It would yield a new primality criterion of the form stated as a theorem in the record, extending classical converse-style tests; a counterexample would expose exactly where such criteria fail.

title: Stolz conjecture
open: Does every smooth, closed spin string manifold of dimension 4k admitting a Riemannian metric of positive Ricci curvature have vanishing Witten genus? Formally: if M is a smooth, closed spin manifold of dimension 4k with 1/2 p_1(M) = 0 and M carries a metric of positive Ricci curvature, must the Witten genus of M vanish?
status: Conjectured by Stolz in 1996; the question of which cases are proven was posed on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 10 and no answers, so no partial-case results are recorded there. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/503553/stolz-conjecture
solved_when: The conjecture is proven in full generality — that is, for every smooth, closed spin manifold of dimension 4k with 1/2 p_1(M) = 0 admitting a positive Ricci curvature metric, the Witten genus is shown to vanish.
why: It would be a Ricci-curvature analogue of the Lichnerowicz theorem, which shows that positive scalar curvature on a spin 4k-manifold forces the A-hat genus to vanish; resolving it would sharpen the link between positive curvature and vanishing elliptic genera.

title: Symmetric function transition matrix and a non-conjecture by Clifford and Stanley
open: What is the dimension of the null-space of the transition matrix $R$ between the power-sum and monomial bases of symmetric functions after subtracting its diagonal $D$? Clifford and Stanley computed the values $d(n)$ for partitions of size $n$ as $1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 19, 24$, but offered no conjecture for the sequence; the problem is to determine or conjecture the behavior of $d(n)$ in general.
status: The entries $R_{\lambda\mu}$ have combinatorial descriptions, e.g. as ordered brick-tableaux of shape $\lambda$ with brick-sizes determined by $\mu$ (see the transition-matrix work of Eğecioğlu and Remmel). The paper on Bottom Schur functions by P. Clifford and R. Stanley (2004) considers $\dim$ of the null-space of $R - D$, computing the sequence above, but makes no conjecture about it. The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 0 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/325899/symmetric-function-transition-matrix-and-a-non-conjecture-by-clifford-and-stanle
solved_when: A formula, recurrence, or asymptotic description (or a well-supported conjecture with structural explanation) of $d(n) = \dim \ker(R - D)$ for all $n$ is given, matching the computed initial terms $1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 19, 24$.
why: A solution would reveal hidden structure in a fundamental transition matrix of symmetric function theory, going beyond the known combinatorial interpretations of the entries themselves.

title: A conjecture of Blakley and Dixon about odd powers of positive matrices
open: Does the inequality conjectured by Blakley and Dixon hold in general? That is, for a symmetric entrywise-nonnegative matrix $S$ and a nonnegative unit vector $u$, is it true that $\langle u, S^k u\rangle^j \ge \langle u, S^j u\rangle^k$ for all odd integers $k \ge j$?
status: Blakley and Dixon posed the conjecture in 1966 and verified it when the right-hand side is sufficiently large; a year earlier, Blakley and Roy verified the $j=1$ case, which also implies the conjecture whenever $j$ divides $k$. No papers citing the 1966 paper and solving the conjecture are known to Google Scholar. The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/236420/a-conjecture-of-blakley-and-dixon-about-odd-powers-of-positive-matrices.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality $\langle u, S^k u\rangle^j \ge \langle u, S^j u\rangle^k$ for all symmetric entrywise-nonnegative matrices $S$, nonnegative unit vectors $u$, and odd integers $k \ge j$, is established.
why: Resolving it would settle a long-standing 1966 conjecture connecting log-convexity-type behavior of moments to entrywise nonnegativity, a basic tool in many matrix analysis arguments.

title: $π(x+y) - π(x) ≤ c·y/\ln(y)$ for some constant $c$
open: Is there an absolute constant $c$ such that $π(x+y) \le π(x) + c·y/\ln(y)$ for all integers $x, y > 1$? That is, does the Second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture $π(x+y) \le π(x) + π(y)$ — believed false (it fails for $y = 3159$ if the k-tuple conjecture holds), but only barely — survive relaxation by a constant factor? And if so, is it likewise known that $π(x+y) \le π(x) + π(y) + c·\sqrt{y}·\ln(y)$ for some constant $c$?
status: The question was posted on Math SE with no answer for a year, then posed on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated (score 9, 1 answers); the original poster reports that Wikipedia and Wolfram state no results affirming or refuting these conjectures, and the record notes the belief that $π(x+y) \le π(x) + π(y)$ fails for some $y$ — specifically for $y = 3159$ if the k-tuple conjecture holds. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/370905/%cf%80xy-%cf%80x-%e2%89%a4-c-y-lny-for-some-constant-c
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the existence of a constant $c$ with $π(x+y) \le π(x) + c·y/\ln(y)$ for all integers $x, y > 1$, together with an answer to the analogous question $π(x+y) \le π(x) + π(y) + c·\sqrt{y}·\ln(y)$.
why: A uniform upper bound on primes in short intervals up to a constant factor would give control over the maximal local density of primes anywhere on the number line, a quantitative weakening of the Second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture that could hold even though the exact conjecture is expected to fail.

title: Status of a conjecture of Hirzebruch
open: If a complex surface is homeomorphic to $S^2 \times S^2$ or $\mathbb{C}P^2 \# \overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}$, must it be biholomorphic to one of the Hirzebruch surfaces — and does the same hold when "homeomorphic" is weakened to "diffeomorphic"?
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow citing a 1994 paper attributing the statement to Hirzebruch; it received 1 answer with a community score of 9, but no definitive resolution is recorded. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/384170/status-of-a-conjecture-of-hirzebruch
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for both the homeomorphic and diffeomorphic versions of the statement, with a reference for whichever variant is established.
why: Settling the diffeomorphic variant in particular would clarify how close the smooth topology of a rational surface determines its complex structure, a basic touchstone for the classification of complex surfaces.

title: Does the sequence formed by Intersecting angle bisector in a pentagon converge
open: Given a non-regular pentagon with no two adjacent angles summing to 360 degrees, iteratively form a new pentagon whose vertices are the intersections of the angle bisectors of the two angles opposite each old vertex (self-intersecting polygons allowed). Does this sequence of pentagons converge?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 9, 1 answers). Original question posed on MSE; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/473957/does-the-sequence-formed-by-intersecting-angle-bisector-in-a-pentagon-converge. No convergence result is recorded.
solved_when: The question of convergence of the sequence $A_nB_nC_nD_nE_n$ is settled for every starting pentagon satisfying the stated hypothesis, with a proof or counterexample.
why: It resolves a natural dynamical-systems question about a geometric iteration on polygons, connecting to the broader study of iterated constructions on polygons.

title: d primality test for specific class of $N=4kp^n+1$
open: Is a conjectured Lucas-sequence primality test for numbers of the form $N=4kp^n+1$ correct? Formally, with $P_m(x)=2^{-m}\cdot((x-\sqrt{x^2-4})^m+(x+\sqrt{x^2-4})^m)$, $N=4kp^n+1$ where $k$ is a positive natural number, $4k<2^n$, $p$ is prime and $n\ge3$, and $a>2$ such that the Jacobi symbols $\left(\frac{a-2}{N}\right)=\left(\frac{a+2}{N}\right)=-1$, the claim is that $N$ is prime if and only if $S_{n-2}\equiv 0 \pmod{N}$, where $S_0=P_{kp^2}(a)\bmod N$ and $S_i=P_p(S_{i-1})$; a further generalization to $N=2kp^n+1$ with $2k<2^n$ is also proposed, and a proof or counterexample is sought.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 9, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/351688/conjectured-primality-test-for-specific-class-of-n-4kpn1; no resolution is recorded there.
solved_when: A rigorous proof or explicit counterexample is given for the stated equivalence (and, secondarily, for the $N=2kp^n+1$ generalization); the proposer has verified the claim computationally for $k\in[1,500]$, $p\le 97$, and $n\in[3,50]$.
why: A proof would yield a fast deterministic primality criterion for this family of Proth-like numbers, while a counterexample would delimit the reliability of a test currently used on empirical evidence alone.

title: A conjecture on intersection of some intervals.
open: If $a\in \mathbb{N}_{\geq3}$, is it true that deleting any single value $b$ with $1\leq b< a$ from the family of intersections makes it nonempty — that is, $\bigcap_{i = 1,\, i\ne b}^{a} \bigcup_{j = 0}^{i-1} \left[\frac{1+aj}{i},\frac{a(j+1)-1}{i}\right] \neq \varnothing$?
status: The full-intersection emptiness (1) was proved at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/131892/a-conjecture-on-intersection-of-some-intervals; the deletion conjecture remains open, with the asker's gap-analysis attempts reaching a dead end. Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 9, 1 answers).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $a\in \mathbb{N}_{\geq3}$ and every $1\leq b< a$, removing the $i=b$ level from the intersection (1) yields a nonempty set.
why: It sharpens the known emptiness result for the full family by showing the empty intersection is a knife-edge phenomenon: every single level is essential, as illustrated by the $a=5$ diagram where removing any one of the top 4 strips creates a region of intersection.

title: Strengthened version of Isoperimetric inequality with n-polygon
open: Is there a strengthened isoperimetric-type inequality for convex polygons? For a convex quadrilateral with side lengths $a,b,c,d$ and area $S$, the known inequality $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 \ge 4S + \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}}\sum(a-b)^2$ holds with best constant $\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}}$; the question is whether, for a convex polygon $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ with side lengths $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ and area $S$, the analogous inequality $\sum_i^n a_i^2 \ge 4\tan\frac{\pi}{n}S + k\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2$ holds, conjecturally with $k = \tan\frac{\pi}{n} - \tan\frac{\pi}{n+2}$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 9, 2 answers); the record states no further partial results. The base inequality $\sum_i^n a_i^2 \ge 4\tan\frac{\pi}{n}S$ follows from the isoperimetric inequality, and the quadrilateral case with best constant $\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}}$ is established in the proposer's paper.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of $\sum_i^n a_i^2 \ge 4\tan\frac{\pi}{n}S + k\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2$ for all convex $n$-gons, with $k = \tan\frac{\pi}{n} - \tan\frac{\pi}{n+2}$ — or a determination of the best constant $k$ for each $n$.
why: It refines the classical isoperimetric bound $\sum_i a_i^2 \ge 4\tan\frac{\pi}{n}S$ by quantifying how irregularity of side lengths forces the sum of squared sides above its minimum, extending the sharp quadrilateral case to general polygons.

title: Is the Tate conjecture known for etale covers of products of curves
open: Let $X$ be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over a finitely generated field $k$. The Tate conjecture — surjectivity of the Chern class map from $\mathrm{Pic}(X) \otimes \mathbb Q_l$ to the Galois invariants of $H^2_{\text{ét}}(X)$ for a prime $l$ invertible in $k$ — is known when $X$ is dominated by a product of curves; does it also hold when $X$ is merely an étale cover of a product of curves? In particular (one may restrict to positive Kodaira dimension), this would follow if every étale cover of a product of curves is dominated by a product of curves — is that the case?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 1 answer). The problem is recorded as a long-tail question outside standard problem lists, with high community interest; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/176879/is-the-tate-conjecture-known-for-etale-covers-of-products-of-curves.
solved_when: Either the Tate conjecture (surjectivity, hence bijectivity, of the cycle class map) is proved for surfaces that are étale covers of a product of curves over a finitely generated field, or the question of whether such covers are dominated by products of curves is resolved (positively implying the conjecture, or negatively reducing it to a distinct problem).
why: Étale covers of products of curves need not themselves be products of curves, so this sits just outside the known dominated-by-a-product case; settling it would extend the Tate conjecture to a genuinely larger class of surfaces, or reveal where the existing method genuinely breaks.

title: Does Vizing's conjecture hold for the infinite graphs
open: Do classical product inequalities for graph invariants, such as Vizing's conjecture relating the domination numbers of a product and its factors, survive when extended from finite graphs to infinite graphs and transfinite-valued invariants? Formally, when is an inequality of the form $i(G*H)\sim f(i(G), i(H))$, with $i$ a graph invariant, $*$ a graph product (tensor, Cartesian, strong, etc.), and $f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, preserved — or made to fail — under such a direct generalization?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 1 answer). The record notes that such inequalities seem vulnerable to the finiteness condition and may fail badly for infinite graphs with transfinite-valued invariants, but no resolution is reported. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/305003/does-vizings-conjecture-hold-for-the-infinite-graphs
solved_when: A characterization (or decisive counterexample) is given of which finite-graph product inequalities, e.g. Vizing's conjecture, remain valid for infinite graphs with transfinite-valued invariants under direct generalization of the original statements.
why: Finite product inequalities are foundational tools in graph theory; understanding exactly how finiteness is used would delimit which classical results can be transferred to infinite graphs and which must be reformulated.

title: Density of the Klarner-Rado Sequence
open: Does the Klarner–Rado sequence (OEIS A005658), which starts with 1 and contains $2n$, $3n+2$, and $6n+3$ whenever it contains $n$, have positive natural density? More precisely, is there a convincing heuristic or rigorous argument that settles Klarner's conjecture in either direction?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 3 answers). The conjecture that the set has positive density is attributed to Klarner via R. Guy's popular article, and Lagarias notes in The Ultimate Challenge book that the conjecture remains open. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/301110/density-of-the-klarner-rado-sequence
solved_when: A proof or disproof that the Klarner–Rado sequence has positive natural density, or a well-justified heuristic that decisively explains the growth rate of the sequence's counting function.
why: The problem is a natural test case for understanding density questions about sets generated by closure under affine maps, a recurring theme in combinatorial number theory.

title: A generalization of Feit–Thompson conjecture, for square-free integers
open: Are there distinct coprime square-free integers $p,q>1$ such that $\frac{p^q-1}{p-1}$ divides $\frac{q^p-1}{q-1}$? The conjecture asserts that no such pair exists, generalizing the Feit–Thompson conjecture from primes to square-free integers.
status: The question was posed on Mathematics Stack Exchange (MSE 3591614, March  23th 2020), where a bounty expired without answers, and was then asked on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 8 and 0 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/357133/a-generalization-of-feit-thompson-conjecture-for-square-free-integers).
solved_when: Either a proof that no distinct coprime square-free integers $p,q>1$ satisfy the divisibility is given, or an explicit counterexample pair is produced.
why: It tests whether the Feit–Thompson conjecture phenomenon is genuinely arithmetic of primes or persists under square-free composition; a counterexample would immediately falsify the natural generalization and reshape expectations about the original conjecture.

title: Order of magnitude of extremely abundant numbers and RH
open: I have always been intrigued by the fact that Riemann's hypothesis is equivalent to the assertion (you can find the scanned paper here ) that the inequality $$\frac{\sigma(n)}n<e^\gamma \log\log n \qquad\qquad\qquad(*)$$ holds for all $n > 5040$ (where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant ). Since $(*)$ is somewhat "quantifiable", I am wondering: Suppose there is an (obviously rather huge) $n$ that violates $(*)$. Then RH is false, so $\zeta(z)$ must have a minimal non trivial zero $z_0$ off the critical line. Taking $n_0$ to be the smallest such $n$, can anything be said about an upper (or, why not, lower) bound of $\Im(z_0)$ or of $\pm\Re(z_0-\frac12)$ in terms of $n_0$? Conversely, if RH is false, so there is such an (obviously rather huge) smallest $z_0$, are there bounds in terms of $|z_0|$ for the smallest $n_0> 5040$ violating $(*)$? It is well-known that if $n_0$ exists, it
status: community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 0 answers)
why: high community interest; long-tail problems outside standard lists

title: Is there a composite number for which this game with composite numbers never ends
open: Does there exist a natural number greater than 1 for which the following iterative game never terminates? Starting from a number that is not a prime power, add to it the next integer having the same number of distinct prime factors; repeat this step at each new value (matching its count of distinct prime factors), with the game ending only upon reaching a number of the form $p^n$ for a prime $p$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question (including the worked example starting at 12, which has two distinct prime factors and receives the next such number, 14) received score 8 and 0 answers. Key works: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/268929/is-there-a-composite-number-for-which-this-game-with-composite-numbers-never-end
solved_when: Either an explicit starting composite number is produced for which the game provably never reaches a prime power, or it is proved that the game terminates at a prime power for every natural number greater than 1.
why: A non-terminating example or a termination proof would reveal how the count of distinct prime factors behaves under this additive process, a concrete and so far untouched question about the distribution of numbers with a fixed number of prime factors.

title: Discriminant of numerator of inverse logarithmic derivative operator iteration
open: Does the numerator of every iterate of the inverse logarithmic derivative operator $T$, defined by $Tf = f/f'$, applied to $x - x^2/2$ have a discriminant that is, up to sign, a perfect square? More precisely, writing $f_n(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ for the numerator of $p_n(x) = T^n(x - x^2/2)$, is $D_n = \pm a_n^2$ for some integer $a_n$ — and do the arithmetic properties of $a_n$ follow a pattern, such as $\nu_2(D_n) = 2^{2n-3}$ for all $n \geq 2$?
status: Posed on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/296328/discriminant-of-numerator-of-inverse-logarithmic-derivative-operator-iteration), where it is community-curated with score 7 and 1 answer; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $D_n = \pm a_n^2$ for every $n$, together with a characterization of the arithmetic of $a_n$; in particular, a proof or counterexample for the conjecture that $\nu_2(D_n) = 2^{2n-3}$ for all $n \geq 2$.
why: The observed initial values ($D_0$ through $D_6$, e.g. $D_6 = 2^{512}5^{20}331^646599695357^2$) suggest a rigid hidden structure in this iteration; explaining it would reveal how the inverse logarithmic derivative operator controls the ramification and factorization behavior of these numerators.

title: Prime constellation conjectures
open: Does the conjecture that every prime constellation not ruled out by residue considerations occurs infinitely often — the purely qualitative weakening of the Hardy–Littlewood prime constellation conjecture that predicts actual densities — have an established name and a known first appearance in the literature? More broadly, what is the canonical circle of conjectures generalizing and refining the twin prime conjecture, including Polignac's conjecture for pairs $(p, p+k)$ with even $k$, the Bunyakovsky conjecture, and Schinzel's hypothesis H?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 7 and 3 answers. No consensus resolution is recorded here.
solved_when: The unnamed qualitative conjecture is identified with a standard name (or shown to have none), together with its first documented appearance in the literature, and the canonical list of related conjectures (Polignac, Hardy–Littlewood, Bunyakovsky, Schinzel's hypothesis H, and any others) is settled.
why: It fixes the terminology and provenance of the web of conjectures around the twin prime conjecture, so that later authors can cite the qualitative claim correctly instead of redefining or misattributing it.

title: A conjecture generalization of Karamata inequality
open: Does the gap between the average of a convex function's values and its value at the average — the Jensen gap — grow under a suitable majorization-like ordering? For a convex real-valued $f$ on an interval $I$, with $x_1 \ge \cdots \ge x_n$ and $y_1 \ge \cdots \ge y_n$ in $I$ satisfying partial-sum conditions (e.g. $x_1 + \cdots + x_i \ge y_1 + \cdots + y_i$ for $i = 1, \dots, n-1$ together with $x_n \le y_n$, or the paired conditions $x_1 + \cdots + x_i \ge y_1 + \cdots + y_i$ and $x_{i+1} + \cdots + x_n \le y_{i+1} + \cdots + y_n$), is it true that $\frac{f(x_1)+\cdots+f(x_n)}{n} - f\!\left(\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}\right) \ge \frac{f(y_1)+\cdots+f(y_n)}{n} - f\!\left(\frac{y_1+\cdots+y_n}{n}\right)$? The motivating case $n=2$ with $f(x)=x^2$ was observed directly, and when $x_1+x_2 = y_1+y_2$ the claim reduces to the classical Karamata inequality.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the problem has received moderate attention (score 7, 2 answers); it originates from an observation on $f(x)=x^2$ and remains outside standard problem lists. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/245092/a-conjecture-generalization-of-karamata-inequality
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for the conjectured comparison of Jensen gaps for all convex $f$ on an interval $I$ and all $n$, under the stated ordering and partial-sum hypotheses (including $x_n \le y_n$ and the paired two-sided partial-sum conditions), generalizing the $n=2$ case with $x_1+x_2 = y_1+y_2$ that yields Karamata's inequality.
why: It would extend the classical majorization framework of Karamata's inequality to comparisons where the totals differ, ordering Jensen gaps rather than function-value sums; a proof would give a new tool for convexity-based estimates, while a counterexample would clarify the limits of majorization-type reasoning.

title: About semiprimal representations of $1$
open: Can the number $1$ always be written as a signed sum $\sum_{k=1}^m (-1)^{i_k} b_{w_k} p_{r_k}$ of $m$ terms, where the primes $p_{r_1},\dots,p_{r_m}$ are mutually different, the primes $b_{w_1},\dots,b_{w_m}$ are mutually different, and each $i_k \in \{1,2\}$ — for every $m \in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ (Conjecture $A_1$)? A stronger form (Conjecture $A_2$, suggested by computation with Peter) drops the exponent choices, and Conjecture $B$ asks whether the number of such representations is infinite for all $m \geq 2$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received score 7 and 1 answer; computational efforts with Peter suggest Conjecture $A_1$ can be strengthened to Conjecture $A_2$.
solved_when: Conjecture $A_1$ is proven for every $m \in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$, or a counterexample is found; and, additionally, the number of representations is shown to be infinite for all $m \geq 2$ (Conjecture $B$).
why: It is a natural additive-representation question about writing $1$ with distinct prime products that sits outside standard problem lists; settling it would clarify how rigid the "mutually different primes" constraint really is for such signed prime sums.

title: on Smith Normal Form for Jucys-Murphy elements (Stanley, Grinberg) - status and generali
open: Has any progress been made on Stanley's 2016 conjectures, posed on the last page of his survey "Smith Normal Form in Combinatorics," concerning the Smith Normal Form of Jucys–Murphy elements (based on computations by Darij Grinberg)? More broadly, are there graphs whose Laplacian matrix — and hence whose Jacobian/sandpile/critical group — can be related to Jucys–Murphy elements?
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 7, 0 answers). Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/484782/conjectures-on-smith-normal-form-for-jucys-murphy-elements-stanley-grinberg
solved_when: The conjectures from the final page of Stanley's survey are resolved (proved or refuted), or an explicit family of graphs is identified whose Laplacian relates to Jucys–Murphy elements.
why: The sandpile/critical group of a graph — viewable as a tropical degeneration of the Jacobian of an algebraic curve — is notoriously hard to compute, so a connection to Jucys–Murphy elements could turn an intractable computation into accessible algebra.

title: Localizing Bondy's metaconjecture on hamiltonicity
open: Is there a meaningful "local" analogue of Bondy's metaconjecture — that any non-trivial condition implying Hamiltonicity also implies pancyclicity (up to a simple family of exceptions) — in which the global hypotheses are replaced by local degree conditions, and if so, what form do the exceptional graphs take?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). Known instances include Dirac [1952] (minimum degree at least $n/2$ implies Hamiltonicity), Bondy [1971] (this condition implies pancyclicity unless $G = K_{n/2,n/2}$), and a corollary of a theorem of Clark [1981]. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/251557/localizing-bondys-metaconjecture-on-hamiltonicity.
solved_when: A precise local condition is formulated and proved (or refuted) as an instance of Bondy's metaconjecture: i.e., a theorem showing that graphs satisfying the local condition are Hamiltonian only if they are pancyclic, with a characterization of the exceptional family of graphs.
why: It would extend Bondy's metaconjecture [1973] from global hypotheses like Dirac's minimum degree condition to local settings, potentially yielding new pancyclicity theorems for sparse or structured graphs where the global condition fails.

title: What is the status of this fifty-year-old conjecture of Kostant
open: Is Kostant's fifty-year-old conjecture, as recorded on page 3.27 of Paul Baum's 1963 thesis, true? Formally: given a torus $T_\ell$ in a compact, connected Lie group $G$ with Weyl group $\Phi$ and subgroup $\Phi'$ of elements preserving $T_\ell$, if $\Phi'$ acts crystallographically on $T_\ell$ and any two points of $T_\ell$ conjugate under $\Phi$ are already conjugate under $\Phi'$, must $T_\ell$ have deficiency zero — equivalently, must the homogeneous space $G/T_\ell$ be formal?
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow (question 222317, score 7) and has received no answers; the conjecture originates from page 3.27 of Paul Baum's 1963 thesis on the cohomology of homogeneous spaces via the Eilenberg–Moore spectral sequence, where it is attributed to B. Kostant. Deficiency is an invariant of pairs of compact Lie groups defined in that thesis, and the most common reformulation of the conclusion is that $G/T_\ell$ is formal.
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for the conjecture as stated: under hypotheses (i) crystallographic action of $\Phi'$ on $T_\ell$ and (ii) $\Phi$-conjugate points of $T_\ell$ being $\Phi'$-conjugate, the conclusion that $T_\ell$ is a subgroup of deficiency zero (e.g., that $G/T_\ell$ is formal) is established or refuted.
why: Resolving it would settle a long-standing question about formality of homogeneous spaces and the behavior of Baum's deficiency invariant, connecting Kostant's conjecture to modern rational homotopy theory.

title: d new primality test for Mersenne numbers
open: Is a Mersenne number $M_q = 2^q - 1$ necessarily prime whenever the sequence defined by $S_0 = 3^2 + 1/3^2$ and $S_{i+1} = S_i^2 - 2 \pmod{M_q}$ returns to its starting value, i.e. $S_{q-1} \equiv S_0 \pmod{M_q}$? More precisely, the conjecture asserts that $M_q$ is prime if and only if any of the following holds: $S_{q-1} \equiv S_0 \pmod{M_q}$; $\prod_{0}^{q-2} S_i \equiv 1 \pmod{M_q}$; or $S_i \not\equiv S_0 \pmod{M_q}$ for all $0 < i < q-1$ — and the forward direction is already proved, so a proof (or refutation) of the converse is what remains.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers). The easy direction — if $M_q$ is prime then $S_{q-1} \equiv S_0 \pmod{M_q}$ — has already been proven; see http://tony.reix.free.fr/Mersenne/ConjectureLLTCyclesMersenne.pdf. The converse remains open. Original question: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/216174/conjectured-new-primality-test-for-mersenne-numbers.
solved_when: The conjecture is settled: a proof that if $M_q$ satisfies any of the three equivalent stated conditions (return of the cycle at step $q-1$, the product condition $\prod_{0}^{q-2} S_i \equiv 1 \pmod{M_q}$, or absence of return $S_i \not\equiv S_0$ for $0 < i < q-1$) then $M_q$ is prime, or a counterexample refuting it.
why: The classic Lucas–Lehmer test for Mersenne numbers rests on the binary tree of the digraph under $x \mapsto x^2 - 2 \pmod{M_q}$; this conjectured test instead exploits a cycle of the same digraph, so proving the converse would validate a genuinely new route to certifying Mersenne primes.

title: An elementary expression for $_3F_2(1,1,9/4;2,2;-1)$
open: Is the series $S=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n\ \Gamma\left(\frac{5}{4}+n\right)}{n^2\ \Gamma(n)}$, equivalently $S=-\frac{5}{16}\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,{_3F_2}\left(1,1,\frac{9}{4};2,2;-1\right)$, expressible in elementary terms? A conjectured candidate is $S\stackrel{?}{=}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}{16}\Bigg(8\sqrt[4]{8}-16-\ln\frac{24\sqrt{69708+49291\sqrt{2}}+3168\sqrt{2}+4481}{4096}+\arctan\frac{24\sqrt{49291\sqrt{2}-13260}}{6913}\Bigg)$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 6, 1 answer). The proposer's derivation is long but non-rigorous, relying on heuristics such as guessing sequence formulas via Mathematica's FindSequenceFunction and OEIS superseeker, and recognizing approximate numeric quantities with RootApproximant and TranscendentalRecognize. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/132269/an-elementary-expression-for-3f-21-1-9-42-2-1
solved_when: The conjectured identity is rigorously proved or disproved — that is, a proof (or refutation) is given of the equality between $S$ and the displayed elementary expression.
why: It would settle whether a nontrivial $_3F_2$ value at $-1$ admits an elementary closed form, a representative case for hypergeometric constants at irrational-leaning parameters; the derivation so far rests on non-rigorous guessing tools and thus proves nothing.

title: Is there an even number $a$ such that $a^{2^{n}}+1$ is prime for infinitely many $n$
open: Does there exist an even number $a$ such that $a^{2^{n}}+1$ is prime for infinitely many $n$? Equivalently from the record, one may ask: for even $a$, are there infinitely many $n$ for which $a^{2^{n}}+1$ is composite?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 6 and 1 answer (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/404209/is-there-an-even-number-a-such-that-a2n1-is-prime-for-infinitely-many).
solved_when: An explicit even integer $a$ is exhibited together with a proof that the set $\{n : a^{2^{n}}+1 \text{ is prime}\}$ is infinite (or, for the companion question, a proof that for even $a$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $a^{2^{n}}+1$ composite).
why: Resolving it would settle a natural generalization of the Fermat-prime phenomenon to even bases, a long-tail question of independent community interest that sits outside standard problem lists.

title: Zero divisors in complex group algebras of residually finite groups
open: Is there a universal function bounding the exponent of the subgroup generated by a zero divisor's support in terms of the size of the support of the element it annihilates? Formally: does there exist $f:\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that whenever $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}[G]$ are non-zero, $\mathbb{C}[G]$ the complex group algebra of a finite group $G$, with $1\in \text{supp}(\alpha) \cap \text{supp}(\beta)$, $|\text{supp}(\alpha)|\leq |\text{supp}(\beta)|$, and $\alpha \cdot \beta = 0$, then $\text{exp}(\langle \text{supp}(\alpha) \rangle) \leq f(|\text{supp}(\beta)|)$, where $\text{exp}(H)$ is the exponent of $H$ and $\text{supp}(\gamma)=\{g \in G \mid \gamma_g \neq 0\}$ for $\gamma=\sum_{g\in G}\gamma_g\, g$?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 6, 1 answers), discussed at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/313639/zero-divisors-in-complex-group-algebras-of-residually-finite-groups.
solved_when: Such a function $f$ is exhibited (or proven to exist), with the bound $\text{exp}(\langle \text{supp}(\alpha) \rangle) \leq f(|\text{supp}(\beta)|)$ holding for all finite groups $G$ and all non-zero $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{C}[G]$ with $1\in \text{supp}(\alpha)\cap\text{supp}(\beta)$, $|\text{supp}(\alpha)|\leq|\text{supp}(\beta)|$, and $\alpha\beta=0$; disproving the existence of any such $f$ closes the problem negatively.
why: A positive answer would imply that the support of any zero divisor in the complex group algebra of any residually finite group generates a finite subgroup, a structural constraint on zero divisors far beyond torsion-free cases.

title: Does the equation $\sigma(\sigma(x^2))=2x\sigma(x)$ have any odd solutions
open: Does the equation $\sigma(\sigma(x^2))=2x\sigma(x)$ have any odd solutions, where $\sigma(x)$ denotes the classical sum-of-divisors function? Formally: determine whether there exists an odd positive integer $x$ satisfying the identity, or prove that none does.
status: The question was posted on Math StackExchange in early August 2020 and, despite several upvotes, received no responses; it was cross-posted to MathOverflow (score 6, 0 answers). A computational search in Sage Cell Server using Pari-GP over $1 < x \leq 10^6$ found only two solutions, $x_1 = 9516 = 2^2\cdot 3\cdot 13\cdot 61$ and $x_2 = 380640 = 2^5\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 13\cdot 61$, both even; the interpreter crashes when a search limit of $10^7$ is specified.
solved_when: An odd positive integer $x$ with $\sigma(\sigma(x^2))=2x\sigma(x)$ is exhibited, or a proof is given that no odd solution exists. (A computational search up to $10^6$ found only the even solutions $x=9516$ and $x=380640$.)
why: A resolution either way would settle a natural arithmetic-analytic question about the sum-of-divisors function iterating over squares, adding a data point on how such divisor-sum identities behave off the even integers.

title: about minimal number of edge crossings in complete bipartite graphs
open: What is the minimum number of edge crossings $cr(K_{m,n})$ in a drawing of the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$, as conjectured in Turán's brick factory problem — and in particular, has an asymptotic approach (letting $n\to\infty$) been successfully attempted?
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow (score 5, 2 answers) by a reader studying the original papers of Zarankiewicz ("On a problem of P. Turan concerning graphs," 1954) and Urbanik ("Solution du problème posé par P. Turán," 1955) after reading the Wikipedia article on Turán's brick factory problem.
solved_when: A determination of $cr(K_{m,n})$, or at minimum a successful asymptotic analysis as $n\to\infty$ with references establishing it.
why: Resolving the conjecture would settle a long-standing, community-vetted open problem originating with Turán that lies outside the standard lists of open problems, and would clarify the extremal crossing behavior of complete bipartite graphs.

title: Is the following weak version of second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture already known
open: Is it known that for every integer $k\ge 1$ there exists a constant $M_k>0$ such that $\pi(ky)+\pi(y)>\pi((k+1)y)$ holds for all real $y\ge M_k$, where $\pi$ is the prime counting function? In other words, does the Second Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture — which asserts $\pi(x)+\pi(y)\ge \pi(x+y)$ for all $x,y\ge 2$, equivalently $\pi(ky)+\pi(y)\ge \pi((k+1)y)$ for all $k\ge 1$ and real $y$ — hold at least eventually in $y$, for each fixed $k$?
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 5 and 1 answer; the proposer searched for related results but could not find this exact statement in the literature (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/312447/is-the-following-weak-version-of-second-hardy-littlewood-conjecture-already-know).
solved_when: The asymptotic inequality $\pi(ky)+\pi(y)>\pi((k+1)y)$ is proved for all $y\ge M_k$ for each fixed $k\ge 1$, or the result is identified in existing literature.
why: It would establish that the Second Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture, which is known to be in tension with the First Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture, holds at least in an eventual, fixed-$k$ regime, clarifying how far the conjecture survives in a weakened form.

title: A conjecture associated with n-gon cut curve of degree m
open: When do the mn points obtained by marking m points on each side of an n-gon all lie on a single curve of degree m? The conjecture asserts that the points $B_{ij}$ on the sides $A_iA_{i+1}$ lie on such a curve if and only if $\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{j=1}^m \frac{\overline{B_{ij}A_i}}{\overline{B_{ij}A_{i+1}}}=1$, where $A_{n+1}=A_1$ — a proposed generalization of a known Carnot-type theorem for cubics stated in a Math StackExchange question.
status: The conjecture was posed by an electrical engineer on MathOverflow as a community-curated open question (score 5, with 1 answer); no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: The conjecture is proved or disproved: a proof (or counterexample) that the $mn$ points $B_{ij}$ lie on a curve of degree $m$ exactly when the stated product of directed ratios equals 1, for general $n$ and $m$.
why: It would extend the Carnot-type theorem for cubics to curves of arbitrary degree cut by arbitrary polygons, giving a clean incidence criterion for when a polygon's marked points lie on a common low-degree curve.

title: Minimizing an expression with sum of digits
open: Is the linear combination of digit sums $P(n) = 10 \cdot S_5(n) + 12 \cdot S_2(n) - 5 \cdot S_3(n)$ always nonnegative, with equality only at $n = 19925000$? More generally, is there a method to minimize $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i S_{b_i}(n)$ for arbitrary coefficients $a_i$ and bases $b_i$ — including the special case $Q(n) = 10 \cdot S_5(3^n - 1) + 12 \cdot S_2(3^n - 1) - 2n$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 5, 2 answers). Numerical evidence suggests the minimum of $P(n)$ is $0$ and the maximum tends to infinity; even candidates like $n = 3^m - 1$ do not push $P(n)$ below $0$. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/503437/minimizing-an-expression-with-sum-of-digits.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $P(n) \geq 0$ for all $n$, with equality characterization at $n = 19925000$; ideally together with a method minimizing $Q(n)$ and the general expression $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i S_{b_i}(n)$.
why: A solution would provide the first general technique for minimizing signed linear combinations of digit sums in different bases, a natural meeting point of Diophantine approximation and additive number theory currently tractable only by case-by-case computation.

title: Heuristics for the very little torsion in the cohomology of Shimura variety
open: What explains the strikingly small amount of torsion in the cohomology of certain locally symmetric spaces? Formally, if $G$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-semisimple group of zero defect (which includes the Shimura variety case), $K \subset G(\mathbb{R})$ a maximal compact subgroup, $\Gamma \subset G(\mathbb{Q})$ a congruence subgroup, $X_\Gamma = \Gamma \backslash G(\mathbb{R})/K$, and $\Gamma_N$ a descending family of congruence subgroups with $\cap \Gamma_N = \{1\}$, what heuristics support the statement $\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{\log |\mathrm{H}^i(X_{\Gamma_N}, \mathbb{Z})_{tors}|}{[\Gamma : \Gamma_N]} = 0$, and what evidence — particularly in the Shimura variety case — is known?
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 5, 0 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/401358/heuristics-for-the-very-little-torsion-in-the-cohomology-of-shimura-variety.
solved_when: A convincing heuristic or conceptual explanation for the vanishing limit above is given, together with evidence (e.g., known cases such as Shimura varieties) supporting the conjecture.
why: This is part of Conjecture 1.3 of N. Bergeron and A. Venkatesh's "The asymptotic growth of torsion homology for arithmetic groups," so resolving it would illuminate the broader conjectural picture of torsion in cohomology of arithmetic groups.

title: The Krzyż Conjecture
open: What is the current status of the Krzyż conjecture, which asserts that for every holomorphic non-vanishing $f:\mathbb{D}\to \bar{\mathbb{D}}$, the coefficients $a_n$ of its power series satisfy $|a_n| \le 2/e$, with equality approached by the extremal function $f(z)=e^{\frac{z^n+1}{z^n-1}}$? In particular, can the conjecture be settled for coefficients $n>5$, where it remains open according to "The Krzyż Conjecture Revisited" (2014), and can the gaps in S. Krushkal's claimed proof be identified or repaired?
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 5, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/297054/the-krzy%c5%bc-conjecture. The paper "The Krzyż Conjecture Revisited" (2014) states the problem is open for coefficients $n>5$. A preprint by S. Krushkal claims a proof but remains unpublished in a reputable journal; the revisiting paper notes that Krushkal's unpublished preprint, "in spite of some gaps, contains a wealth of geometric and analytic ideas which may be useful for a further study of problems of this type."
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $|a_n| \le 2/e$ for all holomorphic non-vanishing self-maps of the disk and all $n$, extending beyond the verified range $n \le 5$; alternatively, a verification that Krushkal's preprint constitutes a complete proof or an identification of its gaps.
why: Settling it would resolve a classical sharp coefficient bound for non-vanishing bounded holomorphic functions, and the geometric and analytic ideas in Krushkal's unpublished preprint are said to be useful for further problems of this type.

title: The set of numbers $a+b$ such that $ma^2+nb^2$ is prime
open: For coprime positive integers $m$ and $n$, does the set of sums $a+b$ arising from positive integers $a,b$ with $ma^2+nb^2$ an odd prime eventually coincide exactly with the integers coprime to $m+n$? Formally, is there always a minimal natural number $N_{mn}$ such that $\{a+b>N_{mn}\mid a,b\in\mathbb N^+\wedge ma^2+nb^2\in\mathbb P_{>2}\} = \{ k > N_{mn} \mid \gcd(k,m+n)=1\}$? (Tests for $k\leq 10^8$ suggest $N_{11}=1$; the record tabulates largest minimal $N_{mn}$ for $k\leq 10^5$, with 0 marking $\gcd(m,n)>1$.)
status: The problem is posed as a community-curated, unanswered MathOverflow question (score 5, 0 answers); no answer or partial result is recorded.
solved_when: For every coprime pair $(m,n)$, a finite threshold $N_{mn}$ is proven to exist such that the equality $\{a+b>N_{mn}\mid ma^2+nb^2\in\mathbb P_{>2}\} = \{k>N_{mn}\mid \gcd(k,m+n)=1\}$ holds; establishing the specific value $N_{11}=1$, suggested by tests up to $k\leq 10^8$, would be a notable instance.
why: A proof would show that primality of such quadratic forms captures exactly the residue condition $\gcd(k,m+n)=1$ beyond a finite window, turning scattered computational data into a structural statement about primes represented by binary quadratic forms.

title: Are concatenations of two consecutive Mersenne numbers which are congruent to 6 mod 7 necessarily co
open: Must every number formed by concatenating the consecutive Mersenne numbers $2^n-1$ and $2^{n-1}-1$ with $2^n-1 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$ be composite, or does a prime exist for this residue? More precisely, is there hidden arithmetic structure forcing a non-trivial factor in the residue-$6$ case, or did the extensive search simply miss one by bad luck?
status: Asked by Enzo Creti on MathOverflow (score 4, 1 answers), following his MSE question: primes were found for all residues modulo $7$ except residue $6$, while residue $1$ occurs only with half frequency. A search up to $n \le 366800$ produced the primes at $n = [2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 12, 19, 22, 36, 46, 51, 67, 79, 215, 359, 394, 451, 1323, 2131, 3336, 3371, 6231, 19179, 39699, 51456, 56238, 69660, 75894, 79798, 92020, 174968, 176006, 181015, 285019, 331259, 360787, 366770]$; exponent $541456$ also leads to a prime. Search details are posted on GitHub; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/294527/are-concatenations-of-two-consecutive-mersenne-numbers-which-are-congruent-to-6.
solved_when: Either a prime concatenation is exhibited with the Mersenne number congruent to $6$ modulo $7$, or a proof is given that all such concatenations are composite.
why: A proof of forced compositeness would reveal unexpected multiplicative structure linking concatenation to Mersenne residues modulo 7, while a prime example would settle a computationally observed anomaly that defies the heuristic frequency of the other residues.

title: $\forall n>3 , \text{gpf}(y_n)>\text{gpf}(y_1)$
open: For a squarefree integer $d > 1$, let $(x_n, y_n)$ be the $n$-th Pell solution of $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$, and let $\mathrm{gpf}(m)$ denote the greatest prime factor of $m$. Is it true for every such $d$ that $\mathrm{gpf}(y_n) > \mathrm{gpf}(y_1)$ for all $n > 3$? More generally, can one prove an effective lower bound on $\mathrm{gpf}(y_n)$ that grows with $n$?
status: This is a community-vetted open problem hosted on MathOverflow (score 4, 1 answer). Evidence for the conjecture includes the case $d = 263$, where $y_1 = 8579 = 23 \times 373$, $y_2 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 11 \times 17 \times 23 \times 31 \times 373$, $y_3 = 5 \times 7 \times 19 \times 23 \times 29 \times 101 \times 127 \times 313 \times 373$, and $y_4 = 2^5 \times 3 \times 11 \times 17 \times 23 \times 31 \times 373 \times 184913 \times 209359$, while subsequent terms appear divisible by very large primes, e.g. $\mathrm{gpf}(y_{17}) = 15297814408905184219513305009152416741 \approx 1.53 \times 10^{37}$. No general proof is recorded. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/513304/conjecture-forall-n3-textgpfy-n-textgpfy-1
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) of the claim that for every squarefree $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{>1}$ and its Pell solutions, $\mathrm{gpf}(y_n) > \mathrm{gpf}(y_1)$ holds for all $n > 3$; ideally accompanied by a quantitative lower bound on $\mathrm{gpf}(y_n)$ in terms of $n$.
why: It would reveal how the prime factorization of Pell solution sequences evolves, turning an observed phenomenon (later $y_n$ carrying very large prime factors) into a theorem, and connect to broader questions on greatest prime factors of linear recurrence sequences.

title: A conjecture like Cayley–Bacharach theorem
open: Does a Cayley–Bacharach-type statement hold for six points on the intersection of a conic and a cubic? Given six points $A, A', B, B', C, C'$ on a conic and a cubic, if the conic through $B, B', C, C'$ meets the cubic again at $A_1, A_2$, the conic through $C, C', A, A'$ meets it again at $B_1, B_2$, and the conic through $A, A', B, B'$ meets it again at $C_1, C_2$, must the six points $A_1, A_2, B_1, B_2, C_1, C_2$ lie on a conic — with the further consequence that if $A_1, B_1, C_1$ are collinear then $A_2, B_2, C_2$ are collinear?
status: The conjecture is posted and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 4, 1 answers) and was checked experimentally in GeoGebra ("ggb"); it includes the general case and the special case where the cubic is three lines. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/217461/a-conjecture-like-cayley-bacharach-theorem
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the general conjecture for six points on a conic and a cubic, including the collinearity consequence; and of the stated special case where the cubic degenerates into three lines, so that the six points $A_1, A_2, B_1, B_2, C_1, C_2$ obtained as intersections with the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ are shown (or not) to lie on a conic with the same collinearity implication.
why: It would extend the classical Cayley–Bacharach phenomenon to this configuration, giving a new incidence theorem for points on conics and cubics that could be used in proofs relying on such residual-intersection constructions.

title: A $2$-fully normal space which is not finitely-fully normal
open: Is every 2-fully normal space also finitely-fully normal? Formally, Mansfield conjectures the existence of a space in which every open cover has a 2-star open refinement, yet some open cover admits no refinement that is simultaneously an $n$-star refinement for all $n\in\omega$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 4, 0 answers). Goldman proved that $n$-fully normal is equivalent to $2$-fully normal, while searches turned up only conjectures about the almost $2$-fully normal property (strongly collectionwise normal) rather than Mansfield's conjecture. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/506499/a-2-fully-normal-space-which-is-not-finitely-fully-normal
solved_when: A construction of a $2$-fully normal space that is not finitely-fully normal is given, or a proof that $2$-fully normality implies finite-full normality.
why: It separates two natural strengthenings of full normality at the first possible level, clarifying the hierarchy of star-refinement properties in covering theory.

title: Optimal covering trails for every $k$-dimensional cubic lattice $\mathbb{N}^k := \{(x_1, x_2, \dots,
open: What is the minimum number of line segments needed in a polygonal chain that visits every point of the $k$-dimensional grid $\mathcal{H}(n,k) := \{0,1,\ldots,n-1\} \times \cdots \times \{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$? Formally, writing $h(n,k)$ for this minimum link count — with $h_l(n,k)$ and $h_u(n,k)$ denoting the known lower and upper bounds, respectively — can the gap between these bounds be narrowed, or $h(n,k)$ determined exactly?
status: Posed on MathOverflow (score 4, 0 answers), where the asker reports a dozen years of work on this class of problems without further improvement; no answer is currently recorded. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/462557/optimal-covering-trails-for-every-k-dimensional-cubic-lattice-mathbbnk
solved_when: An exact characterization of $h(n,k)$ for all $n$ and $k$ (or, short of that, any improvement to the existing bounds $h_l(n,k)$ and $h_u(n,k)$), consistent with the base case $h(n,1)=1$.
why: Closing the gap would settle a natural geometric-optimization question about the cheapest polygonal traversal of lattice point sets, a long-tail problem with community interest that sits outside standard problem lists.

title: A conjecture on consistent monotone sequences of polynomials in Bernstein form
open: Consider a polynomial in Bernstein form of degree $n$, $P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_k {n \choose k} x^k (1-x)^{n-k}$, and recall that the degree-$n$ Bernstein polynomial of a function $f(\lambda)$ has Bernstein coefficients $f(k/n)$, which in general differs from $f$ even when $f$ is a polynomial. Given $f(\lambda):[0,1]\to(0,1)$ with a continuous $r$-th derivative ($r\ge 1$), with $M$ the maximum of the absolute value of $f$ and its derivatives up to the $r$-th, and a sequence of operators $W_{2^0}(g; \lambda), W_{2^1}(g; \lambda), \dots$ mapping continuous functions on $[0,1]$ to bounded functions on $[0,1]$ and converging uniformly to $f$, prove or disprove the stated conjecture.
status: The problem is posted on MathOverflow (score 4, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/427595/a-conjecture-on-consistent-monotone-sequences-of-polynomials-in-bernstein-form and has received no answers; the record is community-curated.
solved_when: The conjecture — formulated for the setup above with $f:[0,1]\to(0,1)$ having $r\ge 1$ continuous derivatives, bound $M$, and the operator sequence $W_{2^i}$ — is either proved in full or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: The record cites high community interest and its nature as a long-tail problem outside standard problem lists; resolving it would settle a community-vetted question on approximation of smooth functions by Bernstein-form polynomial operators.

title: there exist infinite many $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $S_n-[S_n]<\frac{1}{n^2}$
open: Let $S_n := 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \ldots + \frac1n$ denote the $n$-th harmonic number, and let $[x]$ be the largest integer not exceeding $x$. Is the set of natural numbers $n$ for which the fractional part $S_n - [S_n]$ is smaller than $\frac{1}{n^2}$ infinite? The question was previously asked on math.SE without receiving any answers.
status: The problem is community-curated and community-vetted on MathOverflow, where it has a score of 4 and 0 answers (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/258097/there-exist-infinite-many-n-in-mathbbn-such-that-s-n-s-n-frac1n2); it was also asked earlier on math.SE without receiving any answers.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many $n \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $S_n - [S_n] < \frac{1}{n^2}$, i.e. that the fractional parts of the harmonic numbers come within $\frac{1}{n^2}$ of an integer for infinitely many $n$ — or, alternatively, an argument showing that only finitely many such $n$ exist.
why: It probes how well harmonic sums can be approximated by integers, a concrete test case for questions about the distribution of fractional parts of slowly growing sequences where standard equidistribution tools give no information at such a fine $1/n^2$ scale.

title: Find all positive integers $n$ such that $n+\tau{(n)}=2\varphi{(n)}$
open: Are the only positive integers $n$ satisfying $n + \tau(n) = 2\varphi(n)$ precisely $n = 1$ and $n = 9$? Here $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function and $\tau$ is the divisor-counting function; the conjecture is that no further solutions exist.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answers). The original poster verified $n = 1$ and $n = 9$ as solutions and reports extensive search yielding no others, but no proof is known. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/295656/find-all-positive-integers-n-such-that-n-taun-2-varphin
solved_when: A proof (or disproof by explicit example) that the solution set of $n + \tau(n) = 2\varphi(n)$ over the positive integers is exactly $\{1, 9\}$, with any additional solutions fully exhibited.
why: It resolves a natural Diophantine equation mixing additive and multiplicative arithmetic functions, clarifying how the divisor count can perturb the known structure of equations between $n$ and $\varphi(n)$.

title: Solve this diophantine equation: $m^4+n^4=10m^2n^2+1$
open: Are $(m,n)=(0,1),(0,-1),(1,0),(-1,0)$ the only integer solutions of $m^4+n^4=10m^2n^2+1$? That is, does this Diophantine equation admit no integer solutions beyond the four trivial ones?
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow as a conjecture that the four listed solutions are the only ones, with the asker unable to prove it; it is community-curated there (score 3, 1 answer). Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/270728/solve-this-diophantine-equation-m4n4-10m2n21
solved_when: A proof (or disproof via an explicit additional solution) that the integer solutions of $m^4+n^4=10m^2n^2+1$ are exactly $(0,1),(0,-1),(1,0),(-1,0)$.
why: Resolves a concrete Diophantine equation of community interest whose behavior is suspected but unproved, illustrating the phenomenon of equations with no integer solutions despite local solubility.

title: Integer valued polynomials over several variables
open: Can every polynomial in two variables with rational coefficients that takes integer values on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ be built up from one-variable integer-valued polynomials? Formally, writing $f(X,Y)=p_{00}+\sum_{\gcd(i,j)=1}p_{ij}(X^iY^j)$ with $p_{ij}\in\mathbb{Q}[t]$, is the ring of integer-valued polynomials in two variables equal to the ring of all such sums where each $p_{ij}$ is integer-valued on $\mathbb{Z}$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answer): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/320323/integer-valued-polynomials-over-several-variables. No resolution recorded.
solved_when: A proof that the two rings coincide, or an explicit counterexample of an integer-valued two-variable polynomial not expressible as a sum of one-variable integer-valued polynomials applied to monomials $X^iY^j$ with $\gcd(i,j)=1$.
why: It would clarify whether multivariable integer-valued polynomial rings are generated by their one-variable building blocks, a basic structural question about these classical rings.

title: A conjecture regarding odd perfect numbers
open: Does a certain ratio identity connect the Eulerian components of an odd perfect number? Concretely, writing an odd perfect number (if one exists) in Euler's form $n = p^k m^2$ with $p \equiv k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\gcd(p,m)=1$, does the ratio $\frac{D(m^2)}{s(p^k)}$ admit the conjectured form derived from the fundamental equality $\frac{\sigma(m^2)}{p^k} = \frac{2m^2}{\sigma(p^k)} = \gcd(m^2, \sigma(m^2))$?
status: The question was asked on Math StackExchange in June 2018, received no responses there, and was cross-posted to MathOverflow (question 310919), where it is community-curated with score 3 and 4 answers.
solved_when: The conjectured identity involving $\frac{D(m^2)}{s(p^k)}$, where $D(z) := 2z - \sigma(z)$ and $s(z) := \sigma(z) - z$, is proved or disproved for all odd perfect numbers $n = p^k m^2$ in Euler's form.
why: A proof would yield new structural constraints on the Eulerian decomposition of any odd perfect number, adding to the toolkit for attacking the ancient existence question; a disproof would eliminate a proposed identity and clarify which derived equalities actually hold.

title: If there are two primes at an even distance $k$ is there another disjoint pair of primes also at dis
open: If two primes sit an even distance $k$ apart, must there exist a second pair of primes — disjoint from the first — also separated by exactly $k$? Formally: given primes $p,q$ with $q-p=k$ even, do there exist primes $p',q'$ with $q'-p'=k$ and $\{p',q'\}\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing$? (The primes in either pair need not be consecutive.)
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answer). No resolution recorded; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/176219/if-there-are-two-primes-at-an-even-distance-k-is-there-another-disjoint-pair-o
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, of the statement that every prime pair at an even distance $k$ admits another prime pair at the same distance $k$ sharing no elements with it.
why: A positive answer would follow from a weak form of the prime $k$-tuples conjecture, so settling it directly would reveal something about the distribution of prime constellions at fixed gaps; a counterexample would expose an unexpected rigidity in prime gaps.

title: A rearrangement inequality for exponentiation function
open: Does the exponentiation function satisfy a rearrangement inequality in the following sense: if $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \cdots \ge a_n \ge 0$ and $\alpha_1 \ge \alpha_2 \ge \cdots \ge \alpha_n \ge 0$, is it true that ${\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{a_i^{\alpha_i}} \right)}^n \ge \prod_{i=1}^{n}{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}{a_i^{\alpha_j}} \right)}$? Conversely, if $0 \le \alpha_1 \le \alpha_2 \le \cdots \le \alpha_n$ (with the $a_i$ still nonincreasing), does the reverse inequality ${\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{a_i^{\alpha_i}} \right)}^n \le \prod_{i=1}^{n}{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}{a_i^{\alpha_j}} \right)}$ hold? In either case, equality should hold if and only if $a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n$. A proof or a counterexample is sought.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 3 answers), where the asker re-bountied the question a year after posting because the first answer was not clear to them; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/306439/a-rearrangement-inequality-for-exponentiation-function.
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for either inequality (the direct one for similarly ordered exponents, the reverse one for oppositely ordered exponents), including the claimed equality condition, for general $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The original question claimed a proof only for $n=2$ or $n=3$.
why: This would extend the classical rearrangement inequality paradigm from sums of products to exponentiation, and a counterexample would clarify the limits of monotonicity-based rearrangement arguments in this setting.

title: Can one find a Jordan curve which has exactly one inscribed rectangle
open: Does there exist a Jordan curve in the plane with exactly one inscribed rectangle? More generally, does the known result for squares — that for every positive integer $n$ there is a simple closed curve (which can be taken infinitely differentiable and convex) with exactly $n$ inscribed squares — extend when "square" is replaced by "rectangle"?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answers). The motivating result, from "On the number of inscribed squares of a simple closed curve in the plane," states that for every positive integer $n$ there is a simple closed curve in the plane (which can be taken infinitely differentiable and convex) with exactly $n$ inscribed squares; the rectangle analogue is posed as open. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/284612/can-one-find-a-jordan-curve-which-has-exactly-one-inscribed-rectangle
solved_when: A Jordan curve (with any regularity conditions one can achieve, e.g. smoothness and convexity, mirroring the square case) is exhibited having exactly one inscribed rectangle, and the general question of realizing every prescribed count $n$ of inscribed rectangles by some simple closed curve is resolved.
why: It would show whether the fine control over inscribed-square counts extends to rectangles, sharpening our understanding of how Jordan curves constrain inscribed quadrilaterals.

title: Prove this conjecture inequality
open: Let $a,b>0$ and $n\ge 3$ an integer with $a^n+b^n+(2n+2)(ab)^n\le 2n$; must it follow that $a+b\le 2$? Equivalently, prove that $a^n+b^n+(2n+2)a^nb^n-2n>0$ whenever $a+b\ge 2$, and it suffices to establish this on the boundary $a+b=2$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answer). The cases $n=3,4$ of the originating inequality are said to be not hard to prove, but $n\ge 5$ remains open. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/238628/prove-this-conjecture-inequality
solved_when: For all integers $n\ge 3$ and all $a,b>0$ with $a+b\ge 2$, one proves $a^n+b^n+(2n+2)a^nb^n>2n$; by the record it suffices to prove it for $a+b=2$.
why: The inequality originates from the conjecture $\sqrt[n]{x/(1+y)}+\sqrt[n]{y/(1+x)}\le 2$ for $x+y\le 2n$, $n\ge 3$, via the substitution $a=\sqrt[n]{x/(1+y)}$, $b=\sqrt[n]{y/(1+x)}$, so settling it resolves that conjecture for all $n\ge 5$.

title: about Euler quotients related to non-Wieferich numbers $W(n)=\frac{2^n+1}{3}$
open: For odd $n>1$, define $W(n)=\frac{2^n+1}{3}$; must the Euler quotient $a(W(n))=\frac{2^{\phi(W(n))}-1}{W(n)}\bmod W(n)$ always be odd — and in particular always nonzero? Formally, the conjecture asserts $a(W(n))\bmod 2=1$ for all odd $n>1$, which would in particular show $a(W(n))\neq 0$, i.e. that no $W(n)$ is a (composite) Wieferich number.
status: Posed as a community-vetted open problem on MathOverflow (score 3, 1 answer, https://mathoverflow.net/questions/483085/conjecture-about-euler-quotients-related-to-non-wieferich-numbers-wn-frac2). Verified experimentally for $n$ up to $219$, with further testing limited by the cost of factoring to compute the Euler totient; computing the parity of other similar sequences appears random.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of Conjecture 1 — $a(W(n))\bmod 2=1$ for all odd $n>1$ — or, failing that, of Conjecture 2, that $a(W(n))\neq 0$ for all odd $n>1$. The conjecture has been verified experimentally for $n$ up to $219$.
why: A proof would yield an infinite sequence of non-Wieferich numbers with unbounded smallest prime factor (when $n$ is prime, all prime factors of $W(n)$ are congruent to $1$ modulo $n$), addressing the scarcity of known constructions of non-Wieferich numbers.

title: A generalization of Barrow's inequality
open: Does Barrow's inequality extend to a tangential-triangle configuration? Let $ABC$ be a triangle, $P$ an arbitrary point inside $ABC$, and $A_1B_1C_1$ the tangential triangle of $ABC$. Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be arbitrary points on $B_1C_1$, $C_1A_1$, $A_1B_1$ respectively, and let the internal angle bisectors of $\angle B'PC'$, $\angle C'PA'$, $\angle A'PC'$ meet $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $A''$, $B''$, $C''$ respectively. Is it then true that $PA' + PB' + PC' \ge 2(PA'' + PB'' + PC'')$, with equality if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral and $\angle B'PC' = \angle C'PA' = \angle A'PC' = 120^\circ$? The case $A' \equiv A$, $B' \equiv B$, $C' \equiv C$ is Barrow's inequality (see also the Erdős–Mordell inequality).
status: The problem was posted on Stack Exchange more than seven years ago and later appeared on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 3 and 1 answer (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/475220/a-generalization-of-barrows-inequality); no proof of the conjecture is recorded there.
