solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the stated inequality for all triangles $ABC$, interior points $P$, and choices of $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ on the sides of the tangential triangle, together with verification of the claimed equality condition.
why: It would establish a genuine common generalization of Barrow's inequality (itself a sharpening of the Erdős–Mordell inequality) to a much wider configuration involving the tangential triangle.

title: A conjectured upper bound for the mean value of prime divisors inside prime gaps
open: Does the sum of the prime divisors of all integers in the $n$-th prime gap, $\sigma_p(V(n))$ where $V(n)=(p_n+1)(p_n+2)\cdots(p_{n+1}-1)$, satisfy the estimate $\sigma_p(V(n))=2n(\log n)^{3/2}+O(n\log n)$, as suggested by computation up to $n=10^5$? In particular, what is the true order of the mean value $\sigma_p(V(n))/\omega[V(n)]$ of the prime divisors inside the gap?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 0 answers); the problem originated from computations reported there, with a graph of $\sigma_p(V(n))-p_n$ up to $n=10^5$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/376217/a-conjectured-upper-bound-for-the-mean-value-of-prime-divisors-inside-prime-gaps
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the conjectured asymptotic $\sigma_p(V(n))=2n(\log n)^{3/2}+O(n\log n)$, or failing that, a proven upper bound for the mean value $\sigma_p(V(n))/\omega[V(n)]$ of prime divisors inside the gap $g_n$, for example one consistent with the Cramér-type gap bound $g_n=O((\log p_n)^2)$.
why: It refines Grimm's 1969 conjecture ($\omega[V(n)]\ge g_n-1$) from a counting statement to a quantitative estimate on the size distribution of the prime divisors in prime gaps, connecting additive arithmetic functions to the fine structure of prime gaps.

title: Schur positive expression involving border-strip tableaux
open: Is the "cancellation-free" symmetric function $CF_\lambda := \sum_\mu |BST(\lambda,\mu)|\, p_\mu$ — obtained by replacing the signed Murnaghan–Nakayama character sum $\chi^\lambda(\mu) = \sum_{T \in BST(\lambda,\mu)} (-1)^{ht(T)}$ with an unsigned count of border-strip tableaux, and dropping the $z_\mu$ factor — always Schur-positive?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 3, 0 answers); verified computationally for all $|\lambda| \leq 8$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/353150/schur-positive-expression-involving-border-strip-tableaux
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample $\lambda$) of Schur-positivity of $CF_\lambda$ for all partitions $\lambda$; the questioner has verified it for all $|\lambda| \leq 8$.
why: It would give a natural Schur-positive symmetric function built directly from border-strip tableaux, revealing structure hidden by the sign cancellations in the Murnaghan–Nakayama rule.

title: Zero divisors with support size 3 in complex group algebras of residually finite groups
open: Is there a function $f:\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ bounding the exponent of the subgroup generated by $x$ and $y$ in terms of the support size of $\beta$, whenever $\beta \neq 0$ lies in the complex group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ of a finite group $G$, $1 \in \text{supp}(\beta)$, and $(1+x+y)\cdot\beta = 0$ or $(1+x-y)\cdot\beta = 0$ for distinct nontrivial $x,y \in G$? Formally: does there exist $f$ with $\text{exp}(\langle x,y\rangle) \leq f(|\text{supp}(\beta)|)$ under these hypotheses?
status: Community-curated as an open problem on MathOverflow, where it has drawn positive attention (score 3) but remains unanswered (0 answers). No partial results are recorded.
solved_when: Such a function $f:\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ is exhibited (or its existence proved), for which every finite group $G$, every nonzero $\beta \in \mathbb{C}[G]$ with $1 \in \text{supp}(\beta)$, and every pair of distinct nontrivial $x,y \in G$ satisfying $(1+x+y)\cdot\beta = 0$ or $(1+x-y)\cdot\beta = 0$ obey $\text{exp}(\langle x,y\rangle) \leq f(|\text{supp}(\beta)|)$.
why: If true, the support of any zero divisor of the form $1+x+y$ or $1+x-y$ in the complex group algebra of any residually finite group generates a finite subgroup, giving structural control over small-support zero divisors.

title: A sequence based on Catalan–Mihăilescu problem
open: Beyond the two Catalan solutions $3^1-2^1=1$ and $3^2-2^3=1$ (Catalan's 1844 conjecture, proved by Preda Mihăilescu in 2002), how does the equation $3^a-2^b=n$ behave as $n$ varies? Formally, defining $f(n)$ as the number of positive-integer solutions $(a,b)$ of $3^a-2^b=n$, the questions are: is there a simple way to compute $f(n)$; can $f(n)$ take values other than $0$ and $1$ for $n>1$; can $f(n)$ be infinite; are there arbitrarily long runs of $0$'s and $1$'s in the sequence; and what is the asymptotic density of $0$'s?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question has score 2 and 2 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/130316/a-sequence-based-on-catalan-mih%c4%83ilescu-problem); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A characterization or simple computation method for $f(n)$ is given, together with answers determining whether $f(n)$ can exceed $1$ or be infinite for $n>1$, whether the sequence contains arbitrarily long runs of $0$'s and $1$'s, and the asymptotic density of $0$'s.
why: It probes how far the rigidity of the Catalan–Mihăilescu theorem extends to the generalized equation $3^a-2^b=n$, and answers would reveal the structure of values represented by powers of $3$ minus powers of $2$.

title: Is every prime $p \geq 3$ expressible as $2p_1 - p_2$ for distinct primes? (a "difference"
open: Does every prime $p \geq 3$ lie as the middle-distinct term of a non-constant three-term arithmetic progression of primes — that is, do there exist distinct primes $p_1 \neq p_2$ with $p = 2p_1 - p_2$? This is the natural "difference" analogue of Lemoine's conjecture (1895), which asserts that every odd prime $p \geq 7$ (sometimes stated $p > 2$) can be written as $p = 2p_1 + p__2$ for primes $p_1, p_2$, and which remains open despite computational verification to very large bounds.
status: A computational search (segmented sieve of Eratosthenes in C, independently reproduced on a second machine) checked all $455{,}052{,}510$ primes $p$ with $3 \leq p \leq 10^{10}$ and found zero exceptions; the largest "least $p_2$" needed was $4057$, attained at $p = 9{,}517{,}355{,}737$ (example: $13 = 2 \cdot 37 - 61$). The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 2, 2 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/515744/is-every-prime-p-geq-3-expressible-as-2p-1-p-2-for-distinct-primes-a-d
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement: for every prime $p \geq 3$ there exist distinct primes $p_1 \neq p_2$ such that $p = 2p_1 - p_2$.
why: It tests whether every prime sits in a non-constant three-term arithmetic progression of primes, a structured additive pattern in the primes that computational evidence strongly supports; it also connects this "difference" analogue to the long-open Lemoine conjecture.

title: On $\sum_{\substack{p\leq x\\p,p+2\text{ twin primes}}}\frac{(\log p)^m}{p}$, on assumption of the f
open: Under the First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, what is the asymptotic behavior as $x\to\infty$ of the sum $\sum_{p\leq x,\; p,p+2\text{ twin primes}} \frac{(\log p)^m}{p}$, where $m\geq 1$ is a fixed integer and $p$ runs over the lesser of twin primes (OEIS A001359)? In particular, a deduction of the asymptotic for some integer $m\geq 1$ is desired, inspired by Proposition 17 of [1].
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 2 and 1 answer.
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for the sum, valid as $x\to\infty$ for some fixed integer $m\geq 1$, is derived under the assumption of the First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture.
why: It extends a known result for this type of weighted prime sum to the twin-prime setting, and it is unclear whether the exercise appears in the literature even for a single fixed $m$.

title: On the nearest-square function and the quantity $m^2 - p^k$ where $p^k m^2$ is an odd perfect number
open: If $n = p^k m^2$ is an odd perfect number with special prime $p \equiv k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\gcd(p,m)=1$, what can be said about the quantity $m^2 - p^k$ and its relation to the nearest-square function? In particular, since $m^2 - p^k \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, one may write $m^2 - p^k = 4z$ and ask for bounds or structural properties of $z$, where it is known that $4z \geq {10}^{375}$; this is an offshoot of the Dris Conjecture that $p^k < m$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 2, 2 answers); the question was cross-posted from MSE, where user mathlove posted an answer that the asker could not completely understand. Brown (2016) showed that the Dris Conjecture holds in many cases. It is trivial that $m^2 - p^k \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, and the bound $4z \geq {10}^{375}$ was established in an MSE question and answer considering the case $m < p^k$.
solved_when: A characterization or nontrivial bound for $m^2 - p^k = 4z$ is established, sharpening the known lower bound $4z \geq {10}^{375}$ (which was obtained under the case $m < p^k$), or the quantity is otherwise related to the nearest-square function in a provable way.
why: The Dris Conjecture ($p^k < m$, conjectured in Dris (2008) and Dris (2012)) remains open, and understanding $m^2 - p^k$ offers a concrete quantitative handle on the relative sizes of the Eulerian prime-power component and the square component of an odd perfect number.

title: On odd perfect numbers $p^k m^2$ with special prime $p$ satisfying $m^2 - p^k = 2^r t$ - Part II
open: Does the Descartes–Frenicle–Sorli conjecture ($k=1$) hold for odd perfect numbers, or can one prove the Dris conjecture $p^k < m$? Formally: for an odd perfect number $n = p^k m^2$ with special prime $p \equiv k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\gcd(p,m)=1$, determine whether the exponent $k$ on the special prime is always $1$, or at least establish the inequality $p^k < m$.
status: Euler proved that any odd perfect number must have the form $n = p^k m^2$ with $p \equiv k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\gcd(p,m)=1$. Descartes, Frenicle, and subsequently Sorli conjectured $k = 1$ always holds. Dris conjectured $p^k < m$ in his M. Sc. thesis. Brown (2016) proved the weaker inequality $p < m$; Pomerance informed Brown that past proofs for the estimate $p < m$ were incomplete (record truncated). The question was posted on MathOverflow (score 2, 2 answers) after an unanswered MSE posting two weeks prior: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/406701/on-odd-perfect-numbers-pk-m2-with-special-prime-p-satisfying-m2-pk
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every hypothetical odd perfect number $n = p^k m^2$ satisfies $k = 1$; alternatively, a proof of the inequality $p^k < m$ (Dris's conjecture), which would supersede the currently known weaker bound $p < m$.
why: Both the $k=1$ conjecture and the Dris inequality are central structural constraints on the Eulerian form of any odd perfect number; resolving either would sharply narrow the search space for these numbers and settle two long-standing conjectures in the field.

title: Reconstructing analytic tetration with a complex height from a thinner set of points
open: Does the analytic tetration with complex height remain unchanged when it is reconstructed from a thinner, shifted sample of its values? Formally, inserting integer parameters $p,s\in\mathbb Z^+$ into the known double series $t(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{n-k} q^{\binom{n-k}{2}} {z \brack n}_q {n \brack k}_q ({^k a})$ to obtain $t(p,s,z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^{n-k} q^{p\binom{n-k}{2}} {(z-s)/p \brack n}_{q^p} {n \brack k}_{q^p} ({^{pk+s} a})$, is it true that $t(p,s,z) = t(z)$ for all positive integers $p,s$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question has score 2 and 1 answer; see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/259467/reconstructing-analytic-tetration-with-a-complex-height-from-a-thinner-set-of-po
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) that the generalized series $t(p,s,z)$ equals the original tetration function $t(z)$ for all positive integer choices of $p$ and $s$, under the same convergence assumptions as the original series representation.
why: A positive answer would give a strong rigidity/independence property of the analytic tetration: its reconstruction is stable under subsampling and shifting of the tetration values used, which could yield new identities and more flexible series representations of tetration.

title: On a subset of the $abc$ triples
open: Are there only finitely many coprime positive integer triples $(a,b,c)$ with $a+b=c$ and $c > F(abc)$, where $F(p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k}) = n_1\cdots n_k\, p_1\cdots p_k$ is the radical weighted by the exponents? This asks for an $abc$-type finiteness statement for a natural subset of the $abc$ triples, those satisfying $c > \operatorname{rad}(abc)$ strengthened to $c > F(abc)$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 2, 0 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/445553/on-a-subset-of-the-abc-triples. The set of $abc$ triples satisfying the inequality with $\varepsilon = 0$ is known to be infinite.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the set of coprime positive integer triples $(a,b,c)$ with $a+b=c$ and $c > F(abc)$ is finite — the natural criterion, since the record states no quantitative target.
why: The inequality with $\varepsilon = 0$ against the radical is known to admit infinitely many triples, so exponent-weighting is a natural way to recover a finiteness question; resolving it would clarify how far the multiplicative-exponent structure of $abc$ triples alone forces finiteness.

title: How soon can we represent a number as the sum of two primes
open: Given an even number n that is a sum of two primes, how small is the smallest prime p_n such that n − p_n is also prime? More precisely, what is the limiting behavior of the ratio of p_n to n (the asker's experimental data for n ≤ 230751000000 suggests an asymptotic relation for p_n, which is much smaller than n)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow with score 2 and 0 answers; the record links the original question at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/421186/how-soon-can-we-represent-a-number-as-the-sum-of-two-primes, posted there after going unanswered on MSE. No answer is recorded.
solved_when: The limiting value of the normalized smallest Goldbach prime (as stated in the question's final ratio expression) is determined for even n representable as a sum of two primes, ideally with a proof or disproof of the asymptotic relation suggested by data up to n ≤ 230751000000.
why: It quantifies how quickly a Goldbach representation can be found by searching from the smallest prime upward, turning Goldbach's conjecture from an existence statement into one about the location of the smallest witness.

title: Asymptotics of Littlewood polynomials
open: Does there exist a sequence of Littlewood polynomials $f_n(z)=\sum^m \pm z^m$ in the class $\mathscr F$ whose magnitudes on the unit circle are uniformly comparable to $\sqrt{n+1}$, i.e. $A \le |f_n(\theta)|/\sqrt{n+1} \le B$ for all large $n$ with fixed constants $A, B$? The question originates in Littlewood's stated conjectures on the asymptotics of polynomials with $\pm1$ coefficients.
status: Posted on MathOverflow (score 2, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/314561/asymptotics-of-littlewood-polynomials; the poster notes, per Fedor's comment, that J-P. Kahane's work gives an elegant proof for polynomials with unimodular coefficients — his theorem states there exists a sequence $P_n(z)=\sum_{m=1}^{n} a_{m,n} z^m$ with $|a_{m,n}|=1$ — but the original $\pm1$-coefficient question's status and recent survey references remain unconfirmed, and the poster asked whether integer programming methods might apply.
solved_when: An explicit sequence $f_n \in \mathscr F$ is constructed (or proven to exist) satisfying $A \le |f_n(\theta)|/\sqrt{n+1} \le B$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for absolute constants $A$ and $B$ — or the conjecture is refuted.
why: Such polynomials would give flat Littlewood polynomials, a fundamental extremal object in harmonic analysis with connections to signal design and spectral flatness; settling it resolves one of Littlewood's long-standing conjectures on $\pm1$-coefficient polynomials.

title: Weak Leopoldt Conjecture for the Split Prime $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension
open: Is there a proof of the weak Leopoldt conjecture for the split prime $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension — the unique $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $F$ ramified only at a chosen prime $\beta$ dividing $p$, where $F/K$ is a finite extension of an imaginary quadratic field $K$ in which $p$ splits completely? The analogue is known for the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension by Iwasawa's 1973 Annals paper, and the split prime extension shares many cyclotomic-like properties, so the question is whether weak Leopoldt can be established in this setting too.
status: Iwasawa proved the weak Leopoldt conjecture for the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of any number field in his 1973 Annals paper. For the split prime setting, an adaptation of Sinnott's work by Schnepps and Gillard showed the $\mu=0$ conjecture for $p \neq 2,3$. The question was posed on MathOverflow (score 2, 0 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/307620/weak-leopoldt-conjecture-for-the-split-prime-mathbbz-p-extension
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the weak Leopoldt conjecture is given for the split prime $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of any number field $F$ containing an imaginary quadratic field $K$ with $p$ split completely, for an arbitrary choice of prime $\beta \mid p$.
why: The split prime extension is a central non-cyclotomic testing ground for Iwasawa theory; establishing weak Leopoldt there would extend the arithmetic control (e.g. of class groups and Selmer groups) that the cyclotomic case enjoys, and confirm that the cyclotomic analogy carries through in full.

title: Any counter example for this: ${\phi(2^n-1)} \bmod \tau(2^n-1)=0$ for every integer $n \geq 1$
open: Does the number-of-divisors function $\tau$ always divide Euler's totient $\phi$ when both are evaluated at a Mersenne number — that is, is $\phi(2^n - 1) \bmod \tau(2^n - 1) = 0$ for every integer $n \geq 1$? If not, an explicit counterexample $n$ is sought.
status: The question originated on Stack Exchange without responses and was posed on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 2 and 0 answers (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/254323/any-counter-example-for-this-phi2n-1-bmod-tau2n-1-0-for-every-inte). Computation in Wolfram Alpha for $n$ from 1 to 100 found no counterexample, which motivated the question.
solved_when: Either a proof is given that $\tau(2^n-1)$ divides $\phi(2^n-1)$ for all integers $n \geq 1$, or a specific integer $n \geq 1$ is exhibited for which the divisibility fails.
why: The divisibility would reveal unexpected regularity in the divisor structure of Mersenne numbers, informing the study of the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \tau(2^n-1)/\phi(2^n-1)$; a counterexample would expose a structural obstruction.

title: On the conjectured nonexistence of even almost perfect numbers (other than powers of two) and odd pe
open: Does any even almost perfect number exist besides the powers of two? Formally, is there an $M \neq 2^t$ with $\sigma(M) = 2M - 1$, noting Antalan and Tagle showed such $M$ must have the form $M = b^2 2^r$ where $r \geq 1$ and $b$ is an odd composite?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 2, 0 answers), cross-posted to MSE. Known: $M_s = 2^s$ with $s \geq 0$ are almost perfect, $M_0 = 1$ being the only odd almost perfect number currently known; any even almost perfect $M \neq 2^t$ must have the form $M = b^2 2^r$ with $r \geq 1$ and $b$ an odd composite (Antalan and Tagle); only 49 even perfect numbers have been discovered, all of the form $N_e = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ with $2^p - 1$ and $p$ prime; it is unknown whether odd perfect numbers exist, though Euler showed any such $N_o = n^2 q^c$ with $q$ prime and $q \equiv c \equiv 1 \pmod{\cdots}$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/243149/on-the-conjectured-nonexistence-of-even-almost-perfect-numbers-other-than-power
solved_when: A proof that no even $M \neq 2^t$ satisfies $\sigma(M) = 2M - 1$, or an explicit example of such an $M$ (necessarily of the form $b^2 2^r$ with $r \geq 1$ and $b$ an odd composite).
why: It would resolve a natural gap between perfect and almost perfect numbers: the powers of two $M_s = 2^s$, $s \geq 0$, are almost perfect, with $M_0 = 1$ the only known odd almost perfect number, and the parallel question of odd perfect numbers remains open.

title: Infinitely many $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the closed interval $[k, k+99]$ contains from $2$ to $2
open: For how many primes $m$ can we prove that infinitely many blocks of 100 consecutive integers contain exactly $m$ primes? Formally: is there some $m \in \{2,3,\dots,23\}$ for which infinitely many $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ have exactly $m$ primes in the closed interval $[k, k+99]$?
status: The problem was raised on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/435628/infinitely-many-k-in-mathbbn-such-that-the-closed-interval-k-k99-con, motivated by an Italian-language article "Quanti numeri primi in 100 interi consecutivi?" (Matematicamente.it Magazine, Vol. 25(228), 2015 [1]). That article showed that only finitely many $k$ give $m \geq 24$ (in fact, if $m \geq 24$ then $2 \leq k \leq 17$), and — via its Lemma 4 — that infinitely many $k$ give $m = 0$ and $m = 1$. The intermediate cases $2 \leq m \leq 23$ were conjectured to occur infinitely often but remain open, more than 7 years after the article.
solved_when: A proof is given that for at least one $m$ with $2 \leq m \leq 23$, infinitely many $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfy $|[k, k+99] \cap \mathbb{P}| = m$.
why: It would settle one of the basic cases of the natural conjecture that every feasible prime count in a window of 100 consecutive integers occurs infinitely often, completing the picture beyond the already-known cases $m = 0$ and $m = 1$.

title: about primes
open: Given a fixed integer $n_0$ (positive or negative), are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + n_0 = 2^r \cdot q$ for some $r \geq 0$ and some prime $q \geq 3$? For $n_0 = 2$, this specializes to the twin prime conjecture.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answer), where it was posed as a conjecture about primes (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/402286/conjecture-about-primes); it remains open.
solved_when: For an arbitrary fixed integer $n_0$, a proof (or disproof) that infinitely many primes $p$ admit a representation $p + n_0 = 2^r \cdot q$ with $r \geq 0$ and prime $q \geq 3$; in particular, the case $n_0 = 2$ resolves the twin prime conjecture.
why: It generalizes the twin prime conjecture to an infinite family of shifted-prime problems where the shift need only be matched up to a power of 2, so a resolution would represent a major advance on prime-gap questions; even partial cases would illuminate how prime values distribute near linear shifts.

title: in the setting of generalized Diophantine $m$-tuples
open: Does there exist a set of positive integers $\{a_1,\dots,a_m\}$ such that $a_i a_j + 1$ is a perfect square for all $1 \le i < j \le m$ under the asker's proposed generalization of Diophantine $m$-tuples? More precisely, the question asks whether the classical Diophantine $m$-tuple framework, in which infinitely many $4$-tuples exist and no quintuple exists, admits the proposed generalization and what can be said about its solutions.
status: The question was posted by a self-described amateur on MathOverflow, who noted that infinitely many integer Diophantine $4$-tuples have long been known, that the nonexistence of a Diophantine quintuple was conjectured, and that a referenced paper claims the quintuple problem is solved; a linked page collects information on Diophantine $m$-tuples and their generalizations. The post is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answer). Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/268651/question-in-the-setting-of-generalized-diophantine-m-tuples
solved_when: A resolution of the generalized question posed in the record — determining whether such generalized Diophantine tuples exist, and in particular whether an analogue of the no-quintuple phenomenon holds; no explicit quantitative target is stated in the record.
why: It probes whether the recent resolution of the classical quintuple conjecture extends to natural generalizations, which is exactly where long-tail Diophantine problems outside standard lists tend to hide.

title: Is Gardam's support-21 unit in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ (Promislow group) support-minimal
open: Is Gardam's nontrivial unit of support size 21 in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ — where $P$ is the Promislow group — minimal among all nontrivial units, as Gardam remarks is "plausible"? Formally, does every nontrivial unit in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ have support size at least 21?
status: Gardam [1] disproved the Kaplansky unit conjecture by exhibiting a nontrivial unit $\alpha$ of support size 21 in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$, where $P = \langle a,b \mid b^{-1}a^2b = a^{-2},\ a^{-1}b^2a = b^{-2}\rangle$ is the Promislow group. Craven–Pappas [2] had verified the unit conjecture in $K[P]$ for supports of dihedral length at most 3. Computational searches for units and zero divisors of small support in a group-agnostic setting have been carried out by Garg–Mineyev [4], with a structural obstruction to that framework proved by Shin [5]; these do not directly address support minimality inside $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ itself. The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/513417/is-gardams-support-21-unit-in-mathbbf-2p-promislow-group-support-minim
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every nontrivial unit in $\mathbb{F}_2[P]$ has support size at least 21; a disproof requires exhibiting a nontrivial unit of support size less than 21.
why: It would settle the natural quantitative refinement of the Kaplansky unit conjecture in the one group where it is known to fail, giving a sharp lower bound on how small a nontrivial unit can be.

title: Initial conditions to falsify Rowland's conjecture
open: For Rowland's prime-generating recurrence $g(n) = a(n) - a(n-1) = \gcd(n, a(n-1))$, can one characterize the initial values $a(1) = k$ for which the differences $g(n)$ fail to be always 1 or prime? A theorem (or even a conjecture) identifying some structure in the set of such falsifying initial values — beyond the known examples like $k = 532$ and $k = 801$ — would answer the question.
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/455052/initial-conditions-to-falsify-rowlands-conjecture), where it is community-curated with score 1 and no answers. Rowland's paper "A natural prime-generating recurrence" already notes counterexamples such as $k = 532$ and $k = 801$, but no theorem characterizing such initial values is known from the record.
solved_when: A theorem or well-supported conjecture is established describing properties of (a subset of) the initial values $a(1) = k$ for which Rowland's recurrence produces a difference $g(n)$ that is neither 1 nor prime.
why: It would delimit exactly how "natural" Rowland's prime-generating recurrence is — whether primality of the differences is generic or a fragile accident of the initial condition.

title: Stronger conjectured inequality for area of a polygon
open: Is there a strengthening of the classical area–side-length inequality for polygons that accounts for the variation between consecutive sides? In formal terms, does every polygon $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ satisfy $$4\tan\frac{\pi}{n}\,\mathrm{Area}(A_1A_2\cdots A_n)\ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^n(A_iA_{i+1})^2-\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(A_iA_{i+1}-A_{i+1}A_{i+2})^2,$$ as conjectured on the basis of computer checking? As supporting evidence, for an equiangular convex pentagon one has $\mathrm{Area}(ABCDE)=\frac{1}{4}\cot\frac{\pi}{5}\bigl(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2-\frac{(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-d)^2+(d-e)^2+(e-a)^2}{\sqrt{5}}\bigr)$.
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow (score 1, 0 answers) and remains unanswered; the conjecture is supported by computer checking and by the exact identity for equiangular convex pentagons stated above. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/426277/stronger-conjectured-inequality-for-area-of-a-polygon
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via explicit counterexample) of the conjectured inequality for arbitrary polygons $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ is given.
why: A proof would yield a sharper quantitative bound on polygonal area in terms of side lengths and their consecutive differences, refining a known inequality the author proposed four years earlier.

title: Testing polynomials irreducible over the integers
open: Is there a practical criterion, based on counting prime values, that certifies irreducibility of an integer polynomial? Specifically, for $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ of degree $n>0$ with coprime coefficients and greatest fixed divisor $d$, is it true that $f$ is irreducible if and only if $\operatorname{P}^+(d^{-1}\cdot f)>n$ or $\operatorname{P}^+(d^{-1}\cdot(-f))>n$, where $\operatorname{P}^+(g)$ counts the positive primes assumed at distinct integral arguments?
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/321392/testing-polynomials-irreducible-over-the-integers; no answer is recorded. The record states that many irreducible polynomials have a fixed divisor $>1$ and hence $\operatorname{P}^+(f)\leq n$, and reports computational testing of the conjecture on $1{,}000{,}000$ Eisenstein polynomials.
solved_when: The conjecture is proved or disproved: either a proof shows that coprime-coefficient $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ of degree $n>0$ is irreducible exactly when $\operatorname{P}^+(d^{-1}\cdot f)>n$ or $\operatorname{P}^+(d^{-1}\cdot(-f))>n$ (with $d$ the greatest fixed divisor), or a counterexample is exhibited. The motivating theorem — reducible $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ of degree $n>0$ satisfies $\operatorname{P}^+(f)\leq n$, with equality achievable for every $n$ [Acta Arith., 104.2 (2002) 117-127] — gives the baseline bound $n$ that the criterion must exceed. Heuristic support so far: a program tested the conjectured statement on $1{,}000{,}000$ Eisenstein polynomials.
why: It would turn irreducibility testing into a search for prime values, and explain why the fixed divisor (many irreducible polynomials have one $>1$, forcing $\operatorname{P}^+(f)\leq n$) obstructs the naive prime-counting test.

title: If $N = q^k n^2$ is an odd perfect number, and $n < q^{k+1}$, does it follow that $k > 1$
open: If $N = q^k n^2$ is an odd perfect number with Euler prime $q$ and $n < q^{k+1}$, must the exponent $k$ exceed 1? In other words, can the condition $n < q^{k+1}$ coexist with Descartes's and Sorli's conjectured case $k = 1$?
status: The problem is posted and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 0 answers; https://mathoverflow.net/questions/243330/if-n-qk-n2-is-an-odd-perfect-number-and-n-qk1-does-it-follow-tha). Historical context: Dickson (as pointed out recently by Beasley) records Descartes's 1638 letter to Mersenne conjecturing $k=1$, with Frenicle's subsequent observation in 1657; Sorli conjectured $k=1$ on page 89 of his PhD thesis, Algorithms in the study of multiperfect and odd perfect numbers. Brown has announced a proof that $q < n$ and a partial proof that $q^k < n$ holds under many cases; no answer to the posted question is known.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $n < q^{k+1}$ implies $k > 1$ for an odd perfect number $N = q^k n^2$ in Eulerian form; a counterexample with $k = 1$ and $n < q^{k+1}$ resolves it negatively.
why: A positive answer would, together with Brown's announced proof that $q < n$ and partial results toward $q^k < n$, force the biconditionals $q < n \iff \sigma(q) < \sigma(n) \iff \sigma(q)/n < \sigma(n)/q$ and $q^k < n \iff \sigma(q^k) < \sigma(n) \iff \sigma(q^k)/n < \sigma(n)/q^k$, sharpening the structure theory of odd perfect numbers.

title: A symmetric polynomial inequality
open: Does a natural two-level symmetric analogue of Muirhead's inequality hold — namely, if $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ majorizes $(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ for nonnegative reals, is the double symmetric sum $\sum_{sym}\big(\sum_{sym} x_{i_1}^{a_{p_1}}\cdots x_{i_m}^{a_{p_m}}\big)$ at most the corresponding sum over the $y_i$? Formally: for integers $n>2$ and $1\le m\le n$, nonnegative reals $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $y_1,\dots,y_n$ with $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ majorizing $(y_1,\dots,y_n)$, and reals $0\le a_1,\dots,a_n\le 1$, prove $$\sum_{sym}\left( \sum_{sym} x_{i_1}^{a_{p_1}} \cdots x_{i_m}^{a_{p_m}} \right) \leq \sum_{sym}\left( \sum_{sym} y_{i_1}^{a_{p_1}} \cdots y_{i_m}^{a_{p_m}} \right),$$ where the summations run over all $m$-tuples $(i_1,\dots,i_m)$ and $(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ with pairwise distinct entries.
status: Posted as a conjecture on MathOverflow (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/306204/a-symmetric-polynomial-inequality), where the proposer states it as a natural development of the earlier Muirhead-like inequality and offers it without proof; the post has received 2 answers and a score of 0, with no accepted resolution recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the stated inequality is given for all integers $n>2$ and $1\le m\le n$, all nonnegative $x_i, y_i$ with $x$ majorizing $y$, and all exponents $0\le a_i\le 1$.
why: The case $m=n$ recovers the previously established "Muirhead-like inequality," so a proof would extend a classical majorization principle to a broad class of symmetric polynomial sums; a counterexample would expose a genuine boundary of Muirhead-type reasoning.

title: Inequality $(a_1^x+a_2^x+\cdots+a_n^x)^y \ge (a_1^y+a_2^y+\cdots+a_n^y)^x$
open: Is it true that for positive real numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ and exponents $y \ge x$, one always has $(a_1^x+\cdots+a_n^x)^y \ge (a_1^y+\cdots+a_n^y)^x$, with equality exactly when $x=y$? And does this inequality already appear somewhere in the literature?
status: The problem has been posed and community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received 1 answer at score 0 (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/477603/inequality-a-1xa-2x-cdotsa-nxy-ge-a-1ya-2y-cdotsa-nyx); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the inequality and its claimed equality condition for all positive $a_i$ and all $y \ge x$, together with either a reference to a prior appearance or confirmation that it is new.
why: A clean power-sum comparison inequality of this shape would be a useful tool for bounding sums of powers, and settling it removes an attractive, widely-askable conjecture from the long tail of open problems.

title: The difference between two coprime semiprimes
open: Can every positive integer be expressed as the difference of two coprime semiprimes? That is, for each positive integer n, do there exist semiprimes s and t with gcd(s, t) = 1 and s − t = n?
status: The conjecture is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answers) and has been tested numerically up to 1,000,000; a related discussion of differences of coprime composites appears at https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2579578/the-difference-of-two-coprime-composites, with the original record at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/289293/the-difference-between-two-coprime-semiprimes.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit counterexample) of the conjecture that every positive integer is a difference of two coprime semiprimes; numerical verification currently extends up to 1,000,000.
why: It would extend additive prime-variety results (like those on differences of primes) to the semiprime setting with a coprimality constraint, and a disproof would reveal an unexpected obstruction in the additive structure of almost-primes.

title: Proving $k = 1 \implies q = 5$, if $q^k n^2$ is an odd perfect number with Euler prime $q$
open: If an odd perfect number $N = q^k n^2$ (with Euler prime $q$) has exponent $k = 1$ on its Euler prime, must the Euler prime be $q = 5$? Formally, prove the implication $k = 1 \implies q = 5$, thereby establishing the biconditional $k = 1 \iff q = 5$, since the reverse implication $q = 5 \implies k = 1$ was proved by Iannucci (Lemma 12, page 873) — though, per a comment from Pace, Iannucci's result applies to odd perfect numbers with all but at most two prime divisors less than $100$, and such numbers were shown not to exist. A proposed route first establishes $k = 1 \implies I(n^2) \leq 2 - \frac{5}{3q}$ (a short argument, given in a preprint), and then investigates the equality case, since $I(n^2) = 2 - \frac{5}{3q}$ together with $k = 1$ would force $q = 5$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answers). The converse direction $q = 5 \implies k = 1$ is attributed to Iannucci (Lemma 12, page 873), but by Pace's comment that lemma concerns odd perfect numbers with all but at most two prime divisors less than $100$, a class Iannucci went on to show empty; the lemma gives only a restricted form for such numbers. The forward direction remains open, with a preprint establishing $k = 1 \implies I(n^2) \leq 2 - \frac{5}{3q}$, and the equality case $I(n^2) = 2 - \frac{5}{3q}$ (under $k = 1$) shown to imply $q = 5$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/258353/proving-k-1-implies-q-5-if-qk-n2-is-an-odd-perfect-number-with-euler
solved_when: The implication $k = 1 \implies q = 5$ is proved for an arbitrary odd perfect number $q^k n^2$ with Euler prime $q$ (equivalently, the biconditional $k = 1 \iff q = 5$ is established unconditionally).
why: It would pin down the shape of the Euler factor of any odd perfect number, a basic unknown in a centuries-old existence question; the equality case $I(n^2) = 2 - \frac{5}{3q}$ is the key quantitative threshold on the abundancy index of the non-Euler part.

title: on a cyclic quadrilateral associated with central line of triangle
open: Using computer I found a conjecture as follows ( click to check by geogebra ): Conjecture : Let $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ lie on a circle such that $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ are not formed an Isosceles trapezoid. Let $AB$ meets $CD$ at $F$ and $AD$ meets $BC$ at $E$ . Define $\ell(n, m, \triangle T)$ is a line through triangle center $X(n)$ , $X(m)$ of triangle $\triangle T$ , then $\ell(n, m, \triangle ABE)$ , $\ell(n, m, \triangle CDE)$ , $\ell(n, m, \triangle ADF)$ , $\ell(n, m, \triangle BCF)$ form a cyclic quadrilateral for every positive integers $n$ , $m$ ( $n \neq m$ ). Where $X(n)$ refer to Kimberling triangle center . Question : I am looking for a proof the conjecture above.
status: community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answers)
why: high community interest; long-tail problems outside standard lists

title: An triangle inequality $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^\alpha \ge \sum_{i=1}^na_i^\alpha $ if $\alpha >1$
open: Is the classical triangle-side power inequality amenable to a natural $n$-variable generalization? Formally: given $a_1,\dots,a_n>0$ with $S=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ and $b_i=S-(n-1)a_i\ge 0$, does $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^\alpha \ge \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^\alpha$ hold for $\alpha>1$ (and the reverse inequality for $0<\alpha<1$)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answer). Source record: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/334188/an-triangle-inequality-sum-i-1n-b-i-alpha-ge-sum-i-1na-i-alpha-if
solved_when: The generalized inequality is proved (or disproved via counterexample) for all $n$ and all $\alpha>1$, together with the reversed inequality for $0<\alpha<1$. The motivating case — for triangle sidelengths $a,b,c$: $(a+b-c)^\alpha+(b+c-a)^\alpha+(c+a-b)^\alpha \ge a^\alpha+b^\alpha+c^\alpha$ for $\alpha>1$ and $\le$ for $0<\alpha<1$ — was found experimentally by computer and serves as the base instance.
why: It extends a computer-discovered inequality from triangles to arbitrary dimension-like index $n$, testing whether power-mean convexity structure survives under the transformation $a_i \mapsto S-(n-1)a_i$.

title: I conjecture every odd number is a sum of three twin primes — is a bounded-gap version provable
open: Is every sufficiently large odd integer a sum of three primes, each of which has another prime within a bounded distance (say 246, by the bounded-gap theorem)? More precisely, writing $B=\{p\text{ prime}:\exists q\ne p\text{ prime with }|p-q|\le 246\}$, is it a theorem — or within reach of existing circle-method / Maynard–Tao sieve techniques — that every sufficiently large odd integer is a sum of three elements of $B$?
status: By Zhang (2013) and the subsequent work of Maynard, Tao, and the Polymath8 project, it is unconditionally known that $\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n)\le 246$, so $B$ is infinite. The analogous statement with twin primes in place of $B$ remains only conjectural and would imply the twin prime conjecture. The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 0 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/515025/i-conjecture-every-odd-number-is-a-sum-of-three-twin-primes-is-a-bounded-gap-v
solved_when: A proof (unconditional, or conditional on widely accepted hypotheses) that every sufficiently large odd integer is a sum of three elements of $B$, where $B$ is the set of primes having another prime within distance 246.
why: It would give an unconditional additive-combinatorial weakening of the conjecture that every odd number is a sum of three twin primes; the twin-prime version itself would imply the twin prime conjecture via a simple bounded-sumset argument, so it is out of reach, and this bounded-gap surrogate tests how far circle-method and Maynard–Tao sieve tools can be pushed.

title: A 2D lattice generalization related to prime gaps and Cramér's conjecture
open: Must every coprime pair of integers $1 < x < y$ admit a prime of the form $p = nx + my$ with positive integer coefficients $n \le \lceil \ln^2(y)\rceil$ and $m \le \lceil \ln^2(x)\rceil$? A weaker form asks the same when $x$ and $y$ are themselves primes with $x < y$; the logarithmic bounds are structurally inspired by Cramér's conjecture, and by enforcing $x > 1$ with $(x, y)$ as independent weights the problem shifts from a classical 1D prime gap search to a 2D discrete lattice with strict coprimality sieves.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 0 answers); the poser reports computational support (the record is truncated mid-sentence: "I have compu"). No answers or resolutions are recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/509408/a-2d-lattice-generalization-related-to-prime-gaps-and-cram%c3%a9rs-conjecture
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the conjecture: for all integers $1 < x < y$ with $\gcd(x, y) = 1$, there exists a prime $p = nx + my$ with integers $n, m \ge 1$, $n \le \lceil \ln^2(y)\rceil$, $m \le \lceil \ln^2(x)\rceil$; or of the restricted weak form where $x, y$ are primes with $x < y$.
why: A proof would give a Cramér-strength guarantee on prime representations on a 2D weighted lattice with coprimality constraints, generalizing 1D prime gap bounds; a disproof would show logarithmic-square windows are too small once two coprime weights interact.

title: Variants of Nicholson's inequalities for prime numbers, involving the Lambert $W$ function
open: Are the proposed Lambert-$W$ variants of Nicholson's inequalities for primes true — that is, does $(p_{n+1}/p_n)^n < nW(n)$ hold for all integers $n\geq 5$ (with $W$ the principal branch of the Lambert $W$ function and $p_k$ the $k$-th prime), and does $(\log p_{n+1}/\log p_n)^n < e^{-\gamma}\,e/\Omega$ hold for all $n\geq 1$, where $\Omega = W(1)$? If not, can either conjecture be disproved?
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of 0 and no answers (question 351121). The conjectures are proposed as strengthenings of inequalities due to Nicholson [1] and Visser [2], with the Lambert $W$ function's definition and asymptotics invoked as background; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of both conjectures is given: Conjecture 1 for all integers $n\geq 5$, and Conjecture 2 for all integers $n\geq 1$.
why: A proof would establish sharper bounds on prime ratios than Nicholson's and Visser's inequalities, refining the link between prime-spacing estimates and the Lambert $W$ function; a disproof would delimit how far such strengthenings can go.

title: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n!-1$ and $n!+1$ are prime numbers
open: Are there infinitely many integers $n$ for which both $n!-1$ and $n!+1$ are prime? In other words, does the factorial have a twin-prime-like neighborhood that is prime infinitely often?
status: Posed as a community-curated question on MathOverflow (score -4, 1 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/401841/are-there-infinitely-many-n-such-that-n-1-and-n1-are-prime-numbers
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many $n$ exist such that both $n!-1$ and $n!+1$ are prime.
why: Resolving it would illuminate how factorial-based sequences interact with primality, a long-tail question of high community interest that sits outside standard problem lists.

title: Are there infinitely many $k$ such that $6k−1, \; 6k+1, \;$ and $12k−1$ are all prime
open: Can a prime be simultaneously the lower member of a twin prime pair and a Sophie Germain prime — that is, are there infinitely many $k$ such that $6k-1$, $6k+1$, and $12k-1$ are all prime? (The upper member $6k+1$ never works, since $2(6k+1)+1 = 3(4k+1)$ is always a multiple of 3.)
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score -4, 1 answer); the question asks whether the infinitude is conjectured or known, but no resolution is recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/506831/are-there-infinitely-many-k-such-that-6k%e2%88%921-6k1-and-12k%e2%88%921-are-all.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of the infinitude of integers $k \geq 1$ for which all three of $6k-1$, $6k+1$, and $12k-1$ are prime.
why: It would show that the twin prime and Sophie Germain prime conditions can hold simultaneously infinitely often, connecting two central prime constellations beyond what standard conjectures cover individually.

title: What is the definition of the function T used in Atiyah's attempted proof of the Riemann Hypothe
open: What exactly is the Todd function $T(s)$ that Michael Atiyah's paper purportedly proving the Riemann hypothesis relies on? In other words, how did Atiyah define $T$ in his paper "The Fine Structure Constant," which is otherwise difficult to obtain?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question received a score of 107 and 2 answers; the original thread is at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/311280/what-is-the-definition-of-the-function-t-used-in-atiyahs-attempted-proof-of-the.
solved_when: The definition of $T(s)$ as given in Atiyah's paper "The Fine Structure Constant" is stated, or the paper itself becomes available and the definition is extracted from it.
why: The function $T(s)$ and its properties carry the weight of the claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, so anyone attempting to verify or refute Atiyah's argument needs its precise definition.

title: What's the current state of Yang–Mills mass gap question
open: What is the current state of the Yang–Mills mass gap question, and has there been any progress beyond what is described in the introduction article by Jaffe and Witten?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 11, 3 answers). See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/17257/whats-the-current-state-of-yang-mills-mass-gap-question
solved_when: A sourced account of progress (if any) on the Yang–Mills mass gap problem beyond that mentioned in the Jaffe–Witten introduction, or a demonstration of the mass gap itself.
why: Clarifying the true frontier of this Millennium Prize problem tells mathematicians whether and where they can contribute, and separates genuine advances from folklore.

title: A conjecture regarding prime numbers
open:
For $n,m \geq 3$, define $P_n = \{ p : p$ is a prime such that $p \leq n$ and $p 
mid n \}$ — for instance $P_3=\{2\}$, $P_4=\{3\}$, $P_5=\{2,3\}$, $P_6=\{5\}$. Must these sets be distinct, i.e. is $P_n 
eq P_m$ whenever $m 
eq n$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 62, 2 answers); the question can be found at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/287011/a-conjecture-regarding-prime-numbers. The poser notes the case of distinct primes is clear, suspects the case $m \geq 2n$ can be handled by a prime in between, and conjectures the problem reduces to integers sharing the same prime factors; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof that $P_n \neq P_m$ for all $n \neq m$ with $n,m \geq 3$, or an explicit counterexample pair.
why: Resolves whether an integer is determined by the primes up to it that do not divide it; a counterexample would reveal a striking coincidence in the distribution of primes relative to factorizations.

title: Why is the Simple Zeros Conjecture said to be stronger than the Riemann Hypothesis
open: Why is the Simple Zeros Conjecture — the assertion that all zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple — commonly said to be "stronger" than the Riemann Hypothesis? No implication SZC $\implies$ RH is known or readily found, so what justifies this informal claim of comparative strength?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 11, 2 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/394295/why-is-the-simple-zeros-conjecture-said-to-be-stronger-than-the-riemann-hypothes.
solved_when: A clear explanation (or reference) is given of the precise sense in which the Simple Zeros Conjecture is stronger than the Riemann Hypothesis, or a demonstration that no such implication exists and the claim is merely heuristic.
why: Clarifying the logical relationship between these two central conjectures about the zeta function sharpens how the community ranks open problems and prevents a widely repeated but unverified claim from passing as fact.

title: What groups should I test my conjecture on
open: If two finite groups have the same number of elements of every order, must they be isomorphic? More broadly, which pairs of finite groups form a "representative sample" on which such an order-statistic isomorphism criterion should be tested?
status: The conjecture originated as a MathOverflow question (community-curated, score 1, 1 answer), where the asker reported verifying it computationally on all pairs of groups up to size 12 and proving it for abelian groups, using a custom Python library. No resolution beyond this is recorded. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/372254/what-groups-should-i-test-my-conjecture-on
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that equal counts of elements of every order imply isomorphism for arbitrary finite groups, or a finite pair of non-isomorphic groups with identical order statistics is exhibited.
why: A positive answer would give a purely arithmetic, easily computable isomorphism test for finite groups; a counterexample would sharpen understanding of how much of a group's structure its element-order statistics actually determine.

title: Adaptive prime window conjecture, does a previous prime gap correlate with the following one
open: Does the gap to the next prime after an integer $x$ admit a bound driven by the gap to the previous prime? Specifically, for every integer $x>2$, with $p_x$ the largest prime strictly less than $x$, $d_x = x-p_x$, $q_x$ the smallest prime strictly greater than $x$, and $g_x = q_x - x$, is it true that $g_x \leq \left\lceil 2e^{-\gamma}\left[\left(\ln\frac{x}{d_x}\right)^2 + 2\right]\right\rceil$, where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant? The proposer originally formulated the bound only for prime inputs, but reports that computation supports it for arbitrary integers $x$, a stronger claim.
status: The problem is a community-posted conjecture on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/515297/adaptive-prime-window-conjecture-does-a-previous-prime-gap-correlate-with-the-f; the proposer worked on it for nearly a year and reports computational evidence supporting it for all integers, not just primes. No resolution is recorded.
solved_when: The conjectured inequality $g_x \leq \left\lceil 2e^{-\gamma}\left[\left(\ln\frac{x}{d_x}\right)^2 + 2\right]\right\rceil$ is proven for every integer $x > 2$ (or disproved by an explicit counterexample).
why: Such a bound would give an explicit, adaptive upper limit on the next prime gap conditioned on the observed previous gap, a concrete refinement of prime gap estimates beyond worst-case bounds.

title: on the unsolvability of the $\{3 \times 3 \times \cdots \times 3\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k
open: Can every set of $3^k$ points of the form $\mathcal{H}(3,k):=\{3 \times 3 \times \cdots \times 3\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be covered by an optimal polygonal chain $\mathcal{P}\left(\frac{3^k-1}{2}\right)$ of minimum link-length whose two endpoints lie in $\mathcal{H}(3,k)$ if and only if neither endpoint is the point $(1,1,\dots,1)$, i.e. $\rm{S}_1 \not\equiv (1,1,\dots,1) \wedge \rm{S}_{\left(\frac{3^k+1}{2}\right)} \not\equiv (1,1,\dots,1)$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 0 answers); the record cites no published progress beyond the original conjecture and the related Theorem 1 by 1 and Theorem 2.1 by Minimum-Link Covering Trails for any Hypercubic Lattice, which characterize optimal covering trails for hypercubic lattices. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/433060/conjecture-on-the-unsolvability-of-the-3-times-3-times-cdots-times-3-s.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the stated equivalence: an optimal minimum-link-length covering trail with both endpoints in $\mathcal{H}(3,k)$ exists exactly when neither endpoint equals $(1,1,\dots,1)$, for general $k$. The conjecture is suspected to be approachable via Theorem 1 by 1 and Theorem 2.1 by Minimum-Link Covering Trails for any Hypercubic Lattice.
why: It would settle the conjecture posed in 2020 (see Solving the $106$ years old $3^k$ points problem with the clockwise-algorithm, JFMA, 3(2), p. 96) on covering the $3^k$-point lattice with a minimum-link polygonal chain, resolving a long-tail geometric optimization question.

title: about the abc conjecture
open: Does there exist an integer $n_0 \geq 2$ such that the set $$\left\{\frac{c}{rad(abc)^{n_0}}: a, b >0,\; c=a+b,\; \gcd(a, b)=1\right\}$$ is bounded? Formally, this asks whether some fixed exponent $n_0 \geq 2$ on the radical forces the ratio $c/rad(abc)^{n_0}$ to stay uniformly bounded over all coprime triples with $c = a+b$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score -1, 1 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/402356/questions-about-the-abc-conjecture.
solved_when: An explicit integer $n_0 \geq 2$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) for which the above set is bounded; the abc conjecture directly implies this statement, so an unconditional proof would be the natural success criterion.
why: A proof would give a radical-flavored boundedness statement unconditionally, weakening dependence on the abc conjecture for this consequence; failure or persistence of the question would clarify how much of abc's power is genuinely needed.

title: Is the conjecture $min(A,B) \le rad(ABC)$ new and correct
open: Is the conjecture that pairwise coprime positive integers $A+B=C$ must satisfy $\min(A,B) \le \rad(ABC)$ both new and correct? Formally: for positive integers with $\gcd(A,B)=\gcd(B,C)=\gcd(C,A)=1$ and $A+B=C$, does $\min(A,B) \le \rad(ABC)$ always hold, and does this statement already appear in the literature?
status: The question was posted and community-curated on MathOverflow, where it received a score of -2 and 1 answer (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339030/is-the-conjecture-mina-b-le-radabc-new-and-correct).
solved_when: The conjecture is either proved in general or refuted by an explicit counterexample of pairwise coprime positive integers $A, B, C$ with $A+B=C$ and $\min(A,B) > \rad(ABC)$, together with a determination of whether the statement (or an equivalent form) already appears in prior literature.
why: The proposer shows the conjecture would yield a quick proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, reducing it via $x^n \le \rad(x^n y^n z^n) = \rad(xyz) \le xyz$ to the single case $n=3$ (using $z^3 + (z-1)^n < z^n$ for $n > 3$, $z > 1$).

title: Does smooth and proper over $\mathbb Z$ imply rational
open: If a variety is smooth and proper over $\mathbb{Z}$, must it be rational? Fontaine's non-digitized letter to Messing shows that such an $X$ has vanishing nondiagonal Dolbeault groups $H^q(X_{\mathbb{Q}}; \Omega^p)=0$ for $p \ne q$, $p+q \leqslant 3$, and the natural sharpening is to remove the degree restriction.
status: The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 23, 1 answer), where the original poster asks whether the rationality conjecture is widely held, who first made it, and whether it is written down anywhere; the only cited evidence is Fontaine's non-digitized letter to Messing establishing the vanishing $H^q(X_{\mathbb{Q}}; \Omega^p)=0$ for $p \ne q$, $p+q \leqslant 3$. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/97086/does-smooth-and-proper-over-mathbb-z-imply-rational.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every smooth proper scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$ is rational; the natural cohomological variant is resolved by showing or refuting $H^q(X_{\mathbb{Q}}; \Omega^p)=0$ for all $p \ne q$ without the restriction $p+q \leqslant 3$.
why: It would clarify how restrictive arithmetic smoothness over $\mathbb{Z}$ is on the underlying geometry; the vanishing conjecture would extend Fontaine's low-degree obstruction to all degrees, and a single space satisfying the cohomological hypothesis still need not be rational, since fake projective planes mimicking the cohomology of the real projective plane exist — though their finite covers would again be smooth and proper over $\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Nonnegative to Positive Curvature.
open: Why is it so hard to tell whether a closed, simply-connected manifold of nonnegative sectional curvature can also carry a metric of strictly positive sectional curvature? More concretely, what are the principal difficulties and currently blocked paths to the Hopf Conjecture, i.e. whether $S^2\times S^2$ admits a metric of positive curvature — and why does no known obstruction separate the two classes, despite the abundance of nonnegative-curvature examples compared to positive-curvature ones?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question scored 22 and received 1 answer; it reports that, to the asker's knowledge, no obstructions are known distinguishing nonnegative from positive curvature, while examples of nonnegative curvature vastly outnumber examples of positive curvature. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/47942/nonnegative-to-positive-curvature
solved_when: A characterization (or a definite answer in a representative case such as $S^2\times S^2$) of which closed simply-connected nonnegatively curved manifolds admit positive sectional curvature is given — in particular, either a positive-curvature metric on $S^2\times S^2$ or a proof that none exists.
why: The gap between the two example classes suggests a hidden structural distinction that no current invariant captures; finding it — or a positive-curvature metric on $S^2\times S^2$ — would be a major step in understanding the rigidity of positive sectional curvature.

title: Is every finite-order unimodular matrix conjugate to a $0,1,-1$ matrix
open: Is every finite-order matrix $A\in\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$ conjugate within $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$ to a matrix whose entries lie in $\{0,1,-1\}$? That is, if $A^k=1$ for some $k\geq 1$, must there exist $g\in\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$ such that $gAg^{-1}$ has only $0$, $1$, and $-1$ as entries?
status: The problem was raised on MathOverflow, where Mark Sapir remarked that it is a famous open problem; the thread is community-curated (score 13, 2 answers) and includes discussion of what is known and which other parts of mathematics the problem connects to. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/346842/is-every-finite-order-unimodular-matrix-conjugate-to-a-0-1-1-matrix
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that every finite-order element of $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$ is $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$-conjugate to a $\{0,1,-1\}$-matrix, for all $n$; a single explicit $A$ of finite order not conjugate to any such matrix would resolve it negatively.
why: Finite-order unimodular matrices govern symmetries of lattices, and an affirmative answer would give a strikingly simple normal form for all such symmetries; it is a famous open problem, so a resolution would settle a long-standing question in integral linear algebra.

title: Why would dim primitive irrep divide size of some conjugacy class
open: Which conjugacy classes of a finite group should be naturally associated to its irreducible representations through divisibility of class sizes? Concretely, Isaacs et al. (2005, Conjecture C) assert that if χ is a primitive irreducible character of a finite group G, then χ(1) divides |cl_G(g)| for some g ∈ G — can one describe which class(es) witness this, at least for standard families such as S_n, A_n, GL_n(F_q), and is the conjecture still open?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 12, 1 answer). The record notes verification that Conjecture C holds for all irreducible characters, primitive or not, of all groups in the Atlas; the general conjecture and the question of identifying the corresponding classes remain open as posed. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/108406/why-would-dim-primitive-irrep-divide-size-of-some-conjugacy-class
solved_when: Conjecture C is either proved in general or refuted by an explicit counterexample; additionally, for standard groups such as S_n, A_n, and GL_n(F_q), a description is given of which conjugacy class(es) correspond to a given irreducible representation via the divisibility χ(1) | |cl_G(g)|, with representative examples.
why: A description of the correspondence between irreducible representations and conjugacy classes would reveal structural links between the character degree set and the class size set of a finite group, two invariant sets the authors note have numerous parallels and analogies.

title: What keeps asymptotic Goldbach's conjecture out of reach of current technology
open: Why does the binary (asymptotic) Goldbach conjecture — the existence of an $N>0$ such that every integer $n>N$ makes $2n$ a sum of two primes — remain out of reach of current technology, despite the proof of the ternary Goldbach conjecture by H.A. Helfgott and the bounded-gaps breakthrough of Yitang Zhang improved by Tao, Maynard and others? In particular, which obstructions — gaps in our knowledge of exponential sums, or heuristics that resist rigorous treatment — block the circle-method or sieve approaches from proving such an asymptotic result?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question scored 10 and received 1 answer; it is a community-vetted problem outside standard lists, motivated by high community interest. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/161947/what-keeps-asymptotic-goldbachs-conjecture-out-of-reach-of-current-technology
solved_when: A rigorous proof exists that there is an $N>0$ such that for all integers $n>N$, $2n$ is a sum of two primes; short of that, a satisfactory account of the specific technical obstructions (e.g., the exponential-sum estimates or parity phenomena) that currently prevent such a proof.
why: The binary Goldbach conjecture is one of the oldest open problems in additive number theory; explaining the obstruction would clarify exactly which inputs the circle method lacks, and any proof would settle the asymptotic form of the conjecture for all sufficiently large even numbers.

title: Is there always one integer between these two rational numbers
open: For each integer $k\geq 2$, is there always an integer $c$ with $\frac{3^k-2^k}{2^k-1}<c\leq \frac{3^k-1}{2^k}$? Note that for $k\geq 2$ the lower bound is always a proper fraction and never matches an integer.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 9, 3 answers). The asker later posted a short proof on Overleaf ("Edit #28 is perfect!"), noted a connection to Waring's problem, and observed via https://oeis.org/A060692 ("Corresponds to the only solution of the Diophantine equation 3^n = x*2^n + y*1^n with constraint 0 <= y < 2^n") that this is equivalent to the $a+c$ term in the Waring if-statement, while flagging that no proof is recorded that the Diophantine equation is always $\leq 2^n$. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/280192/is-there-always-one-integer-between-these-two-rational-numbers
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for every integer $k\geq 2$ there exists an integer $c$ satisfying $\frac{3^k-2^k}{2^k-1}<c\leq \frac{3^k-1}{2^k}$.
why: Resolving it settles a Waring-type question about writing $3^n = x\cdot 2^n + y\cdot 1^n$ with $0 \leq y < 2^n$, connecting a simple-looking interval statement to a classical Diophantine problem.

title: Has there been any progress on this open problem about co-well-poweredness of accessible categories
open: Does the converse implication hold: if every accessible category is co-well-copowered, must there be a proper class of strongly compact cardinals? More precisely, Makkai–Paré showed, via Theorem 6.3.8 of *Accessible Categories: The Foundations of Categorical Model Theory*, that a proper class of strongly compact cardinals implies colimits are uniformly detectable in every accessible category — and Proposition 6.2.2 shows detectable pushouts give co-well-poweredness (also derivable by imitating Theorem 2.49 of Adámek–Rosický, *Locally Presentable and Accessible Categories*) — and the question is whether the large-cardinal hypothesis is necessary.
status: This is a community-vetted open problem posed on MathOverflow (score 8, 0 answers); no progress or answers are recorded. The background results are Proposition 6.2.2 and Theorem 6.3.8 of Makkai–Paré (*Accessible Categories: The Foundations of Categorical Model Theory*), with the co-well-poweredness conclusion also following by imitating the argument of Theorem 2.49 in Adámek–Rosický (*Locally Presentable and Accessible Categories*). Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/455750/has-there-been-any-progress-on-this-open-problem-about-co-well-poweredness-of-ac
solved_when: A proof or refutation of the converse: either a proof, in ZFC without a proper class of strongly compact cardinals, that every accessible category is co-well-copowered; or a model of set theory in which every accessible category is co-well-copowered yet there is no proper class of strongly compact cardinals.
why: It would calibrate the exact large-cardinal strength needed for a basic size-control property of accessible categories, clarifying whether categorical model theory's foundational results genuinely depend on strong compactness or follow from weaker assumptions.

title: A cohomology associated to a (not necessarily integrable) distribution (Hilbert 16th problem and dyn
open: For a manifold $M$ with a distribution $D$, take the subcomplex $\Omega^*(M,D)=\{\alpha \in \Omega^*(M)\mid \alpha_{|D}=d\alpha_{|D}=0\}$ (the condition $d\alpha_{|D}=0$ is redundant when $D$ is integrable) and form the quotient complex $\Omega^*(M)/\Omega^*(M,D)$, replacing the space of coboundaries (exact forms along the distribution) by its closure in the smooth topology; does the resulting cohomology $H^*(M,D)$ admit the dynamical Lefschetz trace formula of "Hilbert 16th problem and dynamical Lefschetz trace formula" when the flow of a vector field $\tilde{X}$ on $M$ preserves $D$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 8, 0 answers); the problem originates from the MathOverflow post https://mathoverflow.net/questions/335820/a-cohomology-associated-to-a-not-necessarily-integrable-distribution-hilbert, which also links a paper explaining the reason for taking the smooth-topology closure of the coboundaries. No answer or resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation with counterexample) that the dynamical Lefschetz trace formula, as discussed in "Hilbert 16th problem and dynamical Lefschetz trace formula," holds for the cohomology $H^*(M,D)$ of $M$ along $D$ whenever the flow of $\tilde{X}$ preserves $D$.
why: Extending the dynamical Lefschetz trace formula to this distribution-relative cohomology would link fixed-point counting for flows preserving nonintegrable distributions to a concrete cohomological invariant, connecting Hilbert's 16th problem to dynamics in a new setting.

title: Mordell's equation $y^2 = x^3 + k$ and perfect numbers
open: For which rational values of $K$ does Mordell's equation $Y^2 = X^3 + K$ have only finitely many rational solutions? More precisely, is there a usable criterion — extending beyond the known sufficient conditions that apply only when $K \equiv 1$ or $2 \pmod 4$ — for finiteness when $K$ ranges over $\mathbb{Q}$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 6, 3 answers). A known sufficient condition, attributed to a Japanese[?] paper, states that $Y^2 = X^3 + K$ has finitely many solutions in $\mathbb{Q}$ if: (1) $-K$ is not of the form $3t^2 + 1$ or $3t^2 - 1$; (2) $K \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ or $K \equiv 2 \pmod 4$; and (3) $3$ does not divide the class number of the (real/imaginary) quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{K})$. No fuller answer for general rational $K$ is recorded. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/48215/re-mordells-equation-y2-x3-k-and-perfect-numbers
solved_when: A checkable criterion (necessary and sufficient, or a substantial extension of the known sufficient conditions) is given for rational $K$, covering values beyond $K \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $K \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, under which $Y^2 = X^3 + K$ has finitely many solutions in $\mathbb{Q}$.
why: A solution would settle when the arithmetic of these Mordell curves is finite over $\mathbb{Q}$ for arbitrary rational parameter $K$, removing the current restriction tied to the class number of the quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{K})$ and the exclusion of $-K$ of the form $3t^2 \pm 1$.

title: Status of Hadamard matrix conjecture
open: Does a Hadamard matrix exist for every order that is a positive multiple of 4? Equivalently, is the classical Hadamard conjecture — that an $n \times n$ sign matrix with mutually orthogonal rows exists for every $n = 4k$, $k$ a positive integer — true?
status: Community-curated and vetted on MathOverflow (score 20, 4 answers); see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/85201/status-of-hadamard-matrix-conjecture. No definitive resolution is recorded in the record.
solved_when: A Hadamard matrix of order $4k$ is constructed (or its nonexistence proved) for every positive integer $k$; short of that, progress is measured by eliminating the remaining orders $4k$ for which no Hadamard matrix is known.
why: Hadamard matrices sit at the crossroads of design theory, coding theory, and combinatorics; resolving the conjecture would complete a century-old existence picture and settle a standard benchmark problem that many constructions and bounds are calibrated against.

title: A tantalizing Gamma quotient to challenge the Rohrlich-Lang Conjecture
open: The Rohrlich–Lang Conjecture predicts that every polynomial relation among Gamma values at rational arguments over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a consequence of the functional equations of the Gamma function — or, in a narrower form, that any quotient of products of Gamma values over $\mathbb{Q}$ that is algebraic can be evaluated using only the reflection and multiplication formulae. What does this conjecture imply for the specific quotient built from $A := \prod_{k=0}^{5}\Gamma\!\left(\frac{49^k \bmod 78}{78}\right) = \Gamma(\tfrac{1}{78})\Gamma(\tfrac{25}{78})\Gamma(\tfrac{43}{78})\Gamma(\tfrac{49}{78})\Gamma(\tfrac{55}{78})\Gamma(\tfrac{61}{78})$ and its companion product $B$?
status: The problem was posed and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 18, 2 answers). The record cites Lang, S., "Relations de distributions et exemples classiques," Séminaire Delange-Pisot-Poitou, 19e année: 1977/78, Théorie des nombres, Fasc. 2, Exp. N° 40, 6 p.; Collected Papers, vol. III, Springer (2000), 59–65. No resolution is recorded.
solved_when: A determination of whether the quotient of the given products $A$ and $B$ (with all Gamma arguments as displayed) is algebraic, and if so, whether it can be derived using only the reflection and multiplication formulae, is achieved.
why: A concrete analysis of this quotient provides a sharp test case for the Rohrlich–Lang Conjecture, potentially exposing Gamma-value relations that go beyond the classical functional equations.

title: Is the conjecture A+B=C following correct
open: Is the conjecture on A+B=C following correct ? Conjecture: Let $A, B, C$ be three positive integer numbers such that $A+B=C$ with $\gcd(A, B, C) = 1$ . By Fundamental theorem of arithmetic we write: $A=a_1^{x_1}a_2^{x_2}...a_n^{x_n}$ , $B=b_1^{y_1}b_2^{y_2}...b_m^{y_m}$ , $C=c_1^{z_1}c_2^{z_2}...c_k^{z_k}$ Let $d = \min\{x_i, y_j, z_h \}$ where $1 \le i \le n, 1\ \le j \le m, 1\le h \le k$ then $$d \le 5$$ PS: I read above one hunded papers, I observed that in any case $\min\{x_i, y_j, z_h \} \le 3$ Example 1: Ten solutions of Catalan-Fermat equation Example 2: $2^4.3^5.7^6+5^9.11^8=19^1.23^1.47^1.6679^1.3051977^1$ See also: Minimal exponent in prime factorization of n A051904 Nivens Constant
status: community-curated on MathOverflow (score 10, 0 answers)
why: high community interest; long-tail problems outside standard lists

title: Generalization of Legendre`s conjecture
open: Does Legendre's conjecture extend to higher powers in the following sense: for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$, is there an $n_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for all $n \geq n_0(\varepsilon)$ the interval between $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ and $(n+1)^{1+\varepsilon}$ contains a prime? Equivalently, does a prime eventually lie between consecutive values of the $(1+\varepsilon)$-th power of $n$?
status: The question was posed on MathOverflow, where it received community attention (score 8, 2 answers); the asker was unaware of any number-theoretic obstruction to the generalization and did not know whether its truth is established. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/267017/generalization-of-legendres-conjecture
solved_when: A proof, or disproof, that for each $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$ there exists $n_0(\varepsilon)$ such that every $n \geq n_0(\varepsilon)$ admits a prime strictly between $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ and $(n+1)^{1+\varepsilon}$; the case $\varepsilon = 1$ recovers Legendre's conjecture itself.
why: A positive answer would interpolate between known prime-gap technology and the classical Legendre conjecture, clarifying exactly which power gaps between consecutive integers are forced to contain primes; a negative answer for some $\varepsilon$ would reveal a surprising obstruction in the distribution of primes.

title: Vaught conjecture for uncountable languages
open: Does the Vaught conjecture generalize to uncountable languages: if a complete theory in a language of size $\lambda$ (for uncountable $\lambda$) has more than $\lambda$ non-isomorphic models of size $\lambda$, must it have $2^\lambda$ such models? And does the analogous Morley-style strengthening hold, where having more than $\lambda^+$ non-isomorphic models of size $\lambda$ forces $2^\lambda$ of them?
status: Posed as a community-curated open problem on MathOverflow (score 7, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/146261/vaught-conjecture-for-uncountable-languages; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: For every uncountable cardinal $\lambda$, every complete theory in a language of size $\lambda$ with more than $\lambda$ (respectively $\lambda^+$, for the Morley version) non-isomorphic models of size $\lambda$ is shown to have $2^\lambda$ non-isomorphic models of size $\lambda$ — or a counterexample is produced.
why: These statements are the natural cardinal-arithmetic generalizations of the classical Vaught conjecture and Morley's theorem from countable to uncountable languages; settling them clarifies the structure of model-theoretic complexity at uncountable cardinalities.

title: What will be the consequences if second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture turns out to be true
open: What would follow mathematically if the Second Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture (that $\pi(x+y) \le \pi(x) + \pi(y)$) turned out to be true, given that it is generally believed false but remains unproved? In particular, which conjectures and results equivalent to the $k$-tuple (First Hardy-Littlewood) Conjecture would collapse, and which statements would follow if and only if the Second Conjecture holds?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 7, 0 answers); no answer has been given. Source: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/192215/what-will-be-the-consequences-if-second-hardy-littlewood-conjecture-turns-out-to
solved_when: A characterization is given of the consequences of the Second Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture being true — including references to results equivalent to the $k$-tuple Conjecture (which would then be false) and to conjectures equivalent to the Second Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture itself.
why: Since the two Hardy-Littlewood conjectures are mutually incompatible, a proof of the Second would falsify the $k$-tuple Conjecture, undermining the many expected results that depend on it; a map of these dependencies clarifies what is truly at stake in the conjectures.

title: Different flavours of Vassiliev Conjecture
open: Are the various closely related formulations of the Vassiliev Conjecture — the "genuine" version and its neighbors — actually equivalent, and does the genuine version hold? Precisely, letting $\sim_n$ identify knots indistinguishable by Vassiliev invariants of order $\le n$ on the space $\mathcal{K}$ of knots in 3 dimensions, the Genuine Vassiliev Conjecture asserts that any two distinct knots can be separated by some Vassiliev invariant, i.e. that the natural maps $\pi_0(\mathcal{K}) \to \varprojlim_n \pi_0(\mathcal{K})/{\sim_n}$ are injective through the tower of surjections $\pi_0(\mathcal{K}) \to \cdots \to \pi_0(\mathcal{K})/{\sim_n} \to \pi_0(\mathcal{K})/{\sim_{n-1}} \to \cdots \to \pi_0(\mathcal{K})/{\sim_1}$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow, where the question was asked out of puzzlement over how several tightly related kinds of results around Vassiliev invariants connect, the asker suspecting a detail obvious to the community was being missed; the post has score 6 and 1 answer. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/452603/different-flavours-of-vassiliev-conjecture
solved_when: The different flavours of the Vassiliev Conjecture circulating in the literature are clarified and shown to be equivalent (or their precise relationships established), and the genuine conjecture is proved or refuted: either every pair of distinct knots is distinguished by a Vassiliev invariant, or an explicit pair of distinct knots indistinguishable by all finite-order invariants is produced.
