why: Settling the relationships among these variants would remove a real source of confusion in the finite-type invariant literature, and a proof of the genuine conjecture would show that Vassiliev invariants completely classify knots — the central structural question of the theory.

title: An inequality in cyclic polygon and tangential polygon
open: Does a polygonal analogue of the Erdős–Mordell inequality hold for every cyclic polygon and its tangential polygon? Formally, let $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ be a cyclic polygon with tangential polygon $B_1B_2\cdots B_n$, and let $P$ be an arbitrary interior point of $A_1\cdots A_n$; if $d_i$ denotes the distance from $P$ to $A_iA_{i+1}$ and $D_i$ the distance from $P$ to $B_iB_{i+1}$ (indices mod $n$), prove that $\sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i \ge \sec\frac{\pi}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i$, with equality exactly for the regular polygon.
status: The conjecture is posted as community-curated on MathOverflow (score 5, 0 answers) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/244984/an-inequality-in-cyclic-polygon-and-tangential-polygon. The triangle case is proved in "A strengthened version of the Erdős-Mordell inequality", Forum Geometricorum, 16: 317–321, MR 3556993; no proof of the general case is known.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, with counterexample) of the inequality $\sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i \ge \sec(\pi/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i$ is given for all cyclic $n$-gons and their tangential polygons, for arbitrary interior point $P$, together with determination of the equality cases (equality conjectured when the polygon is regular).
why: It extends the classical Erdős–Mordell inequality from triangles to all cyclic polygons and strengthens it, so a proof would establish a uniform geometric inequality family; the triangle case already appears in the literature, leaving the general case the natural open frontier.

title: The action of the unitary divisors group on the set of divisors and odd perfect numbers
open: Do the orbits of the unitary divisor group $U_n$ (with operation $a \oplus b = \frac{ab}{\gcd(a,b)^2}$) acting on the divisor set $D_n$ via $u \oplus d = \frac{ud}{\gcd(u,d)^2}$ have the simple form $U_n \oplus d = d \cdot U_{n/d^2}$ for every square divisor $d \in S_n$? Formally, the conjecture is that each orbit is indexed by a square divisor $d$ of $n$ and equals $d$ times the unitary divisors of $n/d^2$.
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 4, 1 answer). The orbit description remains a "seeming" empirical observation; the identity $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \in S_n} d\,\sigma^*(n/d^2)$ can be proved directly since both sides are multiplicative and equal on prime powers. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/370207/the-action-of-the-unitary-divisors-group-on-the-set-of-divisors-and-odd-perfect
solved_when: The orbit formula $U_n \oplus d = d \cdot U_{n/d^2}$ for each $d \in S_n$ is proved (or refuted with a counterexample). A direct equivalent target is the identity $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \in S_n} d\,\sigma^*(n/d^2)$, where $\sigma^*$ is the sum of unitary divisors, since both sides are multiplicative and agree on prime powers.
why: The orbit structure would yield the divisor-sum identity above, which combined with the fact that $\sigma^*(k)$ is divisible by $2^{\omega(k)}$ for odd $k$ gives a new line of attack on the existence of odd perfect numbers.

title: about primes and Fibonacci numbers
open: Is it true that for every integer $m > 4$ not divisible by $2$ or $3$, there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $F_{m+n} - F_n$ is prime? The numerical evidence is substantial: the smallest such $n$ has been computed for all $m < 3000$, with examples including $[5,1]$, $[7,3]$, $[11,4]$, $[13,5]$, $[17,3]$, …, $[619,1353]$, …, $[2011,6629]$.
status: The conjecture was posted on math.stackexchange and received no answer proving or disproving it; searches for counterexamples (notably by user @Peter) found none, and all supporting values of $n$ for $m < 3000$ are tabulated, with the hard cases listed at the bottom. The primes found this way, converted to Zeckendorf representation, form an alternating sequence of $1$s and $0$s, and a related OEIS sequence concerns prime differences of Fibonacci numbers. The problem is community-curated on MathOverflow with score 3 and 0 answers. Key reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/441001/conjecture-about-primes-and-fibonacci-numbers
solved_when: A proof or disproof is given of the statement that for every positive integer $m > 4$ with $2 \nmid m$ and $3 \nmid m$, some positive integer $n$ makes $F_{m+n} - F_n$ prime.
why: A proof would show that differences of Fibonacci numbers with suitable index gaps form an unexpectedly rich source of primes; a disproof would identify a structural obstruction. Either outcome clarifies how primality is distributed along this natural family of linear recurrences.

title: A conjecture on six planes
open: Do four coplanar points and six planes through pairs of them always force a Miquel-type concurrence? Formally: given points $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ on a plane $\sigma$, and six planes $\sigma_{12}, \sigma_{13}, \sigma_{14}, \sigma_{23}, \sigma_{24}$ with $\sigma_{ij}$ passing through $P_i$ and $P_j$, let $P_{ijk}$ be the common point of $\sigma_{ij}, \sigma_{jk}, \sigma_{ki}$; prove that $P_{123}, P_{124}, P_{134}, P_{234}$ are coplanar.
status: The conjecture was posted on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 3 and 0 answers; the proposer verified it experimentally with GeoGebra and no proof is known. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/234762/a-conjecture-on-six-planes
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) of the stated coplanarity is given, in the general configuration described.
why: It is a natural spatial analogue of Miquel's six-circles theorem and Clifford's circle theorem, so a proof would extend a classical circle-geometry theme to planes in space.

title: Analogue of Fermat's little theorem for Bernoulli numbers
open: Does a Fermat-style congruence hold for Bernoulli numbers? Let $D_{2n}$ denote the denominator of $\frac{B_{2n}}{4n}$, where $B_n$ is the $n$-th Bernoulli number; is it true that $a^{2n} \equiv 1 \pmod{D_{2n}}$ whenever $\gcd(a, D_{2n}) = 1$?
status: Posted on MathOverflow after remaining open on MSE for three weeks; the question is still open there (community-curated on MathOverflow, score 2, 1 answer). See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/414103/analogue-of-fermats-little-theorem-for-bernoulli-numbers.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of the stated congruence $a^{2n} \equiv 1 \pmod{D_{2n}}$ for all $n$ and all integers $a$ coprime to $D_{2n}$ (with $D_{2n}$ the denominator of $\frac{B_{2n}}{4n}$).
why: A proof would give a clean multiplicative-order constraint on the denominators of Bernoulli numbers, connecting them to the structure of the groups $(\mathbb{Z}/D_{2n}\mathbb{Z})^\times$; a disproof would clarify where the analogy with Fermat's little theorem genuinely breaks.

title: Primes and the factorial
open: Does every prime $p>5$ admit a prime $q<p$ with $q\equiv m!\pmod p$ for some $m$ with $2<m<p$, and dually, does every prime $p$ admit a prime $q<p^2$ with $q\equiv m!\pmod{p^2}$ for some $m$ (even with $2<m<p$, as pointed out in a comment)?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 2, 1 answers); discussion at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/243771/primes-and-the-factorial and https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1838931/conjecture-about-primes-and-the-factorial.
solved_when: Both conjectures are proven (or a counterexample found) for all primes; currently both have been verified for all $p<100,000,000$.
why: For large $p$ there are many nonzero solutions to $n\equiv m!\pmod p$ and $n\equiv m!\pmod{p^2}$, and the probability that one of those $n$ is prime increases with $p$, giving heuristic reason to believe both conjectures are true; settling them would clarify how factorials distribute primes modulo $p$ and $p^2$.

title: Testing the Cartan determinant conjecture via Gorenstein algebras
open: Does the Cartan determinant conjecture hold for endomorphism algebras $B := End_A(X)$ arising from Gorenstein algebras $A$ of infinite global dimension with finitely many indecomposable Gorenstein projective modules? Formally, since the Gorenstein-Cartan matrix of $A$ (with entries $Hom_A(G_i, G_j)$ for indecomposable Gorenstein projectives $G_i, G_j$) should agree, up to permutation, with the Cartan matrix of the finite-global-dimension algebra $B$, the conjecture's claim that such a determinant is always 1 can be tested in this setting; and if the general case resists proof, does it at least hold when $A$ is a Nakayama algebra?
status: Community-curated MathOverflow question (score 2, 0 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/279555/testing-the-cartan-determinant-conjecture-via-gorenstein-algebras. It is known that such $B$ has finite global dimension and that there is an equivalence between $add(X)$ and $proj$-$B$, so the Gorenstein-Cartan matrix should coincide with the Cartan matrix of $B$ up to permutation; no answer resolving the conjecture in this setting is recorded.
solved_when: The determinant of the Cartan matrix of every algebra of the form $B = End_A(X)$ constructed as above is shown to be 1; or, failing the general case, a proof is given for all such $B$ with $A$ a Nakayama algebra.
why: A proof would verify the long-standing Cartan determinant conjecture on a new class of finite-global-dimension algebras produced from Gorenstein data; a counterexample would refute the conjecture outright.

title: A generalization of Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture
open: Do the proposed generalizations of the Lander–Parkin–Selfridge conjecture hold? Specifically, given $h(P)=\min(a_1,\dots,a_k)$ for $P=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$ (with $h(1)=1$): (Case 1) if $n\ge 1$, the $A_i \ne B_j$ are positive integers with $\gcd(A_1,\dots,A_n,B_1,\dots,B_n)=1$, and $\sum_{i=1}^n A_i = \sum_{j=1}^n B_j$, must $2n \ge d$ where $d = \min(h(A_1),\dots,h(A_n),h(B_1),\dots,h(B_n))$; and (Case 2) if $n \ne m$, $n,m \ge 1$, and $\sum_{i=1}^n A_i = \sum_{j=1}^m B_j$ with the analogous coprimality condition, must $m+n \ge d$?
status: The problem was posed on MathOverflow, where it is community-curated with score 1 and 1 answer; no resolution is recorded. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/337549/a-generalization-of-lander-parkin-and-selfridge-conjecture
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, by counterexample) of both conjectured inequalities $2n \ge d$ and $m+n \ge d$ under the stated hypotheses is given.
why: It extends the classical Lander–Parkin–Selfridge conjecture from perfect powers to all positive integers via the exponent of the prime factorization, so a resolution would settle a broad family of equal-sum questions in additive number theory.

title: A conjecture on the prime counting function
open: Is the prime counting function $\pi(x)$ eventually midpoint-concave in the sense that $\pi(x)+\pi(y)\le 2\pi\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)$ holds for all sufficiently large $x$ and $y$? More precisely, is there a proof of the conjecture that this inequality holds once both $x$ and $y$ are large enough (with the poster noting it appears to hold when $x/y$ is sufficiently large, assuming $x\ge y$)?
status: The problem was posed and community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answer), where the poster observed that the reverse inequality $\pi(x)+\pi(y)>2\pi\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)$ fails infinitely often by a counterexample of R. Israel. No proof of the eventual inequality is recorded. Key work: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/210537/a-conjecture-on-the-prime-counting-function
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the statement that $\pi(x)+\pi(y)\le 2\pi\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and $y$; the record states no quantitative threshold beyond "sufficiently large."
why: The inequality is a proposed repair of the poster's original conjecture $\pi(x)+\pi(y)>2\pi\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)$, which R. Israel showed fails infinitely often; a proof would settle the eventual midpoint-concavity of $\pi(x)$, a natural question connected to the Second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture.

title: A New Quantitative Lower Bound for Exponential Structures in Coprime Triples
open: For pairwise coprime positive integers $a, b, c$ with $a+b=c$ and $c>2$, let $h(n)$ and $H(n)$ denote the minimum and maximum exponents in the prime factorization of $n$ (with the convention $h(1)=H(1)=+\infty$, so $1/h(1)=1/H(1)=0$). Is it true that for every such triple, $\sum_{x\in\{a,b,c\}} 1/h(x) + \frac{1}{4}\sum_{x\in\{a,b,c\}} 1/H(x) \ge 1$, with equality only for $(1, 12167, 12168)$?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answer). The pattern emerged from a comprehensive computational search over the entire "abc hits" database (for $c < 2^{63}$) and other extremal families, including Fermat–Catalan solutions and 241 abc good triples, with equality observed uniquely at $(1, 12167, 12168)$. Reference: https://mathoverflow.net/questions/507177/a-new-quantitative-lower-bound-for-exponential-structures-in-coprime-triples
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via counterexample) of the inequality $\sum_{x\in\{a,b,c\}} 1/h(x) + \frac{1}{4}\sum_{x\in\{a,b,c\}} 1/H(x) \ge 1$ for all pairwise coprime $a+b=c$ with $c>2$, together with confirmation that equality holds uniquely at $(1, 12167, 12168)$, where $1+23^3 = 2^3\cdot 3^2\cdot 13^2$.
why: The conjecture strengthens an earlier proposal that $\min(h(a),h(b),h(c))\le 3$, giving a quantitative lower bound on how "exponential" coprime triples must be; it would yield a new refinement in the direction of the abc conjecture.

title: "Halfway" approach to Landau's 4th problem (special case of Bateman-Horn)
open: What makes Landau's fourth problem — whether $n^2+1$ is prime for infinitely many $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ — so resistant to attack, given that sieving heuristics suggest roughly the "same" density of such primes as ordinary primes? Formally, since $n^2+1$ is only divisible by Pythagorean primes, each prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ removes 2 residue classes while primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ remove none, yielding $|S(N)| = O(N/\log N)$ for $S(N) = \{n \leq N : n^2+1 \text{ prime}\}$ and likely $\Theta(N/\log N)$ as Bateman–Horn would imply — why does this "halfway" sieving structure not bring us closer to infinitude?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 1, 1 answers). See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/366506/halfway-approach-to-landaus-4th-problem-special-case-of-bateman-horn.
solved_when: A resolution of why the conjecture resists current methods, or ideally a proof that $n^2+1$ is prime for infinitely many $n$, consistent with the expected asymptotic $|S(N)| = \Theta(N/\log N)$.
why: It isolates the obstruction separating accessible sieve upper bounds from the infinitude statement in a canonical special case of Bateman–Horn, illuminating what parity-type barriers block such problems generally.

title: An inequality of real continuous function with f'>0 and f''>0
open: Is it true that for a real function $f$ with $f'>0$ and $f''>0$ on $[m,M]$, the gap between the average of $f$ over any points $x_i \in [m,M]$ and $f$ at their average is bounded by the analogous midpoint gap $\frac{f(M)+f(m)}{2}-f(\frac{M+m}{2})$, with equality only when all $x_i$ coincide at the endpoints?
status: The conjecture was proposed on MathOverflow (question at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/245016/an-inequality-of-real-continuous-function-with-f0-and-f0), where it received 1 answer and a score of 0; it remains unresolved.
solved_when: The inequality $\frac{f(x_1)+\cdots+f(x_n)}{n}-f\!\left(\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}\right) \le \frac{f(M)+f(m)}{2}-f\!\left(\frac{M+m}{2}\right)$ is proved (or refuted by counterexample) for all $n$, all $x_i \in [m,M]$, and all real continuous $f$ with $f'>0$, $f''>0$ on $[m,M]$, together with the claimed equality case ($m=x_1=\cdots=x_n=M$).
why: It would give a sharp, endpoint-only bound on how much convexity-plus-monotonicity can amplify Jensen's gap, a basic quantity in Hermite–Hadamard-type inequalities; a counterexample would show monotone convexity alone is insufficient, clarifying what hypotheses such bounds require.

title: Rearrangement inequality for sum
open: Does the rearrangement inequality survive when the operation between the sequences is addition rather than multiplication? Formally, given finite ordered sequences $a_1 \le \cdots \le a_n$, $b_1 \le \cdots \le b_n$, …, $z_1 \le \cdots \le z_n$ (nonnegative in the multiplicative version; the additive variant is asked for real sequences) and permutations $b_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, b_{\sigma(n)}$ and $z_{\tau(1)}, \ldots, z_{\tau(n)}$, is it true that $a_1 b_{\sigma(1)} \cdots z_{\tau(1)} + \cdots + a_n b_{\sigma(n)} \cdots z_{\tau(n)} \le a_1 b_1 \cdots z_1 + \cdots + a_n b_n \cdots z_n$ with multiplication replaced by summation?
status: Community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answers): https://mathoverflow.net/questions/472263/rearrangement-inequality-for-sum. No further results are recorded.
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for the additive analogue: for ordered real sequences and arbitrary permutations of all but one sequence, either the sorted (identity-pairing) sum always dominates, or an explicit instance violating it is exhibited.
why: It tests how far the classical rearrangement phenomenon extends beyond products, and a clean answer would clarify which order-compatibility structures force extremal pairings in sums.

title: Has Pillai conjecture been proven
open: Has Pillai's conjecture been proven? That is, does every sufficiently large integer admit at most one representation as a difference of perfect powers, and is there a proof of this statement accepted by the number theory community?
status: The question is community-curated on MathOverflow (score 0, 1 answer) at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/354324/has-pillai-conjecture-been-proven; a preprint at https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00698687v9/document claims a proof, but the conjecture is still stated as open in standard references such as Stewart and Tall's *Algebraic Number Theory and Fermat's Last Theorem*, and nowhere is it recorded as proved.
solved_when: A rigorous, peer-accepted proof (or disproof) of Pillai's conjecture exists; in particular, clarification of whether the claimed proof in https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00698687v9/document holds up under scrutiny.
why: Pillai's conjecture is a long-tail Diophantine problem of high community interest that lies outside standard problem lists; settling it would resolve basic questions about how sparse the differences of perfect powers are.

title: Is the Conjecture of Representing Integers as Differences of Semiprimes and Primes Extendable to Pro
open: Fix two distinct positive integers $k \neq l$. Is every positive integer $n$ representable as a difference of two prime products, $n = \prod_{j=1}^l q_j - \prod_{i=1}^k p_i$, with all $p_i, q_j$ prime and $k, l$ fixed in advance? The spotlight case is $l = 2, k = 1$, i.e., whether every positive integer is the difference of a semiprime and a prime.
status: Posed as a community-curated question on MathOverflow (score 0, 0 answers); available at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/480101/is-the-conjecture-of-representing-integers-as-differences-of-semiprimes-and-prim. No answers or partial results are recorded.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for fixed distinct positive integers $k \neq l$, every positive integer $n$ admits such a representation; in particular, a resolution for the case $l = 2$, $k = 1$.
why: It extends classical prime-representation questions like Goldbach from sums of primes to differences involving semiprimes, probing how primes and semiprimes interrelate in additive representations of the integers.

title: A special case of Frankl's conjecture. A question about known results
open: In a union-closed family of subsets of $U=\{1,\dots,n\}$ that contains $U$, $\emptyset$, and all $(n-1)$-element subsets of $U$, must there be an element contained in at least half the sets of the family? In other words, is Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture settled for union-closed families $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq\mathcal{P}(U)$ with $\{U,\emptyset\}\cup\mathcal{P}_{n-1}(U)\subseteq\mathcal{F}'$?
status: The question was posted on MathOverflow (score 0) and has received no answers; the asker's own attempt at induction on $|U|$ failed. See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/403955/a-special-case-of-frankls-conjecture-a-question-about-known-results.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that every union-closed family $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq\mathcal{P}(U)$ satisfying $\{U,\emptyset\}\cup\mathcal{P}_{n-1}(U)\subseteq\mathcal{F}'$ contains an element belonging to at least $\frac{|\mathcal{F}'|}{2}$ of its sets.
why: This is a concrete, structured special case of Frankl's long-standing union-closed sets conjecture, and resolving it would clarify how much of the conjecture is forced already by containing the co-atoms $\mathcal{P}_{n-1}(U)$.
